SUBJECT:

Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program: Final Guidance, Implementation of
Sections 1191 – 1198 of the Social Security Act for Initial Price Applicability
Year 2028 and Manufacturer Effectuation of the Maximum Fair Price in 2026,
2027, and 2028

This memorandum provides interested parties with the final Medicare Drug Price Negotiation
Program (the “Negotiation Program”) guidance for initial price applicability year 2028 and
manufacturer effectuation of the maximum fair price (MFP) in 2026, 2027, and 2028. It includes
four sections:
A. An introduction.
B. A summary of changes and clarifications to the draft guidance released on May 12, 2025.
C. A summary of the public comments received in response to the draft guidance and the
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services’ (CMS’) responses.
D. Final guidance that establishes policies on the topics discussed for initial price
applicability year 2028 and manufacturer effectuation of the MFP in 2026, 2027 and
2028, and a table of contents.
CMS may supplement this guidance with further program instruction to explain how these
policies will be implemented for initial price applicability year 2028 and during 2026, 2027, and
2028.
A. Introduction
Sections 11001(c) and 11002(c) of the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (IRA) direct the Secretary
of the Department of Health and Human Services (hereinafter “the Secretary”) to implement the
Negotiation Program provisions in sections 11001 and 11002 of the IRA, including amendments
made by such sections, for 2026, 2027, and 2028 by program instruction or other forms of
program guidance. In accordance with the law, on May 12, 2025, CMS issued draft guidance for
implementation of the Negotiation Program for initial price applicability year 2028 and
manufacturer effectuation of the MFP in 2026, 2027, and 2028. CMS also voluntarily solicited

* Updated December 16, 2025 to correct a numerical error in footnote 93 on p. 172.

2
comments on the draft guidance. 1 The 45-day comment period for the draft guidance began May
12, 2025 and concluded June 26, 2025. CMS received 122 timely comment letters in response to
the draft guidance, representing a wide range of views from academic experts and thought
leaders, consumer and patient organizations, data vendors/software technology entities, health
plans, health care providers, health systems, individuals, pharmaceutical and biotechnology
manufacturers, pharmacies, pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs), trade associations, and
wholesalers.

CMS is making public copies of the timely comment letters that CMS received on the CMS IRA
website at https://www.cms.gov/priorities/medicare-prescription-drugaffordability/overview/medicare-drug-price-negotiation-program/guidance-and-policydocuments at the same time CMS publishes this final guidance. Comment letters from
individuals not representing organizations have the name, address, and contact information of the
individual removed for privacy purposes.
After consideration of the comments received, and recently enacted provisions in the “Working
Families Tax Cuts Act” (P. L. 119-21), CMS is making certain changes to the policies described
in the draft guidance in this final guidance for initial price applicability year 2028 and
manufacturer effectuation of the MFP in 2026, 2027, and 2028. 2 When required by law, CMS
will develop its policies for 2029 and all subsequent years of the Negotiation Program through
notice-and-comment rulemaking. The public will have an additional opportunity to submit
comments as part of that rulemaking process, and comments submitted in response to the draft
guidance for initial price applicability year 2028 may be considered as part of that rulemaking
process.

B. Summary of Changes and Clarifications in Final Medicare Drug Price Negotiation
Program Guidance 3
CMS appreciates the comments received from interested parties on the draft guidance for initial
price applicability year 2028 that was released on May 12, 2025. This section provides a
summary of the key changes and clarifications made to the draft guidance based on these
comments and other feedback. CMS provides responses to the significant comments received in
section C of this final guidance and has made corresponding changes and clarifications to the
policies described in the draft guidance for initial price applicability year 2028, as summarized
below.
2F

Section 30 – Identification of Selected Drugs for Initial Price Applicability Year 2028:
• Use of Medicare Advantage (MA) Data: In section 30 and throughout this final guidance,
CMS included the use of MA encounter data for Part B items and services in policies
regarding Part B claims. Examples include the calculation of Total Expenditures under
Part B (section 30 of this final guidance) and the determination of the 30-day equivalent
supply for a selected drug (section 60.2.1.1 of this final guidance).
• Fixed Combination Drugs: CMS is not making a change to the fixed combination drug
policy outlined in section 30.1 of this final guidance. However, CMS describes its intent
to address this program integrity risk and that it is continuing to consider the appropriate
policy to implement in rulemaking beginning initial price applicability year 2029.
• Treatment of Vaccines for Infectious Disease(s): CMS revised section 30.1 of this final
guidance to clarify that, for vaccines for infectious disease(s), it will identify a potential
qualifying single source drug as all dosage forms and strengths of the vaccine with the
same antigen component(s) and the same holder of the Biologics License Application
(BLA), inclusive of products that are marketed pursuant to different BLAs. CMS
specified that for each unique potential qualifying single source drug that CMS identifies
based on its antigen component(s), CMS will use the earliest date of licensure for any
BLA or supplemental BLA for that unique potential qualifying single source drug for
purposes of determining the time eligibility.
• Bona Fide Marketing Utilization Data Sources: CMS revised section 30.1 of this final
guidance to include review of average sales price (ASP) data for utilization as a
component of CMS’ determination of bona fide marketing.
• Orphan Drug Exclusion: CMS revised sections 30.1 and 30.1.1 of this final guidance in
accordance with amendments to the Orphan Drug Exclusion enacted in the Working
Families Tax Cuts Act.

CMS notes that sections 50, 80, 100, 110, and 120, are not included in the Summary of Changes because CMS did
not make significant clarifying edits or changes to these sections.

Identification of Negotiation-Eligible Drugs: CMS revised section 30.2 of this final
guidance to describe use of MA expenditures in the calculation of Total Expenditures
under Part B.
Request for a Biosimilar Delay—High Likelihood Determination: CMS revised section
30.3.1.3 of this final guidance to revise the requirements to demonstrate that patents
related to the negotiation-eligible drug that includes the reference product for the
biosimilar biological product (the “Biosimilar”) are unlikely to prevent the Biosimilar
from being marketed before the date specified under the statute, and to include examples
of “clear and convincing” evidence of a high likelihood of marketing of the Biosimilar by
the required deadline.

Section 40 – Requirements for Manufacturers of Selected Drugs:
• Clarification on a Primary Manufacturer’s Decision Not to Enter an Agreement: In
section 40.1, CMS clarified the process when a Primary Manufacturer elects to terminate
participation in the Manufacturer Discount Program and the Medicaid Drug Rebate
Program rather than execute a Negotiation Program Agreement.
• Added Drug Data Processing System (DDPS) Edits Related to MFP Eligibility Not
Resolved Within 90 Days: CMS clarified in section 40.4.2.1 of this final guidance the
potential notification from Primary Manufacturers to dispensing entities regarding claims
with DDPS edits related to MFP-eligibility when such edits are not resolved within 90
days of rejection.
• Justification Code Added to Table 5: In section 40.4.3.1 of this final guidance, CMS
added a Justification Code to Table 5 to address scenarios described in section 1193(d)(2)
of the Social Security Act (“the Act”). Primary Manufacturers should use this code when
transmitting the claim-level payment elements if a claim is determined to be 340B
eligible, and the MFP for that claim is lower than the 340B price of the drug.
• Claim Adjustments for Primary Manufacturers Utilizing the Medicare Transaction
Facilitator Payment Module (MTF PM): In section 40.4.3.2 of this final guidance, CMS
provided additional information for how Primary Manufacturers should respond to
adjustments to original claims.
• Transmission of MFP Refund Payments if a Dispensing Entity is Not Enrolled in the
MTF Data Module (MTF DM): CMS added language to section 40.4.3.3 of this final
guidance that outlines a process for which Primary Manufacturers that have elected to
make payments through the MTF PM may elect to pass through MFP refund payments to
dispensing entities that are not enrolled in the MTF DM.
• Claim-Level Payment Elements for MFP Refund Payments Made Outside of the MTF
PM: CMS revised the claim-level payment elements for MFP refund payments made
outside of the MTF PM in Table 6 in section 40.4.4.2 of this final guidance. These
changes include separating MFP refund transmission date and time into separate elements
and adding another MFP refund amount element to report the amount calculated as the
MFP refund.
• Data Elements that Alone Will Not Constitute Sufficient Evidence that a Claim was
340B-Eligible: CMS made a clarifying edit in sections 40.4.5 and 90.2 of this final
guidance to align the language describing certain information that alone generally will
not constitute sufficient evidence that a claim was 340B-eligible with the claim-level data
elements detailed in Table 2 of section 40.4.2.1 of this final guidance.

•

Clarification on Termination Procedures for 2026, 2027, and 2028: CMS clarified that if
CMS determines a Primary Manufacturer’s notice to terminate the Medicare Drug Price
Negotiation Program Agreement complies with the requirements in section 40.6 of this
final guidance, the Primary Manufacturer's request will constitute good cause for CMS to
terminate the Primary Manufacturer’s applicable agreement(s) under the Medicaid Drug
Rebate Program in accordance with section 1927(b)(4)(B)(i) of the Act and section VII(b)
of the Medicaid National Drug Rebate Agreement (NDRA).

Section 60 – Negotiation Process:
• Determination of the 30-Day Equivalent Supply for a Selected Drug: In section 60.2.1.1
of this final guidance, CMS revised the language to state that for each Part B claim, the
number of 30-day equivalent supplies will be equal to the “days between service” divided
by 30.
• Addition of Wholesale Acquisition Cost (WAC) as a Potential Starting Point: In section
60.3.2 of this final guidance, CMS added WAC for a therapeutic alternative covered
under Part D and/or payable under Part B as a possible option for determining the starting
point for development of the initial offer.
• Analysis of Selected Drugs with Therapeutic Alternatives: In sections 60.3.3.1 and
60.3.3.2 of this final guidance, CMS clarified that the analyses described are conducted
specifically on indications for the therapeutic alternative(s) of a selected drug.
• Collection of ASP Data to Inform Consideration of the Factor Listed at Section
1194(e)(1)(E) of the Act: CMS added a data collection requirement to section 60.3.4 of
this final guidance for Primary Manufacturers to submit updated ASP data for the last two
sales quarters in calendar year 2025 to ensure that CMS has the most recent ASP to
inform the consideration of the factor at section 1194(e)(1)(E) of the Act.
• Negotiation Meetings: In section 60.4.4 of this final guidance, CMS revised the timing of
the negotiation meeting period and the procedures for the meetings, including the
meeting materials and agenda, for initial price applicability year 2028.
• Additional Price Exchange Opportunities: In section 60.4.5 of this final guidance, CMS
revised the deadline by which CMS and Primary Manufacturers may exchange additional
written offers and counteroffers for the MFP within the CMS Health Plan Management
System (“the CMS HPMS”) during the negotiation process for initial price applicability
year 2028.
• Issuance of the Final Offer: In section 60.4.6 of this final guidance, CMS revised the
deadline by which CMS will provide the final offer to Primary Manufacturers for initial
price applicability year 2028.
• Removal of NDC-11 Package Price from the MFP File: In section 60.5 of this final
guidance, CMS explained why the NDC-11 package price will be removed from the MFP
file. CMS did not receive comments on removal of the NDC-11 package price from the
public pricing file.
• Application of the MFP to New National Drug Codes (NDCs), New Drug Applications
(NDAs) / BLAs, and to NDCs with Insufficient Prescription Drug Event (PDE), Fee-forService (FFS) Part B Claims, and MA Encounter Data for Items and Services, or WAC
Data in Calendar Year 2025: In section 60.5.1, CMS clarified the application of MFP for
new NDCs of selected drugs.

6
Section 70 – Removal from the Selected Drug List Before or During Negotiation, or After
an MFP is in Effect:
• Removal from the Selected Drug List Before or During Renegotiation, or After a
Renegotiated MFP is in Effect: CMS made revisions to clarify the application of section
70 of this final guidance to drugs that may be eligible for selection for renegotiation for
initial price applicability year 2028, and drugs that are selected for renegotiation for
initial price applicability year 2028 as discussed in section 130 of this final guidance.
Additionally, CMS made parallel edits from section 30 to include CMS’ review of ASP
for utilization as a component of CMS’ determination of bona fide marketing.
Section 90 – Manufacturer Compliance and Oversight:
• Monitoring of Access to the MFP in 2026, 2027, and 2028: In section 90.2 of this final
guidance, CMS provided further detail on the process CMS will use when determining
whether the MFP had been made available by Primary Manufacturers to specific
dispensing entities.
• Centralized Intake System for Complaints and Disputes: In section 90.2.2 of this final
guidance, CMS provided additional information on the initial threshold review, triage,
and outreach that CMS will complete when an issue is received via the centralized intake
system for complaints and disputes. CMS also clarified that the initiation of a dispute
does not affect the Primary Manufacturer’s obligation to make MFP available and
transmit the claim-level payment elements within the 14-day prompt MFP payment
window.
Section 130 – Renegotiation of a Maximum Fair Price for Initial Price Applicability Year
2028:
• Renegotiation Eligibility for Previously Negotiated Drugs with Part B Utilization: CMS
clarified in section 130.1 of this final guidance that Part B utilization may result in a
selected drug with an agreed-upon MFP becoming eligible for renegotiation and
ultimately selected for renegotiation if such utilization results in the selected drug
meeting the criteria described in section 130.1 and 130.2 of this final guidance and
pursuant to sections 1194(f)(2) and (f)(3) of the Act, respectively.
• Sources of Information Used to Determine a New Indication: In section 130.1.2 of this
final guidance, CMS clarified that CMS may use information from both public and CMSspecific sources to determine whether a new indication has been added to the selected
drug.
• Timing Consideration of New Indications for Renegotiation Eligibility: In section 130.1.3
of this final guidance, CMS added that new indications that emerge on or before the
submission date of the “Negotiation Program Drug Selection Information Collection
Request for Initial Price Applicability Year 2028” (CMS-10844, OMB 0938-1443)
(hereinafter the “Drug Selection ICR”) will be considered when reviewing a selected
drug for renegotiation eligibility for initial price applicability year 2028.
• Criteria for Determining Material Change: In section 130.1.4 of this final guidance, CMS
clarified that CMS will consider a change(s) to a section 1194(e) factor for a selected
drug to be material if the change(s) would reasonably be expected to meaningfully alter
CMS’ consideration of that factor within the context of renegotiation offers and
counteroffers, including the initial offer, as compared with its consideration of offers,

guidance.

Appendix A – Definitions for Purposes of Collecting Manufacturer-Specific Data:
• Definitions Related to Research & Development (R&D) Costs: CMS revised the
definitions related to R&D costs to remove duplication in the descriptions across the
defined terms of direct basic pre-clinical costs, post-Investigational New Drug
Application (IND) costs, other allowable costs, and costs of failed and abandoned
products related to the selected drug to ensure the permissible costs are sufficiently clear
and remove duplication in the descriptions that may cause unintended confusion. CMS
also incorporated technical revisions in the definition of “post-IND costs” for consistency
with revisions to definitions of R&D Costs and prior Federal financial support in the draft
guidance for initial price applicability year 2028 that expanded the collection of R&D
costs and prior Federal support to indications that have not been approved by the Food
and Drug Administration (FDA) and removed instructions for the time periods of the data
reported. CMS removed the word “indications” from the terms defined for consistency
with the revisions CMS included for the definitions of these terms in the draft guidance,
which expanded R&D costs to include costs for indications that have not been approved
by the FDA.
• Definitions Related to Market Data and Revenue and Sales Volume Data: CMS added
definitions for the terms of “ASP” and “ASP Unit”. Use of this data is discussed in
section 60.3.4 of this final guidance and CMS intends to include these in the 30-day
revisions to the Drug Price Negotiation for Initial Price Applicability Year 2028 under
Sections 11001 and 11002 of the Inflation Reduction Act Information Collection Request
(ICR) (CMS-10844, OMB 0938-1452) 4 (hereinafter the “Drug Price Negotiation ICR”).

C. Summary of Public Comments on the Draft Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program
Guidance and CMS’ Responses
General Comments Related to the Implementation of the Negotiation Program
Comment: Many commenters expressed concern that the draft guidance and the Negotiation
Program more broadly would increase uncertainty related to developing new treatments and
undermine market dynamics. Some commenters expressed concern that the draft guidance lacked
transparency; in particular, these commenters added that CMS is not following an Executive
Order to improve transparency of the Negotiation Program and minimize impacts on
innovation. 5 And several commenters further asserted that the draft guidance is inconsistent with
statute and thus unlawful under Loper Bright Enterprises et al. v. Raimondo 6—in particular, by
maintaining the definition of a qualifying single source drug. One commenter recommended
CMS reconsider the draft guidance for initial price applicability year 2028 and make sure to
meaningfully respond to submitted comments received for that draft guidance. One commenter
urged CMS to monitor the impacts of the Negotiation Program on innovation and drug
development, and another commenter encouraged CMS to monitor such impacts on the
development of personalized medicines for small patient subpopulations.
4F

5F

Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their feedback. The U.S. prescription drug market
is the largest in the world—with a track record of fostering innovation. However, patients in the
United States generally pay more for prescription drugs than anywhere else in the world. 7 CMS
believes the Negotiation Program will make prescription drugs more affordable for people with
Medicare and the Medicare program—without restricting innovation and new product research
and development. 8, 9 CMS also expects the Negotiation Program to encourage drug
manufacturers to create business models to stay competitive, fostering the development of new
treatments. Only drugs that have been approved by the FDA for at least 7 years and only
biologicals that have been licensed by the FDA for at least 11 years are eligible for selection as
part of the Negotiation Program, unless they are otherwise excluded in accordance with statute.
Additionally, in accordance with the Working Families Tax Cuts Act and as described in section
30.1.1 of this final guidance, CMS is implementing amendments to the Orphan Drug Exclusion
to expand the eligibility requirements for the Orphan Drug Exclusion and to measure the 7- and

11-year periods described above starting from when a drug or biological product does not or did
not meet the criteria for the Orphan Drug Exclusion. With the changes made by the IRA, CMS
believes prescription drugs will be more affordable, allowing more patients to purchase those
prescription drugs and adhere to their medications. As a result, prescription drug sales likely will
continue to grow and drug manufacturers will reap the rewards of more patients being able to
afford their medications. Finally, CMS believes the Negotiation Program will help improve drug
affordability for people with Medicare therefore improving access to innovative, life-saving
treatments for people who need them.
Additionally, CMS drafted the guidance and is implementing the Negotiation Program consistent
with the statute. CMS appreciates the comments received from interested parties on the draft
guidance for initial price applicability year 2028 released on May 12, 2025. CMS refers
commenters to section B, “Summary of Changes and Clarifications in Final Medicare Drug Price
Negotiation Program Guidance” for a summary of key changes and clarifications. CMS also read
and responded to all significant comments received timely on the initial guidance for initial price
applicability year 2026 and the draft guidance for initial price applicability year 2027 and MFP
effectuation for 2026 and 2027. Similar to CMS’ process in connection with the publication of
the revised guidance for initial price applicability year 2026 and final guidance for initial price
applicability year 2027 and MFP effectuation for 2026 and 2027, 10 CMS is making public copies
of all timely comments received for the draft guidance on the CMS IRA website at
https://www.cms.gov/priorities/medicare-prescription-drug-affordability/medicare-prescriptiondrug-affordability in conjunction with CMS’ publication of this final guidance. Additionally,
CMS notes that the agency has pursued implementation in accordance with the statutory
requirements of the Negotiation Program. Finally, CMS refers commenters to section C,
“Summary of Public Comments on the Draft Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program
Guidance and CMS’ Responses,” in this final guidance for initial price applicability year 2028
for a summary of comments and CMS’ responses.
9F

Comment: A couple of commenters recommended CMS generally minimize the impact the
Negotiation Program may have on patient access to prescription drugs. Another commenter
expressed concern about the inclusion of drugs payable under Part B into the Negotiation
Program for initial price applicability year 2028 and the Negotiation Program’s impact on
patients and providers. This commenter recommended that CMS keep payment amounts at a
level that incentivizes providers to stock and furnish drugs payable under Part B.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their input. CMS believes the Negotiation
Program will help improve drug affordability for people with Medicare, improving access to
innovative, life-saving treatments for people who need them. CMS agrees with the commenters
about the importance of ensuring meaningful access to selected drugs. Finally, the commenter’s
recommendation about payment amount is outside the scope of this guidance. CMS reminds
commenters that Primary Manufacturers are required to establish processes to ensure that Part B
providers have access to the MFP for the selected drug in accordance with section 1193(a) of the
Act.

Comment: A commenter stated that 45 days is an insufficient amount of time to provide
meaningful comments and engage substantively with CMS given the significant range of new
complexities in incorporating drugs payable under Part B into the Negotiation Program. The
commenter added that CMS should provide more meaningful opportunities to comment on issues
specific to initial price applicability year 2028.
Response: CMS thanks this commenter for their concern and notes that the amount of time
provided many interested parties sufficient time to submit thorough and extensive comments.
CMS encourages interested parties to direct further feedback, queries, or meeting requests to the
IRA mailbox (IRARebateandNegotiation@cms.hhs.gov). CMS intends to address MFP
effectuation for Part B in the future, which will provide an additional opportunity for public
input.
Comment: A couple of commenters provided input regarding updates in this final guidance and
the impact on initial price applicability year 2026. One commenter urged CMS to clearly denote
that any significant changes made between the draft and final versions of the guidance are not in
effect for initial price applicability year 2026. Another commenter requested that CMS not make
changes to manufacturer responsibilities providing access to the MFP for 2026 to ensure that
compliance with these requirements is feasible.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their input. Policy changes in this final guidance
are generally limited to initial price applicability year 2028, except for sections pertaining to
manufacturer effectuation of the MFP in 2026, 2027, and 2028 and the formulary successor
regulations that apply to 2027 and 2028. CMS has indicated in the applicable section titles and
throughout the final guidance when policies apply to 2026, 2027, and 2028. For example, in
section 90.2 of this final guidance, CMS describes the following with respect to MFP
effectuation policies for 2026, 2027, and 2028: “The MFP effectuation policies established for
2026 and 2027 in final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027 and manufacturer
effectuation of the MFP in 2026 and 2027 are final policies that remain in effect for 2026 and
2027. In this final guidance, CMS makes updates and includes supplemental information
regarding these policies for 2026 and 2027 and is extending these same policies to 2028 for
drugs covered under Part D. For ease of reference, CMS is restating the MFP effectuation
sections from the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027 and manufacturer
effectuation of the MFP in 2026 and 2027 in this final guidance so that the changes and updates
to those policies can more easily be read in context with the policies in the prior final guidance
that CMS is modifying or supplementing. In this section, CMS adds clarifying language
regarding the agency’s process for determining whether MFP was made available and
information that may be considered during case-specific monitoring and investigation activities.”
Identification of Qualifying Single Source Drugs for Initial Price Applicability Year 2028
(Section 30.1)
Comment: CMS received many comments on its reading of the statute to aggregate all dosage
forms and strengths of a drug with the same active moiety and the same holder of a NDA or of a
biological product with the same active ingredient and the same holder of a BLA, for the
purposes of identifying potential qualifying single source drugs. Many commenters disagreed

11
with CMS’ definition of a qualifying single source drug and asserted that CMS guidance
contradicts the statute and stated that they do not believe that CMS has the statutory authority to
aggregate qualifying single source drugs across multiple NDAs / BLAs. Many of these
commenters claimed that the statute defines a qualifying single source drug in reference to a
distinct NDA or BLA, and a few of these commenters stated that it would be reasonable and
appropriate that such a definition would align with the FDA’s approval and licensure processes
under section 505(c) of the Federal Food Drug and Cosmetic Act (“FD&C Act”) or section
351(a) of Public Health Service Act (“PHS Act”). One commenter claimed that the statute
defines a qualifying single source drug by reference to the definition of a “covered Part D drug”
at section 1860D-2(e) of the Act, which in turn cross-references the definition of a “covered
outpatient drug” at section 1927(k)(2) of the Act. The commenter asserted that, under section
1927(k)(2) of the Act, whether a single source drug is a distinct “covered outpatient drug” is
based on whether the product is approved pursuant to a distinct NDA or BLA, and the only
exception to this rule is for line extensions. 11
10F

Some other commenters expressed appreciation for CMS’ consistent approach to the qualifying
single source drug definition. These commenters believed that CMS’ approach aligns with
statute, and they supported the current definition. One of these commenters stated that the statute
does not require CMS to adhere to the FDA’s licensure categories when identifying qualifying
single source drugs. A few commenters stated that this policy is critical in preventing
manufacturers from gaming the drug selection process and finding inappropriate ways to exclude
drug products from the Negotiation Program that might otherwise be eligible and underscored
that it is consistent with section 1192(d)(3)(B) of the Act. These commenters specified that this
policy will reduce incentives for “product hopping,” wherein a manufacturer would obtain a new
NDA or BLA based solely on modifications that are modest or minor—and which often do not
result in increased efficacy or improved outcomes—in order to effectively reset the 7- or 11-year
periods that must pass before a product is eligible as a qualifying single source drug.
Response: Consistent with CMS’ response on pages 12 and 13 of the final guidance for initial
price applicability year 2027, section 1192(d)(3)(B) of the Act directs CMS to “use data that is
aggregated across dosage forms and strengths of the drug, including new formulations of the
drug, such as an extended release formulation, and not based on the specific formulation or
package size or package type of the drug” for purposes of determining whether a qualifying
single source drug is a negotiation-eligible drug. Similarly, section 1196(a)(2) of the Act directs
CMS to establish procedures “to compute and apply the maximum fair price across different
strengths and dosage forms of a selected drug and not based on the specific formulation or
package size or package type of such drug.” In addition, section 1194(e)(1)(D) of the Act
instructs CMS, for purposes of the negotiation process discussed in further detail in section 60 of
this final guidance, to consider, among other information, “applications and approvals under
section 505(c) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act or section 351(a) of the Public
Health Service Act,” in the plural, for the “drug,” in the singular. The aggregation rules under
sections 1192(d)(3)(B), 1194(e)(1)(D), and 1196(a)(2) of the Act are clear and are designed to
Section 1927(c)(2)(C) of the Act defines a “line extension” as “with respect to a drug, a new formulation of the
drug, such as an extended release formulation, but does not include an abuse-deterrent formulation of the drug (as
determined by the Secretary), regardless of whether such abuse-deterrent formulation is an extended release
formulation.”
11

12
ensure that the Negotiation Program delivers benefits to the Medicare program and its
beneficiaries as intended by the law. Because different dosage forms and strengths, as well as
different formulations, containing the same active moiety / active ingredient may be approved or
licensed under multiple NDAs or BLAs, the suggestion from commenters to define a qualifying
single source drug in reference to a distinct NDA or BLA is inconsistent with sections
1192(d)(3)(B) and 1196(a)(2) of the Act. Contrary to the views of some commenters, such
section 1192(d)(3)(B) of the Act refers to the aggregation of data “across dosage forms and
strengths of the drug, including new formulations of the drug,” thereby necessarily establishing
that the statutory negotiation procedures apply more broadly than to a distinct NDA or BLA.
Unlike the views offered by some commenters, CMS’ understanding of the statutory language
gives full effect to all relevant provisions of the statute, including sections 1192(d)(3)(B),
1192(e), 1194(e)(1)(D), and 1196(a)(2) of the Act; CMS is applying an interpretation of the
statute that follows the statutory criteria for the identification of a qualifying single source drug
under section 1192(e) of the Act and, consistent with sections 1192(d)(3)(B), 1194(e)(1)(D), and
1196(a)(2) of the Act, gives effect to the statutory policy that a drug that may be selected for
negotiation includes multiple dosage forms and strengths and formulations of that drug.
CMS agrees with commenters that complying with the statutory requirement to identify a
qualifying single source drug using data that is aggregated across different dosage forms and
strengths, as described in this final guidance, will decrease incentives for pharmaceutical
manufacturers to engage in “product hopping.” This statutory requirement ensures that products
by the same sponsor with the same active moiety / active ingredient are subject to the same
processes under the Negotiation Program, and that a manufacturer is therefore limited in its
ability to inappropriately exclude from the Negotiation Program drug products that might
otherwise be eligible based on modest or minor modifications. Reducing “product hopping” is
consistent with the purpose of the statute, which is to ensure that the Negotiation Program
delivers benefits to the Medicare program and its beneficiaries. For the above reasons, in this
final guidance, CMS maintains the approach described in the draft guidance for initial price
applicability year 2028 for identifying potential qualifying single source drugs.
Comment: A few commenters recommended that certain drugs be automatically excluded from
the Negotiation Program. A couple of those commenters stated that CMS should immediately
exclude, or as one commenter stated, make a “carve-out” exemption, for all medications used for
the treatment of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)/acquired immunodeficiency syndrome
(AIDS) in the U.S. in order to prevent harm to both persons living with HIV/AIDS and the

should not consider Drugs Covered as Additional Preventive Services (DCAPS) to be qualifying
single source drugs for which payment is made under Part B since DCAPS are not payable under

preventive service under section 1861(ddd)(1) of the Act for the first time. 12 The current set of

of the Act.

Comment: A few commenters stated that influenza vaccines should be excluded from the
Negotiation Program with a couple of commenters stating that the time intensity and complexity
of the influenza vaccine production process contributes to fragility in the influenza vaccine
market, such as a limited number of manufacturers producing these vaccines. A couple of
commenters stated that influenza vaccines are not qualifying single source drugs eligible for
negotiation because commenters state that the active ingredient(s) are the strain antigens, which
vary annually as the strain changes every influenza season. These same commenters stated that
multivalent influenza vaccines are comprised of a combination of different active ingredients and
should therefore be considered fixed combination drugs and be deemed a new qualifying single
source drug. Additionally, these commenters stated that because each new unique active
ingredient(s) requires a new FDA approval and constitutes a new qualifying single source drug,
the influenza vaccine would never be on the market for 11 years and therefore never meet the
timing requirements in accordance with 1192(e)(1)(B)(ii) of the Act.
Response: Nothing in the statute indicates that CMS should categorically exclude vaccines or
products with complex and time intensive production processes from being potential qualifying
single source drugs nor from the Negotiation Program more broadly. In fact, section
1194(c)(3)(A) of the Act makes clear that vaccines are not categorically excluded from the
Negotiation Program. Section 1194(c)(3)(A) of the Act specifies the same applicable percent, for
purposes of calculating the ceiling under section 1194(c)(1)(C) of the Act, for vaccines as it does
short-monopoly drugs. By expressly specifying the same applicable percent for establishing a
ceiling for the MFP of vaccines as it does for short-monopoly drugs, the statute contemplates the
selection of vaccines under the Negotiation Program.
As stated in section 30.1 of this final guidance, in accordance with section 1192(e)(1) of the Act,
CMS will identify a potential qualifying single source drug as all dosage forms and strengths
with the same active moiety or active ingredient and the same holder of an NDA or BLA,
inclusive of products that are marketed pursuant to different NDAs or BLAs. CMS will identify
the active moiety or active ingredient of the drug using public sources such as RxNorm,
OpenFDA, FDALabel, DailyMed, and FDA’s Active Ingredient-Active Moiety
Relationship/Basis of Strength file. CMS may also consult with FDA as appropriate to, for
example, clarify whether a suffix or prefix in an ingredient name represents a genuine difference
in active ingredient. CMS clarifies that in the context of vaccines for infectious disease(s), CMS
will identify a potential qualifying single source drug on the basis of such vaccines’ antigen
component(s) as reflected on such vaccines’ labeling, as accessed in public sources.

qualifying single source drug that is a biological product with more than one FDA application

strengths, formulations or routes of administration from other products that are aggregated as

into the same potential qualifying single source drug for both drugs payable under Part B and/or

For initial price applicability year 2028, CMS will maintain its approach to fixed combination

qualifying single source drugs. A product containing only one (but not all) of the active moieties

the formulations of the fixed combination drug and will be considered a separate potential
qualifying single source drug. Section 30.1 of this final guidance details how CMS intends to
treat fixed combination drugs and gives an example to illustrate the application.

offered by the same NDA / BLA holder will be considered as one potential qualifying single
source drug. As noted above, CMS intends to address fixed combination drugs in rulemaking
beginning in initial price applicability year 2029 and may address co-packaged drugs at that
time.

Bona Fide Marketing (Sections 30.1, 60.7, 70, and 90.4)
Comment: One commenter requested CMS publish the names, or the number, of drugs not
selected for negotiation due to a determination by CMS of bona fide marketing.
Response: CMS thanks the commenter for the suggestion. Consistent with prior initial price
applicability years, CMS will not publish for initial price applicability year 2028 the names of
the qualifying single source drugs removed due to a determination of bona fide marketing in
accordance with section 30.1 of this final guidance. This approach is consistent with the policy
for exclusions from drug selection in sections 30.1.1 through 30.1.3 of this final guidance and a
request for a biosimilar delay in section 30.3.1 of this final guidance.
Comment: Many commenters stated that CMS lacks statutory authority to review “bona fide
marketing” to implement the statutory requirement of determining if a generic or biosimilar is
“approved and marketed” or “licensed and marketed” under sections 1192(c) and (e) of the Act.
These commenters stated that “marketing” is already a term defined in the pharmaceutical
industry, including by FDA and CMS. In addition, these commenters stated that any review of
“marketing” for purposes of drug selection under section 1192(e) of the Act or deselection under
section 1192(c) of the Act must be based on the first “market date.” One commenter stated that
the statute does not address generic drug or biosimilar distribution agreements as relevant to
whether a generic or biosimilar is being marketed as the statute does in other contexts (e.g., a
request for a biosimilar delay). One commenter stated that the Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
would regulate any areas of marketing concern. A few commenters raised concerns about the
impact of a bona fide marketing determination on the biosimilar (including a request for a
biosimilar delay) and generics markets. Additionally, some commenters suggested that CMS
lacks statutory authority to monitor marketing after a drug/biological is determined ineligible for
selection or removed from the selected drug list. A few commenters expressed support for the
approach, including the ongoing monitoring of selected drugs removed from selection.
Response: Consistent with CMS’ response on page 20 of the final guidance for initial price
applicability year 2027, section 1192 of the Act requires CMS to make a determination whether a
generic drug or biosimilar “is marketed” in order to determine whether a listed drug / reference
product should be selected as a qualifying single source drug or whether a selected drug should
be deselected. The statute uses different terminology in section 1192 of the Act than in section
1860D-14B of the Act, which established the new Medicare Part D Drug Inflation Rebate
Program. In the latter provision, the statute referred to the date that a drug is “first marketed.”
The absence of similar terminology in section 1192 of the Act demonstrates that, for purposes of
the Negotiation Program, a generic drug or biosimilar would have a continuing presence on the
market in order to affect the status of a listed drug/reference product. Consistent with the purpose
of the statute to lower prices for Medicare through negotiation or price competition, the statute
contemplates that, in making this determination, CMS would consider whether meaningful
competition exists on an ongoing basis between a listed drug or reference product and a generic
drug or biosimilar. This determination requires more than solely token or de minimis availability
of the products. For example, CMS is aware of situations in which a manufacturer of a brand
name drug or biologic has entered into a market-limiting agreement with a manufacturer of a
generic drug or biosimilar, where the generic drug or biosimilar manufacturer agrees to limit

20
production or distribution of the generic drug or biosimilar, such that only a nominal quantity of
product is allowed to enter the market. The result is a lack of meaningful price competition, and
in that circumstance the generic drug or biosimilar is not “marketed” within the meaning of that
term as it is used in the IRA. Given the Negotiation Program is targeted at single source drugs
and biologics that have been on the market for some time, for which no generic drug or
biosimilar competition currently exists, the statutory directive would not be met if a qualifying
single source drug were to avoid selection or be removed from the selected drug list where
generic drug or biosimilar availability is limited by the Primary Manufacturer. It is consistent
with the purpose of the statute to avoid selection or remove a qualifying single source drug from
the selected drug list only when there is evidence that the selected drug is subject to meaningful
competition. For example, section 1192(e)(2)(A) of the Act provides that an “authorized generic”
drug or biosimilar product “shall be treated as the same qualifying single source drug.” Although
an authorized generic may appear to be competing with the reference drug, authorized generics
are marketed by the brand name drug company or another company under the brand company’s
NDA, meaning that the relationship between the brand drug and its authorized generic is not
meaningful competition. Whether such competition exists between a listed drug or reference
product and a generic drug or biosimilar will depend on the totality of circumstances in existence
at the time that CMS performs its function of making the determination whether a generic or
biosimilar is being marketed. Accordingly, CMS maintains the approach in this guidance of
determining if the manufacturer of the generic/biosimilar is engaged in bona fide marketing of
the generic/biosimilar.
Comment: A few commenters raised concerns with using a “totality of the circumstances”
approach to review bona fide marketing as a vague standard that may vary by case, while a few
other commenters shared support for the bona fide marketing review. One commenter stated that
CMS’ previously stated concern that a manufacturer might “launch into the market a token or de
minimis amount of a generic drug or biosimilar for the selected drug and the manufacturer of that
selected drug could claim that the MFP should no longer apply” is not a scenario they are aware
of ever happening with a biosimilar and a reference product. Another commenter thanked CMS
for acknowledging that in the absence of a limiting agreement a product with “relatively low”
sales may be considered marketing, but the commenter requested that CMS consider “any” such
sales be considered marketed. Another commenter stated that CMS should not overly rely on
PDE data because the commenter states PDE data may not contain the entire universe of relevant
data for all drugs that might be a qualifying single source drug.
Response: CMS thanks commenters for sharing their specific observations of the market and
feedback on potential scenarios for review. Consistent with CMS’ responses on page 21 of the
final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027, CMS reiterates that the determination
whether a generic drug or biosimilar is being bona fide marketed on an ongoing basis is a
totality-of-the circumstances inquiry that will not necessarily turn on any one source of data,
including PDE data. Further, as stated with additional detail in CMS’ response immediately
above, it is consistent with the purpose of the statute to avoid selection or remove a qualifying
single source drug from the selected drug list only when there is evidence that the selected drug
is subject to meaningful competition and not just when there are “any” sales of the generic drug
or biosimilar as suggested by a commenter.

21
Comment: A couple of commenters shared their perspectives about the interplay of the
definition of a qualifying single source drug and bona fide marketing. Specifically, one
commenter suggested that CMS’ “broad” aggregation policy for a qualifying single source drug
paired with CMS’ determination of when bona fide marketing is met through PDE and Average
Manufacturer Price (AMP) data results in de facto agency discretion to determine the product’s
exclusivity period. Alternatively, another commenter suggested that a manufacturer might
manipulate the policies by focusing marketing on new formulations and permitting biosimilar
competition on the older formulation. The commenter suggested that CMS consider the
formulations without a generic drug or biosimilar when considering spending for selection and
after selection retain formulations that lack marketing.
Response: CMS thanks the commenters for their feedback. Regarding a commenter’s assertion
that CMS’ aggregation policy and its bona fide marketing determinations results in de facto
agency discretion to determine the product’s exclusivity period, we respectfully disagree. The
identification of qualifying single source drugs under the Negotiation Program is not a
determination of the regulatory exclusivity periods for drugs and biological products. With
respect to a commenter’s concern that competition on older formulations could result in a
qualifying single source drug avoiding selection or being removed from the list, CMS
acknowledges this, but for consistency, will continue to mirror the approach to aggregation
across dosage forms and strengths of a drug for selection pursuant to section 1192(d)(3)(B) of the
Act. CMS is finalizing the policy for bona fide marking for initial price applicability year 2028
as described in the draft guidance. As stated in section 30.1 of this final guidance, if any strength
or dosage form of a potential qualifying single source drug is the listed drug or reference
product, as applicable, for one or more generic or biosimilar products that CMS determines are
approved or licensed, as applicable, and marketed based on the process described in this final
guidance, the potential qualifying single source drug will not be considered a qualifying single
source drug for initial price applicability year 2028.
Comment: A couple of commenters thanked CMS for sharing examples of potential qualifying
single source drugs with at least one approved generic drug or licensed biosimilar with bona fide
marketing. These commenters also shared feedback on the examples provided. One commenter
raised concerns that the examples were “subjective” and do not provide sufficient predictability
to manufacturers of the bona fide marketing standard. One commenter disagreed with the third
example—according to this comment, this example would result in the wrong outcome where a
particular biosimilar has recently launched, e.g., at risk or based on a settlement without any
patent litigation proceedings as to its biosimilar (notwithstanding the existence of other patent
disputes as to biosimilars of the same reference product), but PDE, AMP, and ASP sales do not
yet reflect the launch.
Response: CMS thanks commenters for their feedback. The examples provided in section 30.1
of this final guidance are for illustrative purposes only to provide interested parties with some
instances of how certain factors might weigh in favor of, or against, a determination of bona fide
marketing. CMS endeavored to provide examples both for a drug payable under Part B and a
drug covered under Part D, along with including the availability of differing factors in the
scenarios. In response to the commenter’s feedback on the third example, as stated with
additional detail in CMS’ response above, in its review for bona fide marketing CMS considers

22
whether meaningful competition exists on an ongoing basis between a listed drug or reference
product and a generic drug or biosimilar and, therefore, a biosimilar with no utilization or one
that has yet to be launched due to pending patent litigation, would not be considered bona fide
marketed because there is no current distribution of the biosimilar and there are potential barriers
to its future distribution. However, CMS reiterates, as stated in section 30.1 of this final
guidance, that CMS’ ultimate determination of any particular drug will be based on the totality of
the circumstances and not on the presence, or absence, of any single factor.
Comment: A couple of commenters requested additional information from CMS about the
notification process to the public, Part D plan sponsors, and manufacturers when a selected drug
is removed from the list of selected drugs. One commenter asked if public notice beyond the
CMS website will be provided and another commenter suggested CMS provide public notice via
the CMS HPMS. Additionally, a few commenters raised concerns about the interplay of prompt
notice of deselection or removal of a selected drug and the impact on formulary coverage, for
example, including if and when removal by a Part D sponsor of a selected drug from a formulary
is permitted.
Response: CMS thanks commenters for their questions. Consistent with section 70 of this final
guidance, CMS will provide public notice by publishing the relevant information on the CMS
website when a selected drug is removed from a selected drug list before or during negotiation,
or after an MFP is in effect after CMS determines the statutory criteria in section 1192(c) of the
Act for generic or biosimilar competition are met for the selected drug. CMS will consider
alerting interested parties about this updated information using its regular channels for the
Negotiation Program, including the CMS HPMS for manufacturers and plans.
Responses to comments regarding Part D formulary inclusion of selected drugs, including the
formulary inclusion exception successor regulation for 2027 and 2028, are discussed in the
comment summaries and responses for sections 110 and 110.1 of this final guidance.
Comment: Some commenters suggested that if a generic drug or biosimilar is determined to be
bona fide marketed after the negotiation period ends but prior to the initial price applicability
year 2028, the MFP should never apply to this selected drug. One commenter provided text
revisions to section 70 of the draft guidance for initial price applicability year 2028 to remove a
selected drug when a generic drug or biosimilar is marketed after the end of the negotiation
period and before the MFP takes effect.
Response: Consistent with our responses on page 131 of the final guidance for initial price
applicability year 2027, section 1192(c) of the Act requires that each negotiation-eligible drug
included on the selected drug list with respect to an initial price applicability year shall be
referred to as a “selected drug” with respect to such year and each subsequent year beginning
before the first year that begins at least nine months after the date on which CMS determines the
statutory criteria in section 1192(c) of the Act are met, unless CMS makes such a determination
before or during the negotiation period. CMS interprets this requirement such that a drug
included on the selected drug list published for initial price applicability year 2028 will remain a
selected drug for initial price applicability year 2028 unless CMS determines on or before
November 1, 2026 (that is, on or before the end of the Negotiation Period for the initial price

23
applicability year 2028) that a generic drug or biosimilar product for the selected drug has been
approved for marketing by the FDA, and that bona fide marketing exists for the generic drug or
biosimilar product; if CMS so determines, the MFP would not apply for initial price applicability
year 2028 and the selected drug would cease to be a selected drug on January 1, 2029. If CMS
determines between November 2, 2026 through March 31, 2028, for a drug selected for initial
price applicability year 2028, that bona fide marketing exists for the generic drug or biosimilar,
the MFP would apply for initial price applicability year 2028 and the selected drug would cease
to be a selected drug on January 1, 2029. If CMS makes this determination between April 1,
2028 and March 31, 2029, then the selected drug will cease to be a selected drug on January 1,
2030, and the MFP will apply for 2028 and 2029. These circumstances are summarized in
section 70 in Table 9 of this final guidance.
Comment: One commenter requested, based on the commenter’s reading of section 1192(c)(1)
of the Act, confirmation that, for a selected drug from initial price applicability year 2027, if a
generic or biosimilar is approved and marketed by March 31, 2027, the MFP is no longer
applicable beginning January 1, 2028, and the selected drug should not be eligible for
renegotiation for initial price applicability year 2028.
Response: CMS confirms, consistent with the response on page 131 of the final guidance for
initial price applicability year 2027, that if CMS determines between November 2, 2025 through
March 31, 2027, for a drug selected for initial price applicability year 2027, that bona fide
marketing exists for the generic drug or biosimilar, the MFP would apply for initial price
applicability year 2027 and the selected drug would cease to be a selected drug on January 1,
2028. In other words, the selected drug remains a selected drug and MFP applies for initial price
applicability year 2027; the selected drug ceases to be a selected drug on January 1, 2028.
Additionally, CMS has revised section 70 of this final guidance to specify if CMS determines
bona fide marketing exists for a drug selected for initial price applicability years 2026 or 2027
prior to the publication of the selected drug list (which includes drugs selected for renegotiation
for initial price applicability year 2028), a drug selected for initial price applicability years 2026
or 2027 is not eligible for renegotiation as specified in section 1194(f)(5) of the Act. After the
publication of the selected drug list including drugs selected for renegotiation for initial price
applicability year 2028, the timeline for removal of the drug selected for renegotiation from the
selected drug list following generic drug or biosimilar approval and marketing, and the
application of the renegotiated MFP follows the same timeline as drugs selected for negotiation
for initial price applicability year 2028.
Further as included in revisions to section 70 of this revised guidance, regardless of when a drug
is removed from selection for renegotiation for initial price applicability year 2028, the
requirements for application of the originally negotiated MFP must be separately determined
based on the price applicability year that the drug was originally selected for negotiation. For
drugs selected for negotiation for initial price applicability year 2026, the MFP remains in effect
in accordance with the table provided on page 166 of the revised guidance for initial price
applicability year 2026. For drugs originally selected for negotiation or initial price applicability
year 2027, the MFP remains in effect as specified in Table 9 of this final guidance.

Comment Solicitation on Data Sources for Utilization Review
Comment: A few commenters responded to CMS’ solicitation for comment in section 30.1 of
the draft guidance for initial price applicability year 2028 regarding which, if any, additional data
sources may include timely utilization data for drugs payable under Part B and/or covered under
Part D. A couple of these commenters suggested that CMS use all available data sources (e.g.,
AMP, ASP, Medicaid State Drug Utilization Data (SDUD), and/or data from a nationally
representative and commercially available database). These commenters also suggested other
sources including: commercial claims providers; pharmaceutical distributor ordering platforms;
pharmacy dispensing records; IQVIA; the FDA Orange Book for safety, effectiveness, and
marketing status; and Part D claims. Additionally, one commenter suggested that manufacturers
should be permitted to submit additional data as needed to demonstrate that the generic or
biosimilar has entered the market.
Response: CMS thanks commenters for their suggestions related to additional data sources with
timely utilization data for drugs payable under Part B and/or covered under Part D. In
consideration of the comments received in response to CMS’ comment solicitation, CMS revised
section 30.1 of this final guidance to specify that CMS, in addition to PDE and AMP data for
utilization review, CMS will review ASP data available for the sales quarters of the fourth quarter
of 2024 through the third quarter of 2025 (e.g., the 12-month period beginning October 1, 2024
and ending September 30, 2025). CMS believes this additional source is necessary for drugs
payable under Part B. Additionally, CMS may consider additional data sources to review
utilization; however, data may not be available in these additional data sources for all drugs. As
available, CMS may consider SDUD and/or data from a nationally representative and
commercially available database. CMS may review these additional data sources for utilization
for drugs payable under Part B and/or covered under Part D for the most recent 12-month period
for the applicable data source, when available to CMS. The utilization review is in addition to the
review of the additional relevant factors under a holistic inquiry as specified in section 30.1 of
this final guidance (and additionally discussed for removal from the selected drug list in section
70 of this final guidance and monitoring for bona fide marketing in section 90.4 of this final
guidance). The revisions to the utilization data review for bona fide marketing specified in
section 30.1 of this final guidance are applicable to sections 60.7, 70, and 90.4, as specified in
these sections of final guidance. CMS will also continue to consider these suggestions in CMS’
policy development for this issue in future rulemaking.
Comment: A few commenters also noted specific concerns that the data, when it is pulled for
purposes of a CMS determination of bona fide marketing for drug selection or removal of a drug
from selection, may not include the full scope of evidence for bona fide marketing because of
delayed timing of initial uptake for biosimilars and generics. A few commenters also raised
concerns that marketing volume and related data are affected by uncontrollable market dynamics
and lagging system processes. Specifically, one of these commenters stated that lags in CMS’
Medicare Hospital Outpatient Prospective Payment System (OPPS) and OPPS addenda files are
not in a manufacturer’s control, which can lead to a disincentive to prescribe a product and in
turn impact the bona fide marketing. Another commenter mentioned delays in Part D formulary
listings. One other commenter stated that data sources may not reflect commercial availability in
particular for low-volume or specialty medicines.

25
Response: CMS thanks commenters for raising their concerns. As specified in section 70 of this
final guidance, a determination of bona fide marketing is based on a review of the totality of the
circumstances. Therefore, an uptick in the data alone is not determinative of bona fide marketing.
We direct commenters to the additional relevant factors specified in section 70 of this final
guidance, which include, for example, whether the generic drug or biosimilar is regularly and
consistently available for purchase through the pharmaceutical supply chain and whether any
licenses or other agreements between a Primary Manufacturer and a generic drug or biosimilar
manufacturer limit the availability or distribution of the generic drug or biosimilar, as articulated
further in section 90.4 of this final guidance.
Orphan Drug Exclusion from Qualifying Single Source Drugs (Section 30.1.1)
Comment: Many commenters asked CMS to specify that the 7- or 11-year periods that must
elapse prior to eligibility as a qualifying single source drug would begin on the date the Orphan
Drug Exclusion ceases to apply to a drug or biological product. That is, a drug or biological
product could not become a qualifying single source drug until 7 or 11 years had passed between
the date on which the drug or biological product, respectively, loses eligibility for the Orphan
Drug Exclusion and the selected drug publication date. Some commenters stated that, because
the term “qualifying single source drug” is defined to expressly exclude drugs that qualify for the
Orphan Drug Exclusion, the best interpretation of the statute is that the product is entirely
exempt from the qualifying single source drug definition and all its requirements. These
commenters also asserted that such interpretation would align with the intent of the Orphan Drug
Exclusion and mitigate the extent to which it may disincentivize rare disease drug development.
In contrast, another commenter acknowledged that CMS is statutorily required to measure the 7and 11-year periods starting from the date of the drug or biological product’s approval or
licensure date.
Some commenters raised concerns with the policy that, to be considered for the Orphan Drug
Exclusion, the drug or biological product must (1) be designated as a drug for only one rare
disease or condition under section 526 of the FD&C Act; and, (2) be approved by the FDA only
for one or more indications within such designated rare disease or condition. These commenters
raised concerns that narrowly exempting only single-indication orphan drugs from the definition
of a qualifying single source drug undermines incentives for post-approval research and threatens
innovation for rare disease treatments. A couple of commenters asserted that CMS should
interpret section 1192(e)(3)(A) of the Act such that drugs or biological products with multiple
orphan drug designations (for multiple rare diseases or conditions) that are approved only for
indications within the scope of a single rare disease or condition would qualify for the Orphan
Drug Exclusion. A couple of commenters acknowledged that CMS does not have the authority to
change the statutory requirement and expressed their support for legislation to amend the
statutory language. A few commenters expressed their general recommendation that CMS should
re-evaluate its interpretation of the Orphan Drug Exclusion to maximize incentives for the
development of orphan drugs. In contrast, one commenter wrote that exempting additional
orphan drugs with designations for multiple uses would further chip away at the list of drugs
eligible for negotiation, resulting in more high-cost drugs for Medicare enrollees.

26
Response: CMS appreciates these commenters sharing their perspectives. On July 4, 2025, the
Working Families Tax Cuts Act was signed into law. Section 71203(a)(2) of the Working
Families Tax Cuts Act amended section 1192(e)(1)(3)(A) of the Act to describe a drug that
qualifies for the Orphan Drug Exclusion as a drug that is designated as a drug for one or more
rare diseases or conditions under section 526 of the FD&C Act and for which the only approved
indication (or indications) is for one or more such rare diseases or conditions (as such term is
defined in section 526(a)(2) of the FD&C Act). Section 71203(a)(3) of the Working Families Tax
Cuts Act also added new section 1192(e)(4) of the Act, which describes the treatment of former
orphan drugs. In accordance with section 71203(b) of the Working Families Tax Cuts Act, the
amendments made in section 71203(a)(3) of the Working Families Tax Cuts Act shall apply with
respect to initial price applicability years (as defined in section 1191(b) of the Act) beginning on
or after January 1, 2028.
Accordingly, CMS is revising section 30.1.1 of this final guidance in accordance with these
amendments. To be considered for the Orphan Drug Exclusion for initial price applicability year
2028, the drug or biological product must: (1) be designated as a drug for one or more rare
diseases or conditions under section 526 of the FD&C Act; and (2) be approved by the FDA only
for one or more indications within such designated rare disease(s) or condition(s). Pursuant to
section 1192(e)(4) of the Act, if, as of the date of a drug or biological product’s earliest approval
or licensure identified under section 1192(e)(1)(A)(ii) or 1192(e)(1)(B)(ii) of the Act and
described in section 30.1 of this final guidance, such drug or biological product met or meets the
criteria for the Orphan Drug Exclusion, as described in section 1192(e)(3)(A) and section 30.1.1
of this final guidance, CMS will measure the 7- and 11-year periods described in sections
1192(e)(1)(A)(ii) and 1192(e)(1)(B)(ii) of the Act, respectively, starting from the first day after
such earliest date of approval or licensure that such drug or biological product does not, or did
not, meet the criteria for the Orphan Drug Exclusion. CMS will identify this day as the earlier of
(1) the date on which the FDA approves such drug or biological product for an indication for a
disease or condition that is not a rare disease or condition for which the drug or biological
product is designated under section 526 of the FD&C Act; or (2) the date on which an orphan
drug designation is withdrawn, if that withdrawal results in the drug or biological product no
longer qualifying for the Orphan Drug Exclusion. For orphan drug designations withdrawn on or
after August 12, 2013, the FDA Orphan Drug Product designation database includes the date of
such withdrawal. For orphan drug designations withdrawn prior to August 12, 2013, CMS will
use August 12, 2013 as the date on which the orphan drug designation is withdrawn for purposes
of identifying the first day after the drug or biological product’s approval or licensure that such
drug or biological product does not qualify for the Orphan Drug Exclusion. Because these
amendments to the Orphan Drug Exclusion apply with respect to initial price applicability years
beginning on or after January 1, 2028, nothing in this section 30.1.1 of final guidance modifies
CMS’ implementation of the Orphan Drug Exclusion with respect to initial price applicability
years 2026 and 2027, the status of selected drugs that were selected with respect to initial price
applicability years 2026 and 2027, or a Primary Manufacturer’s obligation to make any agreedupon MFP available with respect to such selected drugs, including in 2028.
Comment: A few commenters expressed concern that the FDA Orphan Drug Product
designation database and the FDA approvals database will not allow CMS to identify whether an
indication falls within an orphan drug designation, with a couple of these commenters stating

27
that CMS cannot rely on FDA’s databases because those databases principally track orphan
exclusivity rather than orphan drug designation. Commenters expressed appreciation that CMS
will consult with FDA as needed but recommended that CMS should also establish a pathway for
manufacturers and other interested parties to demonstrate that an indication falls within an
orphan drug designation.
Response: CMS appreciates these comments. CMS believes that consulting the FDA Orphan
Drug Product designation database, along with other publicly available databases and
documents, in addition to consultation with FDA, as needed, will allow CMS to successfully
implement the Orphan Drug Exclusion. The Orphan Drug Product designation database contains
drugs with an orphan drug designation. CMS reviews designations and approved indications to
determine whether the indication falls within a designation. Further, CMS will consult with FDA
if needed. CMS acknowledges commenters’ request to have the opportunity to submit supporting
documentation regarding orphan drug designations but believes that is unnecessary at this time.
Plasma-Derived Product Exclusion from Qualifying Single Source Drugs (Section 30.1.3)
Comment: One commenter stated that CMS should adhere to the statutory language describing
the plasma-derived product exclusion at section 1192(e)(3)(C) of the Act. They recommended
that CMS continue to look to multiple sources when determining if a potential qualifying single
source drug qualifies for the plasma-derived product exclusion, including the drug’s approved
label and FDA resources, such as the Approved Blood Products list. They also recommended
CMS use FDA’s Cellular and Gene Therapy Products website 19 to ensure that other plasmaderived products are appropriately captured in this exclusion.
18F

Response: CMS thanks this commenter for the comments and feedback. As stated in CMS’
response on page 23 of the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027, CMS
continues to believe that referring to product information available on the FDA Approved Blood
Products website, including the list of fractionated plasma products, 20 and databases such as
FDALabel 21 and the FDA Online Label Repository 22 are the best ways to identify plasmaderived products for the purpose of implementing the Plasma-Derived Product Exclusion in a
consistent manner. CMS confirms that cellular and gene therapies are not categorically ineligible
for the Plasma-Derived Product Exclusion described in section 1192(e)(3)(C) of the Act, which
applies the exclusion to biological products derived from human whole blood or plasma. As
described by FDA, cellular therapy products include cellular immunotherapies, cancer vaccines,
and other types of both autologous and allogeneic cells for certain therapeutic indications. As
further described by FDA, human gene therapy seeks to modify or manipulate the expression of
a gene or to alter the biological properties of living cells for therapeutic use. 23 Cellular and gene
therapies will be assessed for the Plasma-Derived Product Exclusion using the same criteria
applicable to other biological products.
