Identification of Negotiation-Eligible Drugs for Initial Price Applicability Year 2028
(Section 30.2)
Comment: One commenter recommended adding more drugs to the list of those eligible for
negotiation as currently only the high spending drugs are selected each year. This commenter
stated that there are very expensive drugs for patients that are not in the top 10, for initial price
applicability year 2026, or top 15, for initial price applicability year 2027, which were selected
for negotiation.
Response: CMS thanks this commenter for their feedback and suggestion. As stated in section
30.2 of this final guidance, in accordance with sections 1192(a) and 1192(d)(1) of the Act, a
negotiation-eligible drug for initial price applicability year 2028 is a qualifying single source
drug that is among the 50 qualifying single source drugs with the highest Total Expenditures
under Part D, or among the 50 qualifying single source drugs with the highest Total Expenditures
under Part B and as described in section 30.3 of this final guidance, in accordance with sections
1192(a) and 1192(b) of the Act, CMS will select 15 (or all, if such number is less than 15)
negotiation-eligible drugs for negotiation for initial price applicability year 2028.
Comment: A few commenters expressed concern with CMS’ use of total gross covered
prescription drug costs to identify and rank negotiation-eligible drugs to determine Total
Expenditures under Part D. These commenters all stated concerns that excluding price
concessions and other rebates from gross covered prescription drug costs will result in CMS
identifying and ranking negotiation-eligible drugs without regards to manufacturer rebates or
discounts that Part D plans currently secure on these same products. A couple of commenters
suggested CMS revert to the regulatory definition that was in effect when the Negotiation
Program was enacted defining “gross covered prescription drug costs” as a price net of rebates.
One of the other commenters suggested that using gross drug costs to determine Total
Expenditures under Part D and net drug costs to determine Total Expenditures under Part B
results in a bias towards and overweighting of drugs covered under Part D, which is exacerbated
by CMS including expenditures associated with beneficiaries enrolled in Medicare Advantage in
Total Expenditures under Part D but not in Total Expenditures under Part B. This commenter
recommended that CMS incorporate data on Medicare Advantage expenditures into the
calculation of Total Expenditures under Part B. Additionally, all of these commenters suggested
using net drug costs for Part B and Part D to determine Total Expenditures for drug selection as
that would result in a more accurate reflection of costs for drugs with high Medicare
expenditures. One additional commenter inquired if Total Expenditures under Part D include
amounts paid when Medicare is not the primary payer.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their feedback and suggestions. As stated in CMS’
response on page 23 of the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027, CMS first
notes that any suggestion that CMS amend the regulatory definition of “gross covered
prescription drug costs” at 42 C.F.R. § 423.308 is outside the scope of this final guidance. CMS
acknowledges the commenters’ concern about the impacts of excluding price concessions and
other rebates when identifying and ranking negotiation-eligible drugs. Consistent with the
approach discussed in CMS’ response on pages 23 and 24 of the final guidance for initial price

29
applicability year 2027, in identifying and ranking the negotiation-eligible drugs for initial price
applicability year 2028, CMS will use Total Expenditures under Part D, which are defined at
section 1191(c)(5) of the Act as “total gross covered prescription drug costs,” as defined in
section 1860D-15(b)(3) of the Act. Section 1860D–15(b)(3) of the Act defines “gross covered
prescription drug costs” in relevant part as “the costs incurred under the plan, not including
administrative costs, but including costs directly related to the dispensing of covered Part D
drugs during the year and costs relating to the deductible.” The term is also defined in the Part D
regulations at 42 C.F.R. § 423.308 as, in part, “those costs incurred under a Part D plan,
excluding administrative costs, but including dispensing fees, during the coverage year.” As
discussed in the Contract Year 2024 Final Rule (see 88 Fed. Reg. 22120, 22259-22263 (Apr. 12,
2023)), costs directly related to the dispensing of covered Part D drugs are most logically
calculated as the accumulated total of the negotiated prices that are used for purposes of
determining payment to the pharmacy or other dispensing entity for covered Part D drugs.
Consistent with this policy, CMS will calculate Total Expenditures under Part D for purposes of
the Negotiation Program using PDE data and will not consider any rebates or other price
concessions not reflected in the negotiated price of the drug on the PDE to identify and rank
negotiation-eligible drugs. CMS acknowledges the concern about the use of gross drug costs to
determine Total Expenditures under Part D and net drug costs to determine Total Expenditures
under Part B but reiterates that it is calculating such total expenditures in accordance with the
definition of “total expenditures” at section 1191(c)(5) of the Act. In response to the comment
raising concerns about the use of expenditures associated with beneficiaries enrolled in MA in
the calculation of Total Expenditures under Part D but not in the calculation of Total
Expenditures under Part B, CMS directs readers to the discussion below and in section 30.2 of
this final guidance. In response to the one commenter inquiring whether Total Expenditures
under Part D include amounts paid when Medicare is not the primary payer, the process of
identifying Part D high spend drugs described in section 1192(d)(1)(A) of the Act is discussed in
section 30.2, in which CMS will identify PDE data for each 11-digit National Drug Code (NDC11) of a qualifying single source drug for dates of service during the 12-month period beginning
November 1, 2024 and ending October 31, 2025 in which the data includes payments when
Medicare is not the primary payer. This PDE data includes PDE records in instances when CMS
is not the primary payer.
Comment: One commenter expressed support for the policy in the draft guidance for initial
price applicability year 2028 to exclude expenditures for a drug or biological product that is
bundled or packaged into the payment for another service when calculating Total Expenditures
under Part B. Another commenter asked that CMS consider how it might, within the existing
statutory framework, include bundled drugs that are billed separately (such as end-stage renal
disease drugs) in its calculation of Total Expenditures under Part B, as doing so could present
opportunities for significant program savings. Another commenter requested clarification on how
CMS will determine if a drug or biological product is bundled or packaged into the payment for
another service in order to exclude those expenditures, and if a line-level claim in the carrier feefor-service file has a Healthcare Common Procedure Coding System (HCPCS) code for a
specified drug, is it assumed that the payment associated with that line of the claim is not
bundled or packaged into the payment for another service.

30
Response: CMS appreciates these comments. As described in section 30.2 of this final guidance,
CMS will exclude expenditures for a drug or biological product that are bundled or packaged
into the payment for another service when calculating Total Expenditures under Part B, as
required by section 1191(c)(5) of the Act. CMS will only exclude expenditures for these billing
and payment codes when they are bundled or packaged; that is, CMS will not exclude any
expenditures for a drug that can be bundled or packaged into the payment for another service
when it is separately paid. CMS has identified rare instances where claims for separate payment
have been submitted for drugs payable under Part B when such claims are typically payable only
as part of a bundled payment. CMS will exclude such separately billed claims. CMS notes that
allowed charges in FFS Part B claims are zero for billing and payment codes when they are
bundled or packaged. Therefore, the expenditures associated with the claim line in such data for
a drug that is bundled or packaged would not be included in Total Expenditures under Part B.
CMS can identify such claims for billing and payment codes that are not bundled or packaged
into the payment for another service because they typically have allowed amounts greater than
zero and, in circumstances in which it is required, include an “AY” modifier.
Comment: Many commenters suggested that CMS should account for expenditures on drugs
payable under Part B and administered to MA enrollees when identifying Part B high spend
drugs. These commenters explained that, because over half of Medicare enrollees are enrolled in
MA plans, and overall use of prescription drugs is similar amongst fee-for-service and MA
enrollees, CMS would exclude roughly half of total spending on drugs payable under Medicare
Part B by only using Part B claims data. They expressed concern that the policy in draft guidance
to calculate Total Expenditures under Part B of Title XVIII of the Act using Part B claims data
would therefore skew the negotiation-eligible drug list toward drugs covered under Part D and
away from drugs payable under Part B.
A few of these commenters asserted that including spending on drugs provided to MA enrollees
is the best reading of the statute, arguing that the Act makes clear that Part B benefits received
through MA plans are benefits received “under” Part B, and that Congress intended to treat drugs
payable under Part B in the same way as drugs covered under Part D. A couple other commenters
argued that CMS should not include Medicare spending on drugs provided to both fee-forservice Medicare beneficiaries and MA enrollees in the calculation of Total Expenditures under
Part B because the better reading of the statute is that this spending is excluded. They asserted
that the statute permits CMS to consider only payments made “under Part B” and not payments
made under MA plans, which is Part C of the Medicare statute. One of these commenters also
viewed the exclusion in section 1191(c)(5) of the Act of expenditures for a drug or biological
product that are bundled or packaged to require that MA units are excluded from total
expenditures under Part B since CMS makes capitated payments to MA plans on a per member
per month basis.
A few commenters offered input on the data and methodology CMS could use to calculate MA
expenditures under Part B. A couple of commenters recommended that CMS use MA encounter
data to identify units of a drug at the NDC-11 level and then assign a dollar value to these
encounters by applying the fee-for-service methodology for payment, such as, for example, that
is described at section 1847A of the Act. One of these commenters acknowledged that MA
encounter data lags behind Part B claims data and recommended that CMS either use MA

31
encounter data from an earlier period or require submission of MA encounter data on a more
rapid basis. One commenter suggested that CMS could extrapolate the MA expenditure spend by
multiplying Medicare fee-for-service spending by the ratio of total Medicare enrollment over the
fee-for-service-only population. Another commenter did not recommend a specific methodology
but requested that CMS not require any new reporting requirements for MA plans.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their suggestions. In response to the commenters,
CMS agrees that MA expenditures for drugs payable under Part B and administered to MA
enrollees should be accounted for and included in Total Expenditures under Part B. CMS also
agrees that by leaving that data out, roughly half of total spending on drugs payable under Part B
would be left out because of the number of enrollees in MA plans. Therefore, CMS has updated
this final guidance to include MA encounter data for drugs payable under Part B (hereinafter
“MA encounter data for Part B items and services”) when calculating the Total Expenditures
under Part B of Title XVIII of the Act.
CMS agrees with the commenters stating that the statute supports including MA encounter data
for Part B items and services. Section 1192(d)(1)(B) of the Act defines a negotiation-eligible
drug as including a qualifying single source drug that is “among the 50 qualifying single source
drugs with the highest total expenditures under part B of title XVIII, as determined by the
Secretary.” Likewise, section 1192(b)(1)(A) of the Act states that “the Secretary shall rank
negotiation-eligible drugs described in subsection (d)(1) according to the total expenditures for
such drugs under Part B and D of title XVIII.” Total expenditures under Part B is best understood
as including MA expenditures for drugs payable under Part B, as section 1852(a)(1) of the Act
requires MA plans to provide to enrollees the “benefits under the original [M]edicare [FFS]
program option,” which includes, as relevant here, drugs payable under Part B. CMS notes
further that including MA expenditures for drugs payable under Part B is consistent with the
statutory directive in section 1191(c)(2)(B) of the Act that a “maximum fair price eligible
individual,” includes individuals “enrolled under part B of title XVIII, including [individuals]
enrolled in an MA plan under part C of such title, if payment may be made under part B for such
selected drug.” CMS therefore agrees with commenters stating that exclusion of MA
expenditures for drugs payable under Part B from the computation of Total Expenditures for
drugs payable under Part B would not capture the complete or most accurate Total Expenditures
for drugs payable under Part B.
However, CMS notes that MA encounter data for Part B items and services does not include the
actual amount paid by the MA plan sponsor. Due to this gap in MA encounter data for Part B
items and services, CMS agrees with commenters that CMS may best estimate MA expenditures
for drugs payable under Part B by establishing an approach that uses MA encounter data for Part
B items and services to identify the units of drugs payable under Part B that were administered
under MA and then determining what Medicare would have paid for such units under Medicare
Fee-for-Service (FFS). We describe our methodology for this approach in section 30 of this final
guidance.
Comment: One commenter asked whether Total Expenditures under Part B include amounts
paid when Medicare is not the primary payer. This commenter also asked whether Total

32
Expenditures for drugs payable under Part B includes beneficiary deductible payments in
addition to Medicare payment and beneficiary coinsurance.
Response: CMS will use FFS Part B data to calculate the total allowed charges (meaning the
amount that is inclusive of the beneficiary coinsurance and Medicare payment for the covered
Part B item and service) for purposes of determining Total Expenditures under Part B. FFS Part
B data includes claims for payments when Medicare is not the primary payer. For CMS’
approach to MA expenditures, we refer readers to the preceding response and the approach
described in section 30 of this final guidance.
Comment: One commenter asked whether PDE records with a value of “0=Not specified
(missing values are also possible)” will be excluded from the calculation of Total Expenditures
under Part D and asserted that such values make up roughly 15 percent of the records in the PDE
file for 2023.
Response: As CMS described in draft guidance for initial price applicability year 2028 and this
final guidance, CMS will only use PDE records with a compound code field equal to “1=Not a
Compound” when calculating Total Expenditures under Part D. CMS disagrees with the
commenter that PDE records with a value of “0=Not Specified” make up roughly 15 percent of
PDE records for 2023. CMS has found that, in recent years, the “0=Not Specified” field typically
accounts for less than 0.05 percent of PDE records, and the vast majority (more than 99 percent)
of PDE records are populated with “1=Not a Compound.”
Comment: A few commenters provided their views on whether and how CMS should combine
total expenditures under Part B and Part D when ranking negotiation-eligible drugs. A couple of
commenters stated that CMS’ proposal to combine such expenditures is inconsistent with the
statute and recommended that CMS instead rank negotiation-eligible drugs according to their
separate spending under Part B or Part D. Another commenter raised their concern about
incentives for manufacturers to develop products with split utilization across Medicare Part B
and Part D to evade selection for the Negotiation Program by keeping expenditures below the
threshold for inclusion on the Part B high spend drug list or Part D high spend drug list, even if
the drug’s combined total expenditures would be large enough to place it on the combined Part B
and Part D list. This commenter recommended that CMS develop a step in the drug selection
process where CMS sums utilization for the same product across Part B and Part D before the
calculation of total expenditures and the ranking of drugs across Part B and Part D.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for sharing their perspectives. CMS disagrees with the
commenters who stated that the policy to combine Total Expenditures under Part B and Part D
when ranking negotiation-eligible drugs is inconsistent with statute. Section 1192(b)(1)(A) of the
Act requires that CMS rank negotiation-eligible drugs according to the total expenditures for
such drugs under Part B and Part D. Such statutory language directs CMS to combine Total
Expenditures under Part B and Part D when ranking negotiation-eligible drugs. CMS
acknowledges the commenter’s concern that manufacturers may be incentivized to split
utilization across Medicare Part B and Part D. However, section 1192(b)(1)(A) of the Act directs
CMS to combine Total Expenditures under Part B and Part D when ranking negotiation-eligible

33
drugs. CMS therefore declines to combine Total Expenditures under Part B and Part D before
ranking negotiation-eligible drugs, as suggested by the commenter.
Small Biotech Exception (Section 30.2.1)
Comment: A few commenters asked CMS to establish a dispute resolution process in
implementing the Small Biotech Exception (SBE). A few commenters asked CMS to provide
flexibility and maintain communication with companies throughout the SBE submission process
to ensure complete and accurate data submissions.
Response: CMS declines at this time to create a dispute resolution process for the SBE.
Consistent with CMS’ response on page 24 of the final guidance for initial price applicability
year 2027, the statutory deadlines for the Negotiation Program do not provide enough time to
establish a dispute resolution process before the selected drug publication date. Additionally,
CMS believes that there is enough time during the submission window for manufacturers to
provide the relevant data to support their application for the exception and declines to use a
dispute resolution process for a manufacturer to supplement a submission. As stated in section
30.2.1 of this final guidance, CMS may request additional information from the Submitting
Manufacturer as necessary to make a determination with respect to an SBE request.
Comment: One commenter stated that if a drug has received an SBE and the manufacturer’s
circumstances have not changed in a material way, the manufacturer should not have to re-apply
for an SBE in subsequent years.
Response: Consistent with CMS’ response on page 25 of the final guidance for initial price
applicability year 2027, CMS’ determination that a given qualifying single source drug qualifies
for the SBE for a given initial price applicability year, including initial price applicability year
2027, does not mean that this drug will continue to qualify for the SBE for a future initial price
applicability year. CMS must provide separate information collection requests for each of these
initial price applicability years because of different statutory requirements across these years,
including the limitation for certain acquisitions for an SBE starting with initial price applicability
year 2027 and the inclusion of selected drugs payable under Part B starting in initial price
applicability year 2028.
Comment: One commenter stated that treating drugs payable under Part B and covered under
Part D as a single qualifying single source drug would have negative impacts on the SBE
because large manufacturers might qualify for the SBE for such a drug.
Response: CMS thanks this commenter for their feedback. As stated in section 30.1 of this final
guidance and further explained in CMS’ response above, and consistent with the aggregation
rules under sections 1192(d)(3)(B), 1194(e)(1)(D), and 1196(a)(2) of the Act, a potential
qualifying single source drug will include all dosage forms and strengths with the same active
moiety / active ingredient and the same holder of a NDA / BLA, inclusive of products that are
marketed pursuant to different NDA(s) / BLA(s). Therefore, in cases when different dosage
forms and strengths, as well as different formulations, containing the same active moiety / active
ingredient may be payable under Part B or covered under Part D, CMS will aggregate such

34
dosage forms and strengths or formulations under the same potential qualifying single source
drug.
Section 1192(d)(2)(A) of the Act states that a negotiation-eligible drug will not include a
qualifying single source drug that meets the criteria in either section 1192(d)(2)(a)(i) of the Act
or section 1192(d)(2)(a)(ii) of the Act. For initial price applicability year 2028, and as described
in more detail in section 30.2.1 of this final guidance, the term “negotiation-eligible drug” will
exclude any qualifying single source drug that meets either the criteria for a drug payable under
Part B or for a drug covered under Part D. CMS will make separate determinations with respect
to the Part B criteria pursuant to section 1192(d)(2)(A)(ii) of the Act (the “Part B Track”), and
the Part D criteria pursuant to section 1192(d)(2)(A)(i) of the Act (the “Part D Track”).
To be eligible for an SBE for the Part D Track, the Total Expenditures during 2021 under Part D
for the qualifying single source drug were: (1) equal to or less than one percent of the Total
Expenditures under Part D for all covered Part D drugs during 2021; and (2) equal to at least 80
percent of the Total Expenditures under Part D for all covered Part D drugs during 2021 for
which the Part D 2021 Manufacturer and its controlled group had a Coverage Gap Discount
Program (CGDP) Agreement in effect on December 31, 2021. To be eligible for an SBE for the
Part B Track, the Total Expenditures during 2021 under the Part B for the qualifying single
source drug were: (1) equal to or less than one percent of the Total Expenditures under Part B for
all qualifying single source drugs paid under Part B during 2021; and (2) equal to at least 80
percent of the Total Expenditures under Part B during 2021 for all qualifying single source drugs
of the Part B 2021 Manufacturer and its controlled group for which payment may be made under
Part B.
Selection of Drugs for Negotiation for Initial Price Applicability Year 2028 (Section 30.3)
Comment: A couple of commenters requested greater transparency into the process of selecting
drugs for negotiation. One of these commenters recommended that, well in advance of the
selected drug publication date, CMS should notify manufacturers of drugs that CMS intends to
select and provide each manufacturer an opportunity to dispute such intended selection. This
same commenter recommended that CMS provide the same notification and opportunity to
dispute to each manufacturer of at least the next five drugs that would be selected if one or more
of the drugs CMS intended to select were found ineligible for selection. This commenter also
recommended for CMS to make publicly available the Medicare expenditure data it is using in
its identification of negotiation-eligible drugs for the selection years, as the data in the Medicare
spending dashboards is the only data that is currently publicly available. They stated that their
understanding that this is not the source for CMS’ determination of negotiation-eligible drugs.
The other commenter also stated that manufacturers do not have access to the same data that
CMS has and suggested that CMS provide more detail on how expenditures are actually
aggregated and drugs are ranked, as well as reasons why high expenditure drugs are excluded.
Response: CMS thanks the commenters for sharing their perspectives. The statute requires that
CMS publish the selected drug list no later than February 1, 2026 for initial price applicability
year 2028. Similar to CMS’ response on pages 26 and 27 of the final guidance for initial price
applicability year 2027, CMS believes that disclosing to manufacturers whether their drug is a

35
selected drug before this date is operationally infeasible due to the time constraints required to
meet statutory deadlines and the complexity of the preparation that must be undertaken in
advance of the publication of the selected drug list by February 1, 2026. For example, section
1192(d)(1)(A) of the Act requires that CMS identify negotiation-eligible drugs for initial price
applicability year 2028 using Total Expenditure data during the most recent 12-month period for
which data are available prior to February 1, 2026. As discussed in section 30 of this final
guidance, Total Expenditures under Part D will be calculated using PDE data for dates of service
between November 1, 2024 and October 31, 2025. To allow a reasonable time for Part D plan
sponsors to submit PDE data, CMS will use PDE data for the dates of service during this 12month period that is available to CMS by December 1, 2025. The complexity of the data
analyses and quality checks that must then be performed on the data forecloses the possibility of
notifying manufacturers that their drug is a selected drug or providing a dispute process as
suggested by commenters prior to the publication of the selected drug list for initial price
applicability year 2028. CMS appreciates feedback received on the Medicare Spending
Dashboards. Similar to CMS’ response on page 26 and 27 of the final guidance for initial price
applicability year 2027, these dashboards allow for a longer claims runout to provide time for
claims to be submitted, processed, and finalized than is possible for the data that CMS is
statutorily required to use to identify and rank negotiation-eligible drugs. To provide
transparency and more timely data to interested parties, CMS plans to release quarterly Part B
and Part D drug spending datasets in the near future. 24
23F

CMS is taking additional steps to promote transparency in the Negotiation Program. As
described in section 30.4 of this final guidance, CMS will also publish a list of the up to 50 top
negotiation-eligible drugs (including the up to 15 selected drugs) ranked by combined Total
Expenditures under Part B and Part D, as described in section 30.3 of this final guidance, and
information on the NDC-9s, NDC-11s, and HCPCS codes for these negotiation-eligible drugs, as
applicable. Additionally, CMS will publish the list of drugs selected for renegotiation, if any, no
later than February 1, 2026, as described in section 130.2.2 of this final guidance.
Biosimilar Delay (Section 30.3.1)
Comment: A couple of commenters suggested that CMS provide greater transparency with the
requirements to delay the inclusion of a negotiation-eligible drug that includes the reference
product for biosimilar. Specifically, one commenter urged CMS to have more open
communication with manufacturers so that they can better understand the likelihood of drug
selection and appropriately anticipate the likelihood of biosimilar approval launch timelines for
the biosimilar of a selected drug. Additionally, a few commenters requested that CMS provide
advance notice of a reference product’s potential or actual selection, to the Primary Manufacturer
and/or the manufacturer of the biosimilar, including for example, providing advance notice to a
Primary Manufacturer of potential selection at least one quarter before publication of the selected
drug list. The commenters suggested that the pre-selection notification period would permit
manufacturers of the biosimilar to inquire if a particular Reference Drug is likely to be included
on the selected drug list and properly prepare any delay request or raise any concerns. One
See: https://www.cms.gov/blog/cms-drug-spending-dashboards-and-inflation-reduction-act,
https://data.cms.gov/tools/medicare-part-b-drug-spending-dashboard, and https://data.cms.gov/tools/medicare-partd-drug-spending-dashboard.
24

36
commenter suggested that CMS automatically delay selection of a reference product if a request
for a biosimilar delay is submitted in order to provide CMS adequate time to evaluate the
request. Finally, a couple of commenters requested that CMS provide the underlying data used
for the basis of qualifying single source drug and negotiation-eligible drug determinations. One
commenter also requested CMS publish a list of all reference products for the requests that were
submitted.
Response: CMS thanks the commenters for their suggestions. Consistent with CMS’ response to
similar comments on page 27 of the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027, this
final guidance describes the timing for the submission of a request for a biosimilar delay in
accordance with section 1192(f) of the Act (the “Biosimilar Delay”) and is based on a set
timeline in the statute and operational constraints related to the drug selection process. CMS
must make a full determination and may not immediately delay the selection of a Reference
Drug whilst making a complete determination of the requirements specified in section 1192(f) of
the Act to determine the outcome of a request to delay the inclusion of a Reference Drug by one
initial price applicability year (an “Initial Delay Request”). Further, the deadline for an Initial
Delay Request has been set as close to the selected drug publication date as is administratively
feasible. CMS adopted this timeline under the authority granted to it in section 1192(f)(1)(B)(ii)
of the Act to set the time, form, and manner of Biosimilar Delay requests, and has exercised this
authority to establish a timeline (which is described in sections 30.3.1 and 30.3.1.1 of the final
guidance) that allows CMS to carefully review the Initial Delay Request documentation and, if
applicable, to request follow-up information from the manufacturer of a biosimilar (the
“Biosimilar Manufacturer”) on its Initial Delay Request. The timeline ensures that CMS will
have adequate time to review follow-up data and make a well-informed determination. These
timing and operational constraints do not allow for any additional notice.
Finally, in response to commenters’ requests to publish data used to make determinations
regarding the Reference Drug and to publish the list of all Reference Drugs for submitted Initial
Delay Requests, CMS reiterates the response provided to similar comments on page 22 of the
revised guidance for initial price applicability year 2026. Specifically, the submission of an
Initial Delay Request does not guarantee that a Reference Drug would be a selected drug absent
the Initial Delay Request, nor does it guarantee that the Initial Delay Request will be granted
even if the Reference Drug would be a selected drug absent the Biosimilar Delay. CMS,
therefore, will not publish a list of Biosimilar Manufacturers submitting an Initial Delay Request
or CMS’ determinations. However, as described in section 30.3.1.1 of this final guidance, CMS
will notify each Biosimilar Manufacturer that submits an Initial Delay Request of CMS’
determination regarding such request on or after the date that the selected drug list for initial
price applicability year 2028 is published, but not later than February 28, 2026. CMS will also
notify each Primary Manufacturer of the reference Drug (the “Reference Manufacturer”) named
in a successful Initial Delay Request and will identify the Reference Drug that would have been a
selected drug, absent the successful Initial Delay Request. Further, CMS will publish the number
of Reference Drugs that would have been selected drugs for initial price applicability year 2028,
absent successful Initial Delay Requests, as part of publishing the selected drug list no later than
February 1, 2026.

37
Comment: A couple of commenters asked CMS to allow submissions of requests as close as
reasonably possible to the publication of selected drugs to ensure that decisions are informed by
the most recent developments. These commenters also suggested CMS accept supplemental and
late-breaking information that may impact CMS’ determination. One commenter supported the
use of the January 15, 2026 date for updating CMS on the status of the Biosimilar’s application
for licensure because of the importance of providing the most up-to-date information to CMS
prior to drug selection.
Response: CMS thanks commenters for this feedback. Consistent with the response to the
comments immediately above, the timing for submission of a request for a biosimilar delay is
based upon the statute and operational constraints related to the drug selection process. As noted
by one of the commenters, CMS already includes an additional date for updating CMS on the
status of the Biosimilar’s application for licensure in instances where updates since the
submission of the request for the biosimilar delay may satisfy the eligibility criteria.
Comment: A couple of commenters requested that CMS clarify what types of agreements are
considered to “incentivize” a Biosimilar Manufacturer to request a delay or otherwise disqualify
a Biosimilar from eligibility. One of these commenters also suggested that an agreement should
only disqualify a Biosimilar if the agreement explicitly requires the submission of an Initial
Delay Request by the Biosimilar Manufacturer from the manufacturer of the reference product.
One commenter supported CMS’ review of the requirements regarding agreements to address
what the commenter referred to as “pay for delay” arrangements between the manufacturers.
Response: CMS thanks the commenters for these questions. Consistent with CMS’ responses on
page 29 of the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027 and pages 21 and 25 of the
revised guidance for initial price applicability year 2026, CMS reiterates that section
1192(f)(2)(D)(iv) of the Act excludes certain Biosimilar Manufacturers from the Biosimilar
Delay if CMS determines that the Biosimilar Manufacturer is the same as the Reference
Manufacturer or that the Biosimilar Manufacturer has entered into any agreement with the
Reference Manufacturer that requires or incentivizes the Biosimilar Manufacturer to submit a
Biosimilar Delay, or that restricts the quantity (either directly or indirectly) of the Biosimilar that
may be sold in the United States over a specified period of time. CMS confirms that the
existence of an agreement alone between a Biosimilar Manufacturer and a Reference
Manufacturer does not disqualify the Biosimilar from being eligible for a delay. However, if
CMS determines that the agreement has the characteristics described in section 1192(f)(2)(D)(iv)
of the Act, then CMS cannot provide a Biosimilar Delay.
Comment: A couple of commenters requested that CMS create a dispute resolution process for
CMS’ determination that a Biosimilar does not qualify for the biosimilar delay.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their recommendations. CMS declines at this time
to create a dispute resolution process for the Biosimilar Delay. The statutory deadlines for the
Negotiation Program do not provide enough time to establish a dispute resolution process before
the selected drug publication date. Additionally, CMS believes that there is enough time during
the submission window for manufacturers to provide the relevant data to support their

38
application for the exception and declines to use a dispute resolution process for a manufacturer
to supplement a submission.
Comment: One commenter asked CMS to clarify if CMS intends the phrase “reference product
included in the Reference Drug” to mean the same as “presentation included in the Reference
Drug,” and, if so, the commenter requests CMS to revise the term in the guidance. This
commenter stated that use of “reference product” is inconsistent with FDA and industry
terminology. This commenter suggested the term CMS used in the draft guidance for initial price
applicability year 2028 appears to be intended to capture presentations (e.g., dosage form,
strength, route of administration) in the BLA, but, if CMS intends otherwise, the commenter
requests CMS clarify use of “reference product.”
Response: As specified in section 30.3.1.1 of this final guidance, and consistent with other uses
of “reference product” in the Act (e.g., section 1192(e)(1(B) regarding biosimilars that are
licensed and marketed), the reference product refers to a biological product that is included in the
negotiation-eligible drug as defined in section 30.1 of this final guidance and is the reference
product for a Biosimilar. CMS clarifies that the commenter’s characterization of “presentations”
is different than FDA’s use of the term “presentation”. CMS declines to revise the term(s) used in
this final guidance because “reference product,” as discussed in this response, is consistent with
the statutory term used to discuss the delay of selection for a biosimilar and other uses of the
term in the statute.
Comment: A couple of commenters asked CMS to clarify how CMS determines if the
Biosimilar is “operationally ready”.
Response: In section 30.3.1.3 of this final guidance and for purposes for an Initial Delay
Request, CMS specifies that, consistent with 1192(f)(1)(B)(ii) of the Act, CMS will assess if the
Biosimilar Manufacturer is operationally ready by reviewing the Biosimilar Manufacturer’s
progress against the actions, activities, and milestones that are typical of the normal course of
business leading up to the marketing of a drug as evidenced by both: (1) disclosures about capital
investment, revenue expectations, and actions consistent with the normal course of business for
marketing of a biosimilar biological product before February 1, 2028; and (2) a manufacturing
schedule that is consistent with the public-facing statements and demonstrates readiness to meet
revenue expectations. The Biosimilar Manufacturer should demonstrate this component of the
“clear and convincing evidence” requirement within the statutorily-required documentation
specified in sections 1192(f)(1)(B)(ii)(I)(bb) and (III) of the Act.
Further progress in operational readiness is also considered for purposes of an Additional Delay
Request, as discussed further in the response to the comment about “a significant amount of
progress” below and in section 30.3.1.4 of this final guidance.
Comment: A couple of commenters asked CMS to clarify what meets the requirements to be
“clear and convincing evidence” of a “significant amount of progress” to successfully determine
an Additional Delay Request. A couple of commenters shared feedback on specific evidence for
an Additional Delay request. One commenter suggested that the Biosimilar Manufacturer be
required to share evidence, only when new evidence was available, to reduce the Biosimilar

39
Manufacturer’s burden in submission of the request. Some specific examples suggested by
commenters as examples of clear and convincing evidence of a significant amount of progress
for an Additional Delay Request included: the first cycle of FDA review of the Biosimilar
remains ongoing and FDA has issued a complete response letter to the Biosimilar Manufacturer
denying the Biosimilar but the Biosimilar Manufacturer has resubmitted the BLA.
Response: As discussed in section 30.3.1 of this final guidance, CMS did not grant any Initial
Delay Requests for initial price applicability year 2027; therefore, Additional Delay Requests are
not relevant for initial price applicability year 2028. However, CMS is providing more
information about the Additional Delay Request process within this final guidance to respond to
previous comments requesting information about this topic and CMS will provide more
information in rulemaking applicable to future initial price applicability years.
Sections 1192(f)(1)(B)(ii)(I)(bb) and (III) of the Act specify the documentation CMS must rely
on to determine if the Biosimilar Manufacturer demonstrates that there is clear and convincing
evidence of a high likelihood that the Biosimilar will be marketed by the High Likelihood
Deadline. In section 30.3.1.3 of this final guidance, CMS specifies that to establish clear and
convincing evidence CMS will look for the Biosimilar Manufacturer to demonstrate, within this
documentation, both that: (1) patents related to the Reference Drug are unlikely to prevent the
Biosimilar from being marketed; and (2) the Biosimilar Manufacturer will be operationally ready
to market the Biosimilar.
As discussed in section 30.3.1.4 of this final guidance, CMS will use a holistic review of the
documentation submitted by the Biosimilar Manufacturer with the Additional Delay Request,
including the statutorily-required documentation specified in sections 1192(f)(1)(B)(ii)(I)(bb)
and (III) of the Act to demonstrate the clear and convincing evidence that the Biosimilar will be
marketed before the High Likelihood Deadline, and to determine whether a significant amount of
progress has been made by the Biosimilar Manufacturer towards licensure and marketing of the
Biosimilar since the successful Initial Delay Request submission for such Biosimilar.
Specifically, CMS is looking to see that the Biosimilar Manufacturer has made affirmative
progress towards being operationally ready to market the Biosimilar by the High Likelihood
Deadline. Therefore, it would not be sufficient for a Biosimilar Manufacturer to only provide
CMS with new information when available, as some commenters suggested, as CMS must
holistically review the required documentation to determine if there is clear and convincing
evidence of significant progress from CMS’ initial review. To conduct this new review, similar to
CMS’ initial review for a determination of an Initial Delay Request, CMS will consider the
actions, activities, and milestones that are typical of the normal course of business leading up to
the marketing of a drug as evidenced by both: (1) disclosures about capital investment, revenue
expectations, and actions consistent with the normal course of business for marketing of a
biosimilar biological product before February 1, 2028; and (2) a manufacturing schedule that is
consistent with the public-facing statements and demonstrates readiness to meet revenue
expectations. However, for an Additional Delay Request, CMS is also comparing such actions,
activities, and milestones in comparison to the Biosimilar Manufacturer’s affirmative progress,
holistically, since CMS reviewed such information for purposes of the successful Initial Delay
Request for the Biosimilar.

40
Comment: A few commenters requested that CMS clarify what patents would be considered
“related to the Reference Product.” Additionally, commenters asked CMS to clarify if a carvedout patent-protected indication is not applicable to the Biosimilar.
Response: CMS thanks commenters for questions. Under section 1192(f)(1)(A) of the Act, the
Reference Drug at issue for the Biosimilar Manufacturer’s request for a biosimilar delay must
include the reference product identified in the Biosimilar’s application for licensure under
section 351(k) of the PHS Act that has been approved by FDA or accepted for review.
Accordingly, a patent related to the reference product is a patent that would be related to the
reference product identified in the Biosimilar’s application for licensure under section 351(k) of
the PHS Act that has been approved by FDA or accepted for review. As specified in section
30.3.1.3 of this final guidance, for example, if a Biosimilar Manufacturer has obtained licensure
with biosimilar labeling that omits a patent-protected indication or other patent-protected
information, then such patents that cover the omitted indication or the omitted information would
not be considered to be “applicable to the Biosimilar.”
Comment Solicitations on Patent Documentation
Comment: Many commenters responded to CMS’ request for comments regarding additional or
alternative evidence that may demonstrate that patents related to the Reference Drug are unlikely
to prevent the Biosimilar from being marketed before the High Likelihood Deadline. These
commenters generally suggested that CMS should permit use of additional or alternative
evidence to demonstrate a high likelihood of marketing. Some of these commenters suggested
that CMS rely on documentation of industry-recognized milestones in a patent dispute to
demonstrate clear and convincing evidence of a high likelihood of marketing, for example, that
the court has issued neither preliminary injunction nor permanent injunction preventing launch
within the relevant time period. A couple of these commenters suggested CMS should consider
that issuance of the notice of first commercial marketing from the Biosimilar Manufacturer to the
Reference Product sponsor no later than 180 days before first marketing as evidence of a high
likelihood of marketing. Additionally, some of these commenters suggested that CMS had broad
authority to consider any evidence from the Biosimilar and/or Reference Product Manufacturer
under section 1192(f)(1)(B)(ii)(II) of the Act, and such evidence might include press statements,
investor meetings/reports, and corporate director statements.
Some commenters also provided responses to CMS’ request for comments on whether CMS
should consider public-facing statements in which the Biosimilar Manufacturer asserts that
ongoing patent disputes will be resolved within the relevant time period for the High Likelihood
Deadline. A couple of these suggested that because a Biosimilar Manufacturer or a Reference
Product Manufacturer must provide information in the statutorily-required documentation based
on fiduciary and legal requirements of the originating documentation, that CMS could
reasonably rely on a statement from a fiduciary representative that the Biosimilar would be
marketed by the High Likelihood Deadline. Commenters also suggested CMS consider as
evidence, for example, that a Biosimilar Manufacturer certifies that no valid patents will be
infringed once the Biosimilar is launched, an executive summary of a law firm’s assessment of
the asserted patents’ invalidity and non-infringement, and a Biosimilar’s market entry forecast by
an industry-leading analytics firm based on data-driven forecast of anticipated market entry
based on tracked litigation and mapping of the patent landscape.

Response: CMS thanks commenters for their feedback. CMS appreciates commenters’ concerns
that the current items a Biosimilar Manufacturer may use to demonstrate patent barriers are
unlikely to prevent the Biosimilar from being marketed before the High Likelihood Deadline in

biosimilar delay, for example, if the litigation on patents related to the Reference Product is
ongoing. In response to similar concerns raised by commenters in previous years, CMS reiterates
that CMS remains bound by the statutory constraints that the Biosimilar Manufacturer must
provide “clear and convincing evidence,” to be found in the documentation specified in sections
1192(f)(1)(B)(ii)(I)(bb) and (III) 25 of the Act that the Biosimilar has a high likelihood to be
marketed by the High Likelihood Deadline. Despite the potentially unpredictable nature of the
litigation process, CMS recognizes that representatives of a manufacturer have fiduciary
obligations as company representatives and legal disclosure requirements under the Securities

patent or patent(s) relating to the reference product included in the Reference Drug applicable to
the Biosimilar, and the Biosimilar Manufacturer specifies a launch date for the Biosimilar by a

Analysis (MD&A)” or another section, as appropriate, in a Form 10-K, and (3) information

illustrative but alone may not always constitute “clear and convincing evidence” of a high

Publication of the Selected Drug List (Section 30.4)
Comment: Some commenters were in favor of CMS publishing a list of the up to 50 top
negotiation-eligible drugs (including the up to 15 selected drugs) ranked by combined Total
Expenditures under Part B and Part D by February 1, 2026, for initial price applicability year
2028. The commenters all noted that this would provide transparency and allow manufacturers
and interested parties to better anticipate which drugs will be selected in future initial price
applicability years. One of the commenters recommended that CMS clearly state that the list is
for informational purposes only and potentially subject to change in future years in order to
avoid any confusion. One of the commenters suggested that CMS publish the list of negotiationeligible drugs, and potentially the list of selected drugs, sooner than the February 1 deadline
required by statute, as soon as December or January. This same commenter suggested that CMS
promote transparency by publishing information on the drugs ranked in the top 50 spend in its
published list for a given initial price applicability year, but were excluded on the basis of the
orphan drug exclusion or, at a minimum, by publishing the number of drugs that were excluded
under the orphan drug exclusion. One commenter was opposed to publication of the top 50
negotiation-eligible drugs ranked by combined Total Expenditures under Part B and Part D at all,
noting that publishing such a list is not required by statute. The commenter raised concerns that
this list could lead to plans proactively adjusting formulary placement of drugs that are likely to
be selected, and that generics and biosimilars for drugs that appear on the top 50 list will be less
likely to come to market.
Response: CMS thanks the commenters for their support and feedback. CMS agrees that
publishing the list of the up to 50 top negotiation-eligible drugs (including the up to 15 selected
drugs) ranked by combined Total Expenditures under Part B and Part D, as described in section
30.3 of this final guidance, and information on the NDC-9s, NDC-11s, and HCPCS codes for
these negotiation-eligible drugs, as applicable, will promote transparency into the drug selection
process. CMS affirms that, with the exception of the top 15 drugs on this list, which are the
selected drugs for initial price applicability year 2028, the list of up to 50 top negotiation-eligible
drugs will be published for informational purposes only. The conditions that determine which
drugs meet the statutory requirements for a drug to become a qualifying single source drug,
negotiation-eligible drug, or selected drug for a given initial price applicability are not static, and
this list is therefore not intended to predict or replicate the selected drug list for future initial
price applicability years. In response to the commenter who requested that CMS publish
information about drugs that would have been included in the negotiation-eligible drug list but
for the Orphan Drug Exclusion, CMS reminds the commenter that the Orphan Drug Exclusion is
an exclusion from the definition of a qualifying single source drug under section 1192(e) of the
Act. CMS therefore does not assess whether a potential qualifying single source drug that
qualifies for the Orphan Drug Exclusion would have become a negotiation-eligible drug absent
the Orphan Drug Exclusion.

44

In response to the commenter who suggested that CMS publish the list of negotiation-eligible
drugs, and potentially the list of selected drugs, sooner than the February 1 deadline, as discussed
in CMS’ response on page 26 of the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027, CMS
believes that committing to publishing the selected drug before this date is operationally
infeasible due to the time constraints required to meet statutory deadlines and the complexity of
the preparation that must be undertaken in advance of the publication of the selected drug list by
February 1. Similarly, CMS believes that committing to publishing the list of negotiation-eligible
drugs before this date is also operationally infeasible due to the same reasons.

about CMS’ policies on formulary inclusion and intent to monitor Medicare Part D plans’
compliance with all applicable formulary requirements and treatment of drugs. CMS believes
that publishing the list of the up to 50 top negotiation-eligible drugs (including the up to 15
selected drugs) ranked by combined Total Expenditures under Part B and Part D and information
on the NDC-9s, NDC-11s, and HCPCS codes for these negotiation-eligible drugs, as applicable,
provides important transparency under the Negotiation Program.
Requirements for Manufacturers of Selected Drugs (Section 40)
Comment: One commenter asked CMS to not hold Primary Manufacturers liable for any
violations of Secondary Manufacturers with respect to making the MFP accessible to eligible
entities and that CMS should sign separate agreements with Secondary Manufacturers.
Response: As discussed in CMS’ response on page 35-36 of the final guidance for initial price
applicability year 2027, given that section 1193(a)(1) of the Act instructs CMS to negotiate with
“the manufacturer” to arrive at the MFP for a given selected drug to which “the manufacturer”
would provide access in accordance with the statute, and given that the term “the manufacturer”
appears repeatedly throughout the statutory provisions establishing the Negotiation Program, the
best statutory interpretation is to interpret the term “manufacturer” as a single entity for the
negotiation process, responsible for negotiation of a single MFP for a given selected drug. Thus,
in accordance with section 1193(a)(1) of the Act and other statutory references to “the
manufacturer,” CMS will enter into an Agreement with “the manufacturer” of a selected drug,
where “the manufacturer” is the NDA / BLA holder as described in section 40 of this final
guidance. CMS has adopted the designations of “Primary Manufacturer” and “Secondary
Manufacturer,” respectively, to establish a process to negotiate the maximum fair price with “the
manufacturer” to align with the meaning of the statutory language and establish responsibilities
and requirements of the Primary Manufacturer related to data collection and submission and
MFP availability for the selected drug sold by the Secondary Manufacturer(s).
Confidentiality of Proprietary Information
Comment: A few commenters requested CMS share additional information regarding the
procedures used for protecting confidential information and proprietary information included in
the information submitted by Primary Manufacturers. A few commenters suggested CMS

45
develop and publish data privacy and security protection protocols and safeguards for storage
and access that include use by CMS staff only on a “need-to-know” basis. Another commenter
shared examples of other CMS programs, such as the Medicaid Drug Rebate Program (MDRP),
with systems that include multilayered privacy and security protections to safeguard sensitive
manufacturer data, including pricing information. One commenter noted that CMS does not
specify a data destruction schedule for the data submitted through the Negotiation Program.
Response: CMS thanks the commenters for their comments on safeguarding data submitted by
manufacturers. Consistent with CMS’ response starting on page 37 of the final guidance for
initial price applicability year 2027, CMS reaffirms its commitment to protect sensitive and
confidential data submitted by Primary Manufacturers and continues to acknowledge the
importance of data security. Upon establishment of the Negotiation Program, starting with
procedures and data related to initial price applicability year 2026, CMS implemented internal
controls to ensure the safeguarding of these data and to provide select CMS staff with access that
appropriately aligns with their role and duties. CMS includes below the information previously
provided in response to similar comments received for initial price applicability years 2026 and
2027 and CMS believes this information is both adequate to detail the protocols and safeguards
used in handling manufacturer-submitted data and, as discussed in further detail below, is
consistent with other CMS programs suggested by the commenters because of agency-wide CMS
requirements.
Over the course of the negotiation process, Primary Manufacturers will submit information to
CMS via the CMS HPMS or, in some instances, Box. 26 Box provides a secure way to share
content and improve collaboration both within CMS and with our partners. Box has been
authorized as a High Federal Information and Security Modernization Act (FISMA)
categorization, which means it can support the storage of all CMS data types, inclusive of
personally identifiable information (PII), protected health information (PHI), and agency
sensitive information. Inviting collaborators through named email addresses of authorized
individuals is the preferred method for this collaboration to ensure the confidentiality and
integrity of the content being shared.
25F

The CMS HPMS adheres to all applicable policies, procedures, controls, and standards required
by the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS)/CMS information security and privacy
programs to ensure the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of manufacturer information and
government information systems. The CMS HPMS system is the primary CMS system for
exchange of information between CMS and Medicare Advantage and Medicare Prescription
Drug Plans, and as such is designed to receive and keep confidential proprietary and
commercially sensitive information. As required by CMS, the CMS HPMS integrates security
into every aspect of the system development life cycle. The CMS HPMS is subject to the
agency’s Security Assessment and Authorization (SA&A) process, a rigorous methodology
during which the system must demonstrate a sound and comprehensive information security
posture. To achieve and maintain an Authority to Operate (ATO), the CMS HPMS routinely
undergoes system penetration testing as well as a Security Control Assessment (SCA), where
independent auditors perform a detailed assessment to ensure that the system’s security controls
If CMS specifies an alternative secure location to Box, CMS will provide updated instructions and information to
Primary Manufacturers.
26

46
meet the CMS Acceptable Risk Safeguards (ARS). An individual must apply for and obtain a
CMS-issued user account and password to access the CMS HPMS. In addition to the CMSissued user ID and password, internal CMS staff must use an HHS identification badge (referred
to as a “PIV card”) when accessing the website on the CMS network, while all users accessing
the system from outside of the CMS network must use multi-factor authentication. The CMS
HPMS further employs role-based access, ensuring that each user is granted access only to those
functions required by their position. The CMS HPMS is hosted at a CMS approved cloud service
provider. The system is protected by a suite of firewall and intrusion detection services, including
Akamai Content Delivery Network (CDN), which serves as an additional web application
firewall that offers robust distributed denial of services protection and access control. The CMS
HPMS utilizes a multizone architecture comprised of a presentation zone, an application zone,
and a data zone, designed to provide further defense against security attacks. CMS will employ
encryption at rest in the database for sensitive manufacturer data (e.g., proprietary information,
including trade secrets and confidential commercial or financial information) in addition to
encryption in transit. The CMS HPMS adheres to the CMS Information Security Incident
Handling Procedures, which are supplemented by the CMS HPMS Security Incident Handling
Procedures. These documents outline the procedures for managing known or suspected security
or privacy incidents, including, but not limited to, roles and responsibilities, escalation
procedures, and guidelines for notifying impacted individuals or organizations. CMS may
provide additional information regarding record retention and destruction of section 1194(e) data
collected and stored in the CMS HPMS in future rulemaking or in updates to the CMS Record
Management Policy, as appropriate.

described in section 40.2.1 of this final guidance, CMS will treat information on non-Federal

information obtained from a person that is privileged or confidential, the Trade Secrets Act at 18

U.S.C. § 1905 requires executive branch employees to protect trade secrets and certain other

Comment: A couple of commenters encouraged CMS to publish the maximum amount of

confidentiality of proprietary information. CMS appreciates the need to balance transparency in

including manufacturers’ proprietary data. As discussed in section 60.6 of this final guidance,
CMS will release a narrative explanation of the negotiation process and redacted information
regarding the section 1194(e) data received, exchange of offers and counteroffers, and the

process will abide by the confidentiality policy described in section 40.2 of this final guidance
and will redact proprietary information, PHI / PII, and information that is protected from

Providing Access to the MFP in 2026, 2027, and 2028 (Section 40.4 and 90.2)
Comment: One commenter expressed concern that pharmacies would be reimbursed by Part D
plan sponsors and PBMs below the MFP for selected drugs. The commenter requested that CMS
ensure Part D plan sponsors and PBMs reimburse pharmacies at the MFP, plus a dispensing fee,
and without pharmacy price concessions. This commenter also asserted that the IRA does not
expressly prohibit the Secretary from ensuring that pharmacies are not reimbursed less than the
MFP for selected drugs and that the amended definition of negotiated price does not include
price concessions. One commenter suggested that CMS require that plan reimbursement for
selected drugs include an enhanced dispensing fees for selected drugs to cover increased
operating costs of pharmacies related to dispensing selected drug.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their recommendations. CMS expects plans and
PBMs to engage in sustainable and fair reimbursement practices with all pharmacies to ensure
access to selected drugs, consistent with their statutory obligations, for individuals with Part D.

48
CMS will closely monitor for whether further programmatic adjustments are needed to address
any contrary practices that emerge. As described in section 60.1 of this final guidance, CMS
interprets section 1194 of the Act to establish a single MFP, updated pursuant to section 1195(b)
of the Act, for a selected drug with respect to its price applicability period. As noted in CMS’
response to a similar comment on pages 39-40 of the final guidance for initial price applicability
year 2027, under section 1860D-2(d)(1)(D) of the Act, as amended by section 11001(b) of the
IRA, the negotiated prices used in payment by each Part D plan sponsor for each selected drug
must not exceed the applicable MFP plus any dispensing fees for such drug. CMS is not
establishing requirements for dispensing fees for selected drugs at this time but will monitor
complaints and audits related to this issue. CMS encourages plan sponsors to work with
pharmacies to ensure adequate and fair compensation for dispensing selected drugs.
Furthermore, CMS intends to closely monitor plan reimbursement for selected drugs including
pharmacy price concessions, and as described in section 110 of this final guidance, monitor plan
compliance with other requirements (e.g., the formulary inclusion requirement under section
1860D-4(b)(3)(I) of the Act).
Comment: Some commenters expressed support for CMS’ centralized approach to facilitating
data and payment through the MTF DM and MTF PM, arguing that this centralized structure
promotes standardization, predictability, and reduces operational burden on stakeholders
responsible for implementing these programs while asserting that there are currently no private
market solutions that offer the MTF’s end-to-end capabilities. A few commenters recommended
that CMS should maintain and invest in the MTF infrastructure during the initial years of

A few commenters suggested that any future private market solution for the MTF should serve as
an alternative to rather than a replacement for the MTF PM. A couple of commenters
recommended that CMS wait until initial price applicability year 2028 concludes before seeking
feedback on private market alternatives for MFP effectuation. One commenter expressed that
CMS’ policies related to MFP effectuation, including use of the MTF, are operationally complex
and will be less efficient and more expensive than existing private market solutions. This

Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their suggestions related to the request for input
regarding potential private market solutions that could offer an alternative to the MTF and the

49
extent to which interested parties perceive a need for ongoing MTF support over time. At this
time, Primary Manufacturers and dispensing entities that have entered into network pharmacy
agreements with Part D plan sponsors will be required to enroll in the MTF DM, and we expect
that Primary Manufacturers will use the MTF platform (including the voluntary MTF PM) to
support access to the MFP for a selected drug starting January 1, 2026. CMS plans to continue to
support MTF operations through 2028 and intends to monitor potential private sector alternative

Comment: One commenter recommended CMS allow plans to negotiate rates for selected drugs
that are lower than the MFP, rather than being required to adopt the MFP.
