must not exceed the MFP plus any dispensing fees for such drug. CMS has not prohibited plans
from negotiating rates for selected drugs that are lower than the MFP.
Comment: One commenter asserted that the IRA required CMS to ensure prospective access to
the MFP for selected drugs. One commenter recommended that CMS support a strategy for
manufacturers to prospectively provide access to the MFP rather than providing access to the
MFP through the retrospective MTF process. A few of commenters stated that, if required by a
manufacturer to purchase retrospectively, pharmacies would have to purchase the drugs at a
higher price and be exposed to financial shortfalls until receiving the MFP refund retrospectively.
One of these commenters asserted that this process would lead to more independent pharmacies
going out of business. A couple of commenters requested that CMS remove the retrospective
access to the MFP framework from the guidance and adopt a framework for prospective access
to the MFP. One commenter requested that in future initial price applicability years, CMS should
explore an MFP effectuation process that occurs upstream in the payer process and does not
place financial constraints on pharmacies. One commenter recommended CMS consider the use
of voluntary claims identifiers for selected drugs prospectively purchased at the MFP.
Response: CMS appreciates the perspectives shared by these commenters. As CMS stated in
response to similar comments on page 43 of the final guidance for initial price applicability year
2027 and manufacturer effectuation of the MFP in 2026 and 2027, a Primary Manufacturer may
provide access to the MFP prospectively or retrospectively. In section 40.4 of this final guidance,
CMS maintains that a Primary Manufacturer must provide access to the MFP in one of two
ways: (1) prospectively ensuring that the price paid by the dispensing entity when acquiring the
drug is no greater than the MFP; or (2) retrospectively providing reimbursement for the
difference between the dispensing entity’s acquisition cost and the MFP. Recognizing that there
may be advantages and disadvantages to both approaches, CMS encourages Primary
Manufacturers and dispensing entities to work together to reach agreements as to whether the
dispensing entity will access the MFP prospectively or retrospectively for a given MFP-eligible
claim. As described in sections 40.4.2 and 40.4.3 of this final guidance, the MTF will support
Primary Manufacturers and dispensing entities using either option. Specifically, the MTF will
support data exchange and optional payment facilitation for Primary Manufacturers using the
MTF’s optional payment facilitation functionality, provide a process for Primary Manufacturers

50
to document retrospective MFP refunds made outside of the MTF’s optional payment facilitation
functionality, and provide a process to exclude MFP refunds on claims when the prospective
approach was used. In response to concerns that dispensing entities would be exposed to
financial shortfalls until receiving the MFP refund retrospectively, CMS is committed to the goal
of assuring prompt payment to dispensing entities, consistent with other prompt pay rules in Part
D, and is requiring the Primary Manufacturer to transmit payment of an amount that provides
access to the MFP within 14 days of the MTF transmitting to the Primary Manufacturer data
elements confirming an individual is eligible for the MFP. Please refer to sections 40.4 and 90.2
of this final guidance for more information. Additionally, section 40.4.2.2 of this final guidance
describes a process for dispensing entities to self-identify as dispensing entities that anticipate
material cashflow challenges because of potential delays created by reliance on retrospective
MFP refunds within the 14-day prompt MFP payment window, and section 90.2.1 of this final
guidance describes a requirement for Primary Manufacturers to include their process for
mitigating cashflow concerns for such dispensing entities in their MFP effectuation plans.
Comment: One commenter requested CMS publicly report metrics on pharmacy enrollment and
other aspects of the MTF DM and PM rollout before initial price applicability year 2026 and
publish more detailed information on the MTF testing scope and timeline process.
Response: CMS thanks the commenter for this suggestion. CMS is committed to continued
stakeholder engagement as preparations for MFP effectuation in 2026 continue, including
providing information and support for stakeholders during enrollment, onboarding, and testing of
the MTF. CMS anticipates continuing to release pertinent information on a regular basis through
our dedicated MTF webpages, listservs, and monthly stakeholder calls. CMS is dedicated to
working closely with those stakeholders most directly involved in 2026 MFP effectuation
(namely, Primary Manufacturers with selected drugs for initial price applicability year 2026 and
the entities dispensing those drugs) on MTF enrollment, onboarding, and testing prior to January
1, 2026.
Comment: A few commenters provided feedback on the MTF development process, including
requests related to meeting cadences with CMS to work on solution development and
implementation, to request direct engagement with the MTF PM, and to provide feedback on the
testing schedule for the MTF, among other topics
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their comments. MTF development continues to
proceed on schedule, and throughout the MTF development process, CMS has remained
committed to continuing engagement with manufacturers during development, onboarding, and
testing of the MTF ahead of the effective date for MFPs of selected drugs for initial price
applicability year 2026 and will continue this engagement with manufacturers as the MTF is
implemented and additional manufacturers and selected drugs are added as part of future initial
price applicability years. Specifically, CMS has hosted and continues to host monthly
manufacturer calls, which include a time set aside for question and answer and discussion with
manufacturers. CMS has hosted individual technical working sessions with initial price
applicability year 2026 Primary Manufacturers and has routinely answered technical questions
submitted via email. Manufacturer end-user testing began in July and is proceeding with routine
testing phases, office hours, and individual manufacturer engagement through Fall 2025, which

51
will incorporate additional testing of both the MTF DM and MTF PM. CMS is routinely
publishing new information on MTF development as it is available, including published
development milestones, Interface Control Documents, FAQs, and support resources (including
videos and user guides with technical instructions).
Comment Solicitation on a Fact-Based Assessment When Determining Whether a Primary
Manufacturer Provided Access to the MFP
Comment: CMS received some comments in response to CMS’ comment solicitation in section
90.2 of the draft guidance for initial price applicability year 2028, regarding CMS’ plan to
undertake a fact-specific assessment when determining whether a Primary Manufacturer
provided access to the MFP to a dispensing entity with respect to a selected drug. One
commenter expressed concern that the factors CMS considers for its fact-specific assessment are
overly broad, particularly the factor of “whether the retrospective refund amount…is sufficient to
account for commercially reasonable costs the dispensing entity is likely to encounter in the
supply chain.” Other commenters echoed similar concerns, asking for clarification on
“commercially reasonable costs” and asserting that factor should be limited to statutory
obligations. One commenter warned that the commercially reasonable costs criterion may
provide incentives for abusive practices and manipulation by supply chain entities. A couple of
other commenters stated that “commercially reasonable costs” should include all costs to
dispense, and pharmacies should not be expected to dispense MFP drugs below their full and
complete costs to acquire and dispense.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their feedback. In response to the concerns raised,
and as a result of efforts by CMS to build out the operational process for assessing whether or
not the MFP has been made available, CMS has provided additional detail on the approach
outlined in this final guidance that CMS will use when evaluating whether or not a Primary
Manufacturer has provided access to the MFP to a dispensing entity as part of general oversight
activities and when making case-specific determinations with respect to whether MFP was made
available in specific circumstances. First, CMS describes in section 90.2 of this final guidance
that, in the absence of information available to CMS indicating otherwise, CMS will consider
WAC to be an appropriate proxy for a dispensing entity’s acquisition cost when monitoring and
assessing compliance with a Primary Manufacturer’s obligation to effectuate the MFP. Therefore,
in the absence of information indicating otherwise, CMS will consider provision of the standard
default refund amount (SDRA) (defined as WAC minus the MFP) to meet the Primary
Manufacturer’s obligation to make MFP available.
Additionally, CMS has provided additional information on the process that CMS will use when
engaged in a case-specific determination as to whether the Primary Manufacturer provided
access to the MFP to a dispensing entity with respect to a selected drug when reviewing cases as
a result of a complaint, an audit, or other compliance monitoring or investigations. CMS will
consider contextual information available to the agency, including, as applicable: the invoice
amount from the dispensing entity (if available); documentation maintained by the Primary
Manufacturer supporting its MFP refund amount (as described in section 40.4.3.1 of this final
guidance); the MFP refund amount provided by the Primary Manufacturer, based on the amount
indicated in the “Total MFP Refund Amount” field on the Primary Manufacturer’s claim-level
payment elements, where available, or as determined based on other supporting documentation

52
in the event the claim-level payment elements are deemed to be inaccurate; other documentation
regarding the dispensing entity’s actual acquisition costs such as documentation of an
arrangement for prospective purchase at the MFP or other alternative arrangement evidencing
acquisition cost (e.g., establishment of an agreed-upon proxy for MFP refund calculation as
described in section 40.4.1 of this final guidance); and the commercial reasonableness of costs
incurred by the dispensing entity related to the procurement of the selected drug (if available).
Supply chain costs would be considered as part of CMS’ review of the commercially reasonable
costs incurred by the dispensing entity related to the procurement of the selected drug, if
available.
Comment: CMS received a couple of comments regarding the type of information that may be
considered when assessing whether or not the MFP has been made available. One commenter
argued that pharmacies should not be forced to submit invoices for any reason and urged CMS to
clarify that manufacturers may not request pharmacy invoices for drugs purchased through a
wholesaler. This commenter also requested clarification that manufacturers should not use
pricing data from other pharmacies or pricing metrics such as Predictive Acquisition Cost (PAC),
Maximum Allowable Cost (MAC), or National Average Drug Acquisition Cost (NADAC) when
determining acquisition cost for a specific dispensing entity. Another commenter requested
clarification that complaint submissions without evidence will not be accepted.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their input. CMS provides relevant content in
section 90.2 of this final guidance, and encourages dispensing entities to review accounts
receivable to assess whether the Primary Manufacturer has accurately paid all claims the
dispensing entity believes are MFP eligible. While CMS encourages dispensing entities and
manufacturers to work together to resolve any discrepancies, this guidance does not require that
pharmacies provide manufacturers with invoices during this process. As described in section
90.2.1 of this final guidance, should a dispensing entity submit a complaint for review and
investigation by CMS, CMS may require supporting documentation (e.g., invoices, purchase
orders) in the course of assessing the complaint. CMS does not intend to make such
documentation directly available to manufacturers (though information shared by the dispensing
entity may be used by the agency in making a determination as to MFP availability and
calculating civil monetary penalties (CMPs), which will be disclosed to Primary Manufacturers);
CMS refers these commenters to the Privacy Statement included in the Drug Price Negotiation
Program Complaint and Dispute Intake Form 27 that notes, among other things, that “information
transmitted in [the complaint and dispute intake] form will be stored in a secure environment and
only accessible by authorized users.”

Retrospective Refund (Section 40.4.1)
Comment: A few commenters provided feedback opposing the retrospective refund model
discussed in section 40.4.1 of the draft guidance for initial price applicability year 2028, noting
that they preferred a prospective MFP purchase model, where a dispensing entity would acquire
the drug at the MFP cost, as opposed to a retrospective refund model, citing the potential
financial strain that a retrospective refund model placed on dispensing entities. Additionally, a
few commenters provided considerations for CMS on how to improve MFP effectuation in a
retrospective refund model, highlighting recommended changes to the 14-day prompt MFP
payment window and considerations for providing the dispensing entities with access to the MFP
more quickly.
Response: CMS appreciates the perspectives shared by these commenters. CMS reiterates that a
Primary Manufacturer may provide access to the MFP prospectively or retrospectively. In
section 40.4 of this final guidance, CMS maintains that a Primary Manufacturer must provide
access to the MFP in one of two ways: (1) prospectively ensuring that the price paid by the
dispensing entity when acquiring the drug is no greater than the MFP; or (2) retrospectively
providing reimbursement for the difference between the dispensing entity’s acquisition cost and
the MFP. Recognizing that there may be advantages and disadvantages to both approaches, CMS
encourages Primary Manufacturers and dispensing entities to work together to reach agreements
as to whether the dispensing entity will access the MFP prospectively or retrospectively for a
given MFP-eligible claim. As described in sections 40.4.3 and 40.4.4 of this final guidance, the
MTF will support Primary Manufacturers and dispensing entities using either option.
Regarding MFP refund payment timing, CMS will apply the standards set forth in current Part D
prompt pay reimbursement regulations regarding payment by plan sponsors to pharmacies to
Primary Manufacturers for their transmission of MFP refunds for selected drugs. That is, CMS
will require that a Primary Manufacturer transmit a payment of an amount that provides access to
the MFP to pharmacies, mail order services, and other dispensing entities within 14 days. The
14-day prompt MFP payment window provides Primary Manufacturers with the same 14-day
timeframe to transmit payment as applies for Part D plan sponsors under existing Part D prompt
pay rules. Additionally, section 40.4.2.2 of this final guidance describes a process for dispensing
entities to self-identify as dispensing entities that anticipate material cashflow challenges because
of potential delays created by reliance on retrospective MFP refunds within the 14-day prompt
MFP payment window.
Comment: Some commenters provided feedback supporting the use of WAC as a standardized
pricing metric in the calculation of the SDRA and cited that WAC offered a reliable refund
amount for both dispensing entities and manufacturers. One commenter noted that CMS should
clarify that the WAC price used in the calculation of the SDRA should be the amount at the time
of adjudication and not the WAC price at the time the MFP refund is transmitted. Some
commenters requested that CMS state that the MFP refund amount cannot exceed the SDRA and
that the use of WAC as a standardized pricing metric in the SDRA calculation should be required
to effectuate MFP refund payments. One commenter did not support a WAC-based calculation,
stating that acquisition cost is often lower than WAC because of discounted pricing available to
providers through Group Purchasing Organization (GPO) contracting. One commenter asked that
CMS impose a timeline of six months within which manufacturers must notify pharmacies of

56
changes to WAC (as the SDRA) in advance, so that pharmacies may financially plan for the
impact of the WAC change.
Response: CMS appreciates commenters’ feedback regarding the use of WAC to calculate the
SDRA. In section 40.4.1 of this final guidance, CMS states that the MTF DM will use WAC, as
published in pharmaceutical pricing database compendia on the date of service of the Part D
claim, as the standardized pricing metric to calculate the SDRA. CMS maintains that WAC is the
best option to calculate the SDRA because WAC is a widely available pricing metric, published
and regularly updated in common pharmaceutical pricing database compendia that would be
accessible and transparent to interested parties in the MFP effectuation process, and does not
require the sharing of confidential, proprietary data, such as contracted pricing, discounts, and
rebates between parties. CMS believes using WAC to calculate the SDRA generally best
approximates the acquisition costs of dispensing entities and offers a reliable refund amount for
both manufacturers and dispensing entities that agree to use such a standardized pricing metric.
CMS notes that the inclusion of WAC as a standardized pricing metric in the calculation of the
SDRA as outlined in section 40.4.2 of this final guidance is informational and that the Primary
Manufacturer can choose to refund an amount different than the SDRA if the Primary
Manufacturer determines some other amount is appropriate and sufficient to make the MFP
available. As such, CMS is not establishing requirements regarding the timing and reporting of
WAC to pharmaceutical pricing database compendia by Primary Manufacturers.
Comment: Some commenters provided feedback that CMS should consider the SDRA to be a
“true default” and that manufacturers should not be required to issue refunds above the
calculated and provided SDRA as reported on the claim level data elements described in section
40.4.2 of the draft guidance for initial price applicability year 2028. Additionally, some other
commenters noted that manufacturers should not be required to reimburse at an amount above
the SDRA if the dispensing entity requests such reimbursement and that CMS should clarify that
the MFP refund payment amount should be capped at an amount no higher than the SDRA. One
commenter noted that the MFP refund amount should be negotiated and agreed upon between the
manufacturer and the dispensing entity if it is an amount other than the SDRA.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their feedback. CMS reiterates the obligation to
calculate and pay an appropriate amount to ensure the dispensing entity has access to the MFP
rests with the Primary Manufacturer, as required under section 1193(a)(3) of the Act. A Primary
Manufacturer can choose to refund an amount different than the SDRA if the Primary
Manufacturer determines some other amount is appropriate to make the MFP available. When
assessing whether a Primary Manufacturer provided access to the MFP to a dispensing entity
with respect to a selected drug, absent information available to CMS indicating otherwise, CMS
will consider provision of the SDRA (which is equal to WAC minus the MFP) to meet the
Primary Manufacturer’s obligation to make MFP available. CMS encourages interested parties to
review section 90.2 of this final guidance for information regarding CMS’ approach to
monitoring and making determinations regarding provision of access to the MFP. If a dispensing
entity believes that it has not received a retrospective refund payment that effectuates the MFP,
CMS recommends the dispensing entity remediate with the manufacturer directly. If remediation
between the parties cannot be carried out, Primary Manufacturers and dispensing entities may

57
use the complaints process within the complaint and dispute system, as described further in
section 90.2.2 of this final guidance.
Comment: A few commenters expressed concerns that using the dispensing entities’ actual
acquisition cost as a determinant in the evaluation for assessing MFP effectuation is problematic
particularly because it may contain costs that are passed on from supply chain trading partners
that the manufacturer should not be responsible for reimbursing. Further, commenters requested
that CMS should clarify that manufacturers are not responsible for costs passed on to dispensing
entities from supply chain trading partners. A couple of commenters noted that requiring
manufacturers to reimburse dispensing entities at actual acquisition cost could result in gaming
among supply chain trading partners to artificially inflate MFP refund payments. One commenter
recommended that CMS track which dispensers or types of dispensers are claiming acquisition
costs above WAC and specify what documentation is required by a dispensing entity when
claiming an acquisition cost above the SDRA.
Response: The Primary Manufacturer is ultimately responsible under the statute for establishing
and paying the appropriate MFP refund amount to ensure access to the MFP. CMS believes that
allowing a Primary Manufacturer flexibility to determine its preferred methodology for
calculating its MFP refund payments aligns with the Primary Manufacturer’s statutory obligation
to calculate and pay an appropriate amount to ensure the dispensing entity has access to the
MFP, as required under section 1193(a)(3) of the Act. CMS outlines in section 90.2 of this final
guidance its process for evaluating whether a manufacturer has made MFP available.
Regarding the comments related to supply chain fees and the gaming concerns of trading
partners inflating acquisition cost to increase MFP refund payments, in section 90.2 of this final
guidance, CMS describes its process for determining whether the MFP has been provided in
specific cases. As reflected in section 90.2 of this final guidance, this determination process
includes an assessment of the commercial reasonableness of costs incurred by the dispensing
entity related to the procurement of the selected drug. Primary Manufacturers may consider
CMS’ process for determining whether the MFP has been provided when determining an MFP
refund amount that sufficiently meets their statutory obligation. As outlined in section 90.2 of
this final guidance, when assessing whether a Primary Manufacturer provided access to the MFP
to a dispensing entity with respect to a selected drug, absent information available to CMS
indicating otherwise, CMS will consider provision of the SDRA (which is equal to WAC minus
the MFP) to meet the Primary Manufacturer’s obligation to make MFP available.
MTF Data Facilitation (Section 40.4.2)
Comment: Many commenters expressed concern with the 14-day prompt MFP payment
window. Some commenters stated that the payment window does not provide enough time for
manufacturers to process the expected volume of MFP claims accurately and thoroughly. One
commenter suggested the prompt payment window should exclude weekends and holidays. A
couple of commenters recommended using timelines between 30 days and 38 days. One
commenter stated that the 14-day prompt MFP payment window is not mandated by statute. A
few commenters stated that the 14-day prompt MFP payment window is too long and could
cause cash flow concerns for dispensing entities. One commenter recommended the payment

58
window begin within 14 days of the dispensing entity adjudicating the claim with the plans or
PBMs, rather than beginning when the MTF sends the claim-level data elements to the Primary
Manufacturer. A couple of commenters suggested allowing dispensing entities and manufacturers
to agree on a different prompt MFP payment window if payment is not being made through the
MTF PM.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their input. Section 1193(a)(3) of the Act places
the obligation on the Primary Manufacturer to ensure that the MFP is made available to
pharmacies, mail order services, and other dispensing entities that dispense the selected drug to
MFP-eligible individuals described in section 80 of this final guidance. Consistent with CMS’
response on pages 50 and 51 of the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027, CMS
will apply the standards set forth in current Part D prompt pay reimbursement regulations
regarding payment by plan sponsors to pharmacies to Primary Manufacturers for their
transmission of MFP refunds for selected drugs. That is, CMS will require that a Primary
Manufacturer transmit payment of an amount that provides access to the MFP to pharmacies,
mail order services, and other dispensing entities within 14 days. The 14-day prompt MFP
payment window provides Primary Manufacturers with the same 14-day timeframe to transmit
payment as applies for Part D plan sponsors under existing Part D prompt pay rules. This timely
MFP refund payment will support dispensing entities to continue efficient operations and prevent
undue financial hardship. Additionally, section 40.4.2.2 of this final guidance describes a process
for dispensing entities to self-identify as dispensing entities that anticipate material cashflow
challenges because of potential delays created by reliance on retrospective MFP refunds within
the 14-day prompt MFP payment window, and section 90.2.1 of this final guidance describes a
requirement for Primary Manufacturers to include their process for mitigating cashflow concerns
for such entities in their MFP effectuation plans.
The 14-day prompt MFP payment window begins when the MTF DM sends the claim-level data
elements to the Primary Manufacturer. While this may result in MFP refund payments in excess
of 14 days from time of claim submission by the dispensing entity to the Part D plan sponsor,
this policy allows CMS to include claim-level data elements that have been twice validated for
an individual’s MFP-eligibility by the Part D plan and by DDPS and ensures the Primary
Manufacturer has the minimum necessary information to effectuate the MFP so no additional
validation of MFP-eligibility of an individual needs to be performed. CMS finalized in
rulemaking a change effective in contract year 2026 to shorten the current 30-day window for
plans to submit initial PDE records to seven days for selected drugs to facilitate more timely
payment of MFP refunds to dispensing entities.
Sections 40.4.3 and 40.4.4 of this final guidance outline that the MTF PM facilitation of
retrospective payment is voluntary for Primary Manufacturers, and that dispensing entities and
Primary Manufacturers may reach an agreement outside of the MTF PM to make MFP refund
payments, regardless of whether the Primary Manufacturer is using the MTF PM; however, the
14-day prompt MFP payment window still applies.
Comment: A couple of commenters expressed appreciation for the ability of dispensing entities
to indicate that they expect to experience material cashflow concerns. One commenter suggested
criteria for dispensing entities to qualify for having material cashflow concerns. One commenter

59
expressed appreciation for shortening the window for Part D plans to submit initial PDE records
into the DDPS system from 30 days to 7 days which could expedite MFP refund payments to
dispensing entities. Some commenters stated concern with holding manufacturers responsible for
mitigating dispensing entities’ cashflow challenges, with a couple of commenters noting that
there is no statutory basis for such responsibility. A few commenters suggested using a model
where CMS pre-funds a pool from which refunds are promptly paid to dispensing entities to
mitigate cashflow concerns, similar to the model used for the Manufacturer Discount Program
(MDP).
Response: CMS appreciates this feedback. As discussed in section 40.4.2.2 of this final
guidance, CMS will allow dispensing entities to self-identify as anticipating material cashflow
concerns at the start of the initial price applicability year due to the reliance on retrospective
MFP refunds within the 14-day prompt MFP payment window. At this time, CMS did not specify
other criteria by which dispensing entities qualify for such designation. This information will be
provided to Primary Manufacturers to assist in the development of their MFP Effectuation Plans.
Consistent with section 1193(a)(5) of the Act and as described in section 90.2.1 of this final
guidance, CMS will require Primary Manufacturers to include their approach to mitigating
material cashflow concerns in their MFP Effectuation Plans. CMS agrees timely movement of
funds is important and appreciates that prefunding would offer advantages. The IRA did not
include an appropriation to ‘prefund’ MFP refund payments. In accordance with section
1193(a)(3)(A) of the Act, it is the sole responsibility of the Primary Manufacturer to provide
dispensing entities access to the MFP for selected drugs.
Comment: A couple of commenters suggested that all PDE records for selected drugs should be
passed to the Primary Manufacturer regardless of the presence of DDPS edits that are not listed
in Appendix B of this final guidance. A couple of commenters requested that all DDPS edits,
including those not listed in Appendix B of this final guidance, should be resolved before
sending to Primary Manufacturers.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their input. As discussed in section 40.4.2 of this
final guidance, CMS will receive PDE records for all claims for selected drugs with an MFP
dispensed to MFP-eligible individuals during a price applicability period. Data elements for a
PDE record will not be sent to the Primary Manufacturer until the PDE record can be verified as
reflecting that a selected drug was dispensed to an MFP-eligible individual. As discussed in
section 40.4.2 of this final guidance, CMS will use the list of DDPS edits in Appendix B of this
final guidance in determining whether to transmit a PDE record to a Primary Manufacturer. In
cases where DDPS edits directly relate to the determination and verification of MFP eligibility
for the purposes of the Negotiation Program, such as missing NDCs or dispensing entity
identifiers, the MTF will not send these claims to the Primary Manufacturer for MFP refunds
until those issues are resolved.
MTF Payment Facilitation (Section 40.4.3)
Comment: Some commenters expressed concern or provided comment related to the financial
burdens of the MFP effectuation process on dispensing entities, with a couple of commenters
expressing concerns with how MFP refund payments are effectuated. Commenters requested that

60
CMS work collaboratively with the pharmacy and provider community to establish mitigation
strategies to avoid cash flow disruptions. Some commenters provided feedback related to the
methods described in section 40.4.3 of the draft guidance for initial price applicability year 2028
that interested parties can consider in addressing the cash flow concerns of dispensing entities.
Some commenters requested that CMS “prefund” MFP refund payments from manufacturers to
dispensing entities through the MTF and a few commenters recommended that CMS consider
modeling the MFP refund payment process after CGDP. A couple of commenters shared
feedback related to CMS prohibiting the charging of fees or the placement of administrative
burden on dispensing entities by interested parties in the MFP effectuation process. One
commenter requested that CMS leverage its statutory authority to pre-fund a “MFP” discount
pool to mitigate pharmacy cashflow concerns. Another commenter recommended that CMS
utilize an approach utilizing a “pass through” of CMS pre-funded MFP refund amounts to
dispensers on behalf of Primary Manufacturers at the time of claim adjudication with
manufacturers invoiced at a later date.
Response: CMS appreciates this feedback. Consistent with CMS’ previous response on pages
78-79 of the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027, CMS agrees that timely
movement of funds is important and appreciates that prefunding would offer advantages.
However, the IRA did not include an appropriation to ‘prefund’ MFP refund payments. In
accordance with section 1193(a)(3)(A) of the Act, it is the sole responsibility of the Primary
Manufacturer to provide dispensing entities access to the MFP for selected drugs. CMS notes
that there are distinct differences in the agency’s role outlined in statutory requirements for the
Negotiation Program and the agency’s role outlined in statutory requirements for CGDP under
section 1860D-14A of the Act. CMS reiterates that the goal of the MTF PM is to provide an
efficient and unified payment flow through the connection of statutorily affected parties where a
payment flow does not currently exist today.
In addition to requiring Primary Manufacturers to transmit MFP refund payments within the 14day prompt MFP payment window, CMS finalized in rulemaking a change effective in contract
year 2026 to shorten the current 30-day window for plans to submit initial PDE records to seven
days for selected drugs to facilitate more timely payment of MFP refunds to dispensing entities.
As described in section 40.4.2.2 of this final guidance, during MTF DM enrollment, CMS is
asking dispensing entities to self-identify whether they are a dispensing entity that anticipates
having material cashflow concerns due to the reliance on retrospective MFP refunds within the
14-day prompt MFP payment window. This information will be provided to Primary
Manufacturers to assist in the development of their MFP effectuation plans, as described in
section 90.2.1 of this final guidance. Consistent with section 1193(a)(5) of the Act, CMS requires
Primary Manufacturers to include their approach to mitigating material cashflow concerns in
their MFP effectuation plans. In section 40.4.3 of this final guidance CMS outlines
considerations for interested parties to consider when addressing pharmacies that have identified
as having material cash-flow concerns.
As stated in section 40.4.3 of this final guidance, neither Primary Manufacturers nor dispensing
entities shall have to pay any fees to the MTF PM in connection with the pass through of MFP
refund payments, including but not limited to user fees or transaction fees, as CMS intends to

61
bear the cost of operationalizing the MTF PM for 2026, 2027, and 2028. As outlined in section
40.4.3 of this final guidance, regardless of whether the MFP refund is passed through the MTF
PM or outside of the MTF PM, neither Primary Manufacturers nor their contracted entities shall
charge any transaction or other fees to dispensing entities for the pass through of the MFP refund
to the dispensing entity.
Comment: Many commenters requested clarification on different aspects of how credits and
debits will be managed by the MTF credit/debit ledger system. One commenter requested
visibility into the credit and debit ledger for accounting purposes. A couple of commenters
requested that CMS clarify that a record of full reversals will be provided to the manufacturer
and that CMS transmit the record to the manufacturer first before applying a full reversal of the
previously paid amount. A couple of commenters requested that CMS clarify that any
adjustments that occur to claim data within the 14-day prompt MFP payment window restart the
payment window based on the transmission of the adjusted record. A couple of commenters
requested that CMS provide access to the credit/debit ledger system after termination from the
Negotiation Program or termination from MTF PM participation. One commenter requested that
the MTF PM maintain a balance of credits and debits for payments made outside of the MTF PM
as well as for payments made through the MTF PM.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their input. In response to interested parties’
requests for additional clarity on how reversals and adjustments will be addressed by Primary
Manufacturers that elect to pass payment through the MTF PM, section 40.4.3.2 of this final
guidance describes how MFP refund payments will be reconciled using a credit/debit ledger
system for claims that are reversed or require payment adjustment for Primary Manufacturers
that pass payment through the MTF PM. CMS clarified in section 40.4.3.2 of this final guidance
that for full reversals, the MTF DM will issue a record to the Primary Manufacturer indicating
that a full reversal has occurred on a claim. Further, in the case of a credit accrual in the MTF
PM as a result of the issuance of a full reversal after the claim-level payment elements have been
transmitted, a receipt file will be issued to the Primary Manufacturer to provide notice of the
accrued credit, unless no MFP refund payment was authorized, in which case the credit amount
would be equal to zero. In response to comments related to the expectations for timing of the
transmission of claim-level payment elements on adjusted claims, CMS reiterates in section
40.4.3.2 of this final guidance that each set of claim-level data elements is required to be
responded to within the 14-day prompt MFP payment window, regardless of whether a new
adjusted set of claim-level data elements is issued before the claim-level payment elements of the
original claim are transmitted by the Primary Manufacturer. That is, the 14-day prompt MFP
payment window for an original claim is not reset when an adjusted set of claim-level data
elements is issued, and both the original and adjusted set of claim-level payment elements have
different and unique 14-day prompt MFP payment windows that are based on the date of
transmission of the associated claim-level data elements to the Primary Manufacturer. CMS
believes that this aligns with the policy described in section 40.4.2.1 of this final guidance, that
Primary Manufacturers are required to transmit claim-level payment elements “for each claim
identified in the claim-level data elements”.
For Primary Manufacturers that pass payments through the MTF PM, the ledger will operate two
pathways for reconciliation, the first pathway being an automatic credit to be applied for a

62
reversal record indicated by receipt of a PDE reversal record from DDPS, and the second
pathway being an indication on the claim-level payment elements, as described in section
40.4.3.1 of this final guidance, that a previously transmitted set of claim-level payment elements
requires an adjustment as determined by the Primary Manufacturer in its provision of access to
the MFP. In both pathways, a credit, if applicable, will be applied for that Primary Manufacturer
at the dispensing entity NPI-level that the MFP-eligible claim originated from, and to which
selected drug the MFP refund payment was made. Credits will then be netted out of future MFP
refund payments on the selected drug to the credited dispensing entity for Primary Manufacturers
that choose to pass payment through the MTF PM. Regarding visibility into credits and debits at
termination, in section 40.4.3.2 of this final guidance, CMS outlines that CMS, or its designated
contractor, will provide the Primary Manufacturer with an accounting of any outstanding credits
remaining in the credit/debit ledger system as of the date of termination, at a time and in a
manner to be described by CMS in upcoming guidance or technical instruction. Lastly, as stated
in section 40.4.3.2 of this final guidance, CMS intends that dispensing entities and participating
Primary Manufacturers will be able to view the status of available credits and MFP refunds
through their MTF portal and further technical specifications will be outlined in technical
guidance.
The MTF will not maintain a credit/debit ledger for transactions that occur between interested
parties outside of the MTF PM, whether because a Primary Manufacturer that has elected to
participate in the MTF PM and a dispensing entity have a mutually agreed-upon process for MFP
effectuation outside of the MTF PM, or because the Primary Manufacturer chooses to not utilize
the MTF PM at all. For payments not passed through the MTF PM, section 40.4.4 of this final
guidance outlines the Primary Manufacturer’s responsibility to indicate on the claim-level
payment elements reversals and adjustments to previously paid claims; however, the MTF will
not maintain balances of credits or debits for such Primary Manufacturers. The Primary
Manufacturer will be responsible for establishing a generally accepted accounting principles
(GAAP) compliant system to account for adjustments and reversals to previously paid MFP
refunds.
Comment: A couple of commenters provided feedback related to the receipt file that CMS
intends to provide to manufacturers participating in the MTF PM. A few commenters noted that
CMS should clarify that manufacturers are not responsible for technical failures of the MTF PM
in effectuating payments.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their feedback. CMS will consider suggestions
related to the receipt file as we continue to develop the technical specifications of the files and
reports that are exchanged between interested parties. Regarding the comments related to MTF
PM technical failures, section 100.1 of this final guidance notes that CMS will take into
consideration when determining a Primary Manufacturer’s CMP liability, technical failures
related to transmission of payments outside of the Primary Manufacturer’s control as well as
other factors for consideration as evidenced by the Primacy Manufacturer in the Primary
Manufacturer’s response to CMS’ Notice of Potential Noncompliance.
Comment: A couple of commenters requested the addition of a Justification Code to Table 5 in
section 40.4.3.1 of draft guidance for initial price applicability year 2028 that is dedicated to

63
addressing specific scenarios where the 340B price of a selected drug is greater than the MFP.
According to the commenters, the intent of having this code is to communicate that a reduced
MFP refund payment is being made because of (1) the claim being determined to be 340B
eligible and (2) the 340B price being greater than the MFP. The commenters believe that
Justification Code “2” is too broad to capture this circumstance.
Response: In response to commenters’ request, CMS has added a Justification Code to Table 5 in
section 40.4.3.1 of this final guidance to address the scenario described. Justification Code “8”,
“Amount Other than Standard Default Refund Amount Transmitted – Section 1193(d)(2)
Scenario”, has been added to the available list of codes. Primary Manufacturers should use this
code when transmitting the claim-level payment elements if a claim is determined to be 340B
eligible, and the MFP for that claim is lower than the 340B price of the drug.
Comment: Some commenters provided feedback regarding technical specifications that they
would like to see incorporated into the MTF payment facilitation framework. A couple of
commenters provided feedback related to the handling of unclaimed funds, seeking clarification
for how unclaimed funds will be handled and how the return of unclaimed funds will be
communicated to Primary Manufacturers. Some commenters noted their support for the MTF
PM and the proposed retrospective refund process.
Response: CMS is contracting with the MTF Contractor to administer the functions described in
this final guidance with respect to the MTF PM. CMS expects specifications related to the
functionality, interface, and technical specifications of the MTF PM to develop in partnership
with the MTF Contractor and expresses gratitude to the commenters sharing thoughts and
recommendations for features they would like to see related to the operation of the MTF PM.
CMS will consider these recommendations as technical development with the MTF Contractor
evolves.
Regarding unclaimed funds, CMS describes in section 40.4.3 of this final guidance the process
and will reiterate here that all unclaimed funds for payment provided through the MTF PM will
be returned to the Primary Manufacturer, CMS will not accrue any interest on unclaimed funds,
and any disputes related to unclaimed funds will be reconciled directly between the Primary
Manufacturer and the dispensing entity. CMS intends to provide further clarification through
technical instructions as the MTF PM contractor develops the operational considerations for the
processing of unclaimed funds for Primary Manufacturers that utilize the MTF PM.
Comment: A couple of commenters provided feedback that manufacturers should not be
required to participate in the MTF PM. One commenter noted that Primary Manufacturers should
not be responsible for the payments of Secondary Manufacturers. CMS received a couple of
comments reinforcing the commenters’ concerns that Primary Manufacturers must participate in
the MTF PM, stating, “Allowing manufacturers not to participate in the MTF PM could
potentially require pharmacies to negotiate alternative and unique payment arrangements with
each manufacturer. Such scenario would be unduly burdensome and costly for pharmacies.”
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their feedback. Primary Manufacturers have a
statutory obligation to effectuate the MFP, and as described in sections 40.4 and 90.2 of this final

64
guidance, Primary Manufacturers are required to establish a process to ensure the MFP is made
available to MFP-eligible individuals and dispensing entities. While section 1193(a)(3) of the Act
places the obligation on Primary Manufacturers to provide access to the MFP to dispensing
entities, it does not expressly specify how Primary Manufacturers must make MFP accessible.
Therefore, participation in the MTF PM is voluntary for Primary Manufacturers. A Primary
Manufacturer may elect to use the MTF PM to pass through MFP refund payments to dispensing
entities. CMS declines the suggestion to make participation in the MTF PM mandatory.
Comment: A few commenters requested that dispensing entity enrollment in the MTF be
mandatory, and that Primary Manufacturers only be responsible for facilitating payments through
the MTF PM if that is how the Primary Manufacturer has elected to effectuate the MFP to
dispensing entities to avoid having to develop standalone processes with dispensing entities
outside of the MTF PM.
Response: In the CY 2026 Parts C&D Final Rule 31 and as codified at 42 C.F.R. § 423.505(q),
CMS requires Part D plan sponsors to include in their network pharmacy agreements a provision
requiring dispensing entities to be enrolled in the MTF DM. Dispensing entity enrollment in the
MTF DM is needed for necessary operations related to administration of the Negotiation
Program and the Part D program, including creating and sending electronic remittance advices
(ERAs) or remittances, facilitating continued access to selected drugs that are covered Part D
drugs, and ensuring accurate Part D claims information and payment. Further, CMS added
language to section 40.4.3.3 of this final guidance that outlines a process by which Primary
Manufacturers that have elected to make payments through the MTF PM may elect to pass
through MFP refund payments to dispensing entities that are not enrolled in the MTF DM.

Nonduplication with the 340B Ceiling Price (Section 40.4.5 and 90.2)
Comment: Many commenters requested that CMS provide greater clarity on how manufacturers
should identify 340B claims, expressing opposition to the 340B nonduplication approach that
CMS described in the draft guidance for initial price applicability year 2028 and stating that it
creates operational and compliance challenges and risks for supply chain entities. One
commenter recommended that CMS expressly affirm that manufacturers may develop and rely
on their own good-faith nonduplication methodologies and confirm that reasonable, auditable
approaches, when thoughtfully designed and consistently implemented, will be deemed sufficient
for compliance. The commenter raised concerns that manufacturers may face legal risk despite
acting in good faith to fulfill their obligations for nonduplication between the 340B ceiling price
and the MFP. One commenter stated that an identification mechanism that is voluntary for 340B
covered entities will not serve as a realistic solution because, they asserted, covered entities have
no compelling reason to report their 340B claims and that CMS should rely on civil monetary
penalties as an enforcement framework. A couple of commenters recommended CMS prohibit
identification of 340B units after a period of time in order to avoid duplication of discounts.
31
CMS, Final Rule, “Medicare and Medicaid Programs: Contract Year 2026 Policy and Technical Changes to the
Medicare Advantage Program, Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program, Medicare Cost Plan Program, and

https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/04/15/2025-06008/medicare-and-medicaid-programs-contractyear-2026-policy-and-technical-changes-to-the-medicare.

Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their input and acknowledges the concerns
expressed. As explained in section 40.4.5 of this final guidance, CMS is not charged with
verifying or otherwise reviewing whether a particular drug claim is a 340B-eligible claim and
will not, at this time, assume responsibility for nonduplication of discounts between the 340B
ceiling price and MFP. CMS reiterates the requirement for the Primary Manufacturer to transmit
payment of an amount that provides access to the MFP within 14 days of the MTF DM sending
the data elements verifying the selected drug was dispensed to an MFP-eligible individual to the
Primary Manufacturer. CMS also notes that nothing in this guidance modifies a manufacturer’s
statutory obligations under section 340B(a)(1) of the PHS Act, including the obligation to
provide the 340B ceiling price to eligible entities. Nothing in this guidance alters a
manufacturer’s liability under section 340B of the PHS Act for an overcharge violation and
sanctions for failure to provide the 340B ceiling price to eligible entities pursuant to section
340B(d)(1)(B)(vi) of the PHS Act and 42 C.F.R. § 10.11. Accordingly, CMS expects
manufacturers to work with dispensing entities, covered entities and their 340B Third Party
Administrators (TPAs), and other prescription drug supply chain stakeholders to facilitate access
to the lower of the MFP and the 340B ceiling price consistent with their statutory obligations.
Comment: Many commenters recommended that CMS require the use of claims modifiers for
340B claims, a few of these commenters suggesting that CMS could enforce this requirement via
Part D plan contracts or by conditioning receipt of MFP refunds and Part D payment on the
dispensing entity’s appropriate use of either a 340B or non-340B modifier. Another commenter
requested that, if CMS does not require affirmative 340B and non-340B claim modifiers, CMS
and Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) jointly state that dispensing entities
must provide manufacturers with claim-level data for all 340B-eligible claims with respect to
selected drugs for which an MFP is in effect. In contrast, one commenter opposed any policy that
would require the use of 340B claims modifiers, stating that a point-of-sale modifier is
incompatible with the virtual inventory system used by pharmacies as part of the 340B Program.
This commenter noted that dispensing entities may be unable to make the necessary
determinations at the point-of-sale, therefore limiting submission of these codes in a timely
manner. One commenter referenced an analysis on the usage of 340B modifiers and remarked
that 340B claim modifiers are not reliable, even when required. One commenter noted that even
if an identifier is added to a claim, it could be removed at some point when the data transfers
between entities including pharmacies, third-party administrators, and pharmacy benefit
managers. One commenter noted that dispensing entities would be unlikely to use the modifier as
this would provide plans with insight into which claims are 340B claims and the plan could
reimburse the dispensing entity at a lower rate than it otherwise would. One commenter
requested that CMS report how many claims that pass through the MTF DM include the 340B
indicator.
Many commenters recommended that CMS create—or facilitate the creation of—a 340B claims
“clearinghouse” that could identify units subject to a 340B discount and ensure nonduplication of
the MFP and 340B ceiling price in addition to or instead of requiring a claim modifier. One
commenter stated that the clearinghouse would enable covered entities (or TPAs acting on their
behalf) to retrospectively submit 340B claims data, and data from the clearinghouse could be
shared with the manufacturer so they could provide the difference between the MFP and the

66
340B price to the covered entity for 340B-eligible claims. A few commenters noted that the
Oregon Medicaid program has successfully implemented this model for the purpose of
nonduplication of 340B discounts and Medicaid rebates, and this approach has eased provider
burden while allowing for retrospective claim identification. One commenter stated that if the
clearinghouse is not established, CMS should develop a standardized process for manufacturers
to coordinate with TPAs. One commenter stated that if CMS has concerns about mandating
covered entities to report data to a clearinghouse, it could make submission to the clearinghouse
voluntary. By contrast, a few commenters suggested that CMS work with the Health Resources
and Services Administration (HRSA) to establish penalties for covered entities that do not submit
claims data to the clearinghouse in a specified timeframe. Another commenter suggested that
CMS create a conduit within the MTF to facilitate the direct transfer of 340B claims data from
covered entities to manufacturers and assist in nonduplication of 340B and MFP claims. One
commenter argued that any clearinghouse would only be effective for government-paid claims
because commercial 340B claims would not be identified by the clearinghouse and it would
therefore create additional fragmentation in the system. Another commenter stated that covered
entities should report all 340B sales, not just Medicare sales to a clearinghouse and that
manufacturers should be able to receive 340B claims data from the clearinghouse to verify that
the total number of 340B claims reported by each covered entity match the 340B discounts
provided to that covered entity on each drug. A few commenters noted that this clearinghouse
could also be used to remove units that covered entities identified as 340B eligible from the
Medicare Part D Drug Inflation Rebate Program.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their recommendations. In response to the
recommendations for and against the use of a Part D claim modifier for 340B claims, CMS
acknowledges feedback that requiring such a modifier has the potential to pose operational
challenges, increase administrative burden, and may not always be accurate. Consistent with
CMS’ response on page 60 of the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027 and
manufacturer effectuation of the MFP in 2026 and 2027, CMS is not pursuing a policy at this
time to require the use of such a modifier and reiterates that use of the 340B submission
clarification code described in section 40.4.2.1 of this final guidance is optional for dispensing
entities based on current National Council for Prescription Drug Programs (NCPDP) standards.
In response to the commenters who recommended that CMS create a 340B claims
“clearinghouse” that could collect data on 340B-eligible claims that would be used for
nonduplication of the MFP and 340B ceiling price, CMS appreciates the detailed insight
provided by commenters. CMS will not, at this time, assume responsibility for such 340B ceiling
price and MFP nonduplication functions, whether through a “clearinghouse” or through other
means, but will monitor this approach and will continue to explore the feasibility of
incorporating 340B-related transactional data from 340B covered entities or their TPAs
identifying claims eligible under section 1193(d)(1) of the Act into MTF processes in the future.
For example, CMS is considering ways to incorporate asynchronous 340B data into MTF
processes in the future.
Comment: A couple of commenters argued that the 340B Drug Pricing Program relies on the
ability of covered entities to purchase covered outpatient drugs upfront at the 340B ceiling price,

67
draft guidance, covered entities will be harmed by CMS’ decision to not take an active role in

One commenter stated that if Primary Manufacturers sell drugs prospectively at the MFP,
covered entities could use virtual inventory systems that are used for 340B-eligible drugs to track
drugs purchased at the MFP and dispense only to MFP-eligible individuals.

to develop and rely on private market solutions to comply with nonduplication of the 340B
ceiling price and the MFP.
One commenter stated that CMS asserts that effectuating the 340B price falls under HRSA’s
purview, not that of CMS, but that construct should not apply in situations involving refunds to
effectuate the 340B price for drugs purchased at the MFP, since the entire MFP effectuation
system is outside of HRSA’s purview.
Response: CMS appreciates the feedback from interested parties on this topic. Consistent with
CMS’ response on page 65 of the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027 and
manufacturer effectuation of the MFP in 2026 and 2027, CMS reiterates that CMS is not charged
with verifying or otherwise reviewing whether a particular drug claim is a 340B-eligible claim.
CMS reiterates that nothing in this guidance modifies a Primary Manufacturer’s statutory
obligations under section 340B(a)(1) of the PHS Act, including the obligation to provide the
340B ceiling price to eligible entities. Nothing in this guidance alters a Primary Manufacturer’s
liability under section 340B of the PHS Act for an overcharge violation and sanctions for failure
to provide the 340B ceiling price to eligible entities pursuant to section 340B(d)(1)(B)(vi) of the
PHS Act and 42 C.F.R. § 10.11. CMS will monitor the extent to which MFP is made available
where appropriate, and CMS will also monitor the extent to which the manufacturer faces
challenges with nonduplication between the 340B ceiling price and the MFP.
Comment: One commenter requested that CMS clarify the language used in footnote 77 of the
draft guidance for initial price applicability year 2028. The commenter argued that the footnote
stated that section 340B(a)(1) of the PHS Act imparts authority to the manufacturers to make any
determinations regarding the proper identification of 340B-eligible patients. The commenter
asserted that the current 340B eligibility determination for individuals is discussed in section
340B(a)(5)(B) of the PHS Act, however, it only refers to the covered entity’s responsibility in
patient eligibility determination, while footnote 77 of draft guidance suggested a manufacturer
privilege of patient 340B eligibility determination. The commenter argued that the footnote could
create confusion or conflict between manufacturers and health centers about determining 340B
eligible individuals.
Response: CMS thanks this commenter for the input. Footnote 77 of the draft guidance for
initial price applicability year 2028 included the language, “CMS does not determine nor verify
340B eligibility and expects manufacturers and covered entities to continue to be responsible for
statutory obligations pursuant to section 340B(a)(1) of the PHS Act regarding proper
identification of 340B-eligible patients and covered outpatient drugs dispensed to such patients.”
The footnote refers not only to proper identification of 340B-eligible patients but also covered
outpatient drugs dispensed to such patients. CMS is clarifying that this language indicates that
manufacturers have statutory obligations related to offering the 340B ceiling price on covered
outpatient drugs to eligible covered entities. CMS is not suggesting which entity determines a
patient’s 340B eligibility. CMS has also clarified the last sentence of the footnote in section
40.4.5 of this final guidance to more broadly refer to section 340B of the PHS Act rather than the
specific obligations pursuant to section 340B(a)(1) of the PHS Act.

70
Comment: A few commenters stated that the draft guidance for initial price applicability year
2028 provides Primary Manufacturers with excessive latitude with respect to 340B
nonduplication, and therefore, providers will be in a position where a Primary Manufacturer does
not provide access to either the 340B price or the MFP. These commenters raised concerns that
provider access to appropriate pricing could therefore hinge on burdensome complaint and
dispute resolution processes and refund payments to providers would be excessively delayed.
One commenter recommended that CMS provide financial support to providers as complaints
and disputes are being resolved and require Primary Manufacturers to provide MFP refunds
promptly unless the Primary Manufacturer is certain of and can provide documentation that the
claim was identified as 340B-eligible and the 340B ceiling price was lower than the MFP.
Another commenter recommended that Primary Manufacturers’ nonduplication plans are shared
with covered entities so that covered entities can prepare and share any concerns with the
Primary Manufacturers in advance. One commenter recommended that CMS require Primary
Manufacturers to share the documentation the Primary Manufacturer provides to CMS related to
340B eligibility determinations, stating that such documentation may be useful to providers
should potential complaints or disputes emerge.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for sharing their perspectives and concerns. As
described in section 40.4.5 of this final guidance, the Primary Manufacturer is required to
transmit payment of an amount that provides access to the MFP of a selected drug to the
dispensing entity within the 14-day prompt MFP payment window, and section 1193(d)(1) of the
Act only applies if: (1) the claim for the selected drug is a 340B-eligible claim; and (2) the 340B
ceiling price is lower than the MFP for the selected drug. As described in sections 40.4.3.1 and
40.4.4.2 of this final guidance, in cases where a Primary Manufacturer receives claim-level data
elements for a selected drug that it reasonably believes is subject to the exception under section
1193(d)(1) of the Act, the Primary Manufacturer would indicate so when reporting claim-level
payment elements to the MTF and declining to transmit payment in an amount that provides
access to the MFP within the 14-day prompt MFP payment window. In this scenario, the Primary
Manufacturer would be required to provide documentation demonstrating the claim was 340Beligible and the 340B ceiling price was lower than the MFP upon request from CMS as described
further in section 90.2 of this final guidance. CMS refers the commenter who requested that
CMS provide financial support to providers as complaints and disputes are being resolved to
section 90.2.2 of this final guidance and the policy therein stating that the initiation of a dispute
on a claim does not negate the Primary Manufacturer’s statutory responsibility to make the MFP
available to the dispensing entity for an MFP-eligible claim subject to a dispute.
As described in section 90.2.1 of this final guidance, some information from manufacturer MFP
effectuation plans will be made available to dispensing entities through the MTF user interface,
and all Primary Manufacturers’ plans must include description(s) of the types of documentation
and data they anticipate collecting, maintaining, and delivering to CMS, if requested, for the
purposes of auditing and compliance with the requirement to make the MFP available.
Information about the Primary Manufacturer’s process regarding nonduplication of 340B claims
is provided in Section 4, Question 6, of the Drug Price Negotiation Program MTF DM Primary
Manufacturer MFP Effectuation Plan Form. This section and question will be collected solely for
CMS’ use for program monitoring and oversight and will not be made public. That is, the
Primary Manufacturer’s response to this question will not be shared with dispensing entities or

71
other stakeholders. CMS reiterates that nothing in this final guidance modifies a manufacturer’s
continued responsibility for statutory obligations pursuant to section 340B(a)(1) of the PHS Act,
including the obligation to offer the 340B ceiling price to eligible entities, nor the federal
agencies responsible for enforcing requirements under section 340B(a)(1) of the PHS Act and
section 1193(d)(2) of the Act.
Comment: A few commenters requested that HHS exercise enforcement discretion with respect
to Primary Manufacturers’ nonduplication efforts if the Primary Manufacturer can demonstrate it
has engaged in reasonable, good faith efforts with a covered entity to fulfill the manufacturer’s
obligations under section 1193 of the Act and section 340B(a)(1) of the PHS Act, as applicable,
or if compliance is inhibited by factors outside of the manufacturer’s control. One commenter
requested clarity on the dispute resolution process, including clarity on which federal agency will
be responsible for adjudicating complaints related to nonduplication with the 340B price and
how disputes related to a 340B rebate model would be resolved. One commenter recommended
CMS provide clear guidance for complaints and disputes related to 340B nonduplication that can
be handled at the claim level.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their feedback. Consistent with CMS’ response on
page 62 of the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027, the complaint and dispute
system will be set up with two “tracks” within one overall system – one track for complaints and
one track for disputes. The disputes process established in section 90.2.2 of this final guidance is
intended to cover specific, identifiable challenges to a technical aspect of the MTF and process
and is not intended to address 340B compliance concerns. Primary Manufacturers have the
option to indicate in their report of claim-level payment elements if they did not pay an MFP
refund on a particular claim because they identified it as a 340B claim and the 340B ceiling price
is lower than the MFP. To account for the instance in which a Primary Manufacturer believes it
provided an MFP refund through the MTF PM on a claim that had already been made available
at a lower 340B ceiling price after the MFP refund had been processed (i.e., the manufacturer
provided a duplication of discounts), the MTF’s crediting functionality within the credit/debit
ledger system will be available to enable the Primary Manufacturer to reconcile these
duplications retroactively. The MTF DM will provide functionality for Primary Manufacturers to
submit instructions for the MTF to apply a credit for the previously provided MFP refund in
these scenarios such that Primary Manufacturers will have access to functionality to address
duplicated discounts retroactively if needed.
The complaint process will be available to the public as well as Primary Manufacturers and
dispensing entities, regardless of their degree of participation in any aspect of the MTF and will
encompass any issues that do not qualify as disputes. A dispensing entity may submit a complaint
to the MTF that the MFP was not made available, including with respect to claims that the
Primary Manufacturer claimed were subject to section 1193(d)(1) of the Act based on the
Primary Manufacturer’s reported claim-level payment elements. CMS may investigate
complaints related to MFP effectuation, including to assess whether an MFP refund was owed
rather than the exception in section 1193(d)(1) of the Act applying. CMS intends to limit
investigations and findings in such circumstances to (1) whether the MFP is lower than the 340B
price; and (2) if so, whether the MFP was made available. As part of that investigation, CMS will
review the extent to which the Primary Manufacturer reasonably believed that the exception in

72
section 1193(d)(1) of the Act applied and the role that any operational barriers played in the
Primary Manufacturer being able to take timely action to meet its statutory obligation to make
MFP available, as applicable, with respect to these claims. If CMS determines that the MFP
should have been made available for the claim and was not, CMS will follow the process
established in section 100.1 of this final guidance. Regarding the commenters’ requests that
manufacturers be held harmless in certain cases, CMS refers this commenter to sections 100 and
100.1 of this final guidance. Section 100 of this final guidance states that CMS intends to
exercise the authority to impose CMPs for instances of noncompliance that substantively
obstruct Negotiation Program processes and/or availability of the MFP. Section 100.1 of this
final guidance states that, upon discovery and confirmation of a Primary Manufacturer’s failure
to make MFP available, CMS intends to send the Primary Manufacturer a Notification of
Potential Noncompliance that will include information on the potential violation and an
opportunity for corrective action. CMS intends to establish a process in which the Primary
Manufacturer will have 10 business days to respond to the Notice of Potential Noncompliance to
provide additional context, evidence refuting the violation, proof of mitigation of
noncompliance, and/or other factors for CMS’ consideration. CMS intends to consider the
materials provided by the Primary Manufacturer when determining the Primary Manufacturer’s
CMP liability, including any technical failures outside the control of the Primary Manufacturer
related to the transmission of payment.
Comment: One commenter noted that, although CMS makes clear that using an NPI on its own
would be insufficient to identify a claim as 340B, the claim-level data elements from the MTF
DM include the NPI for prescribers and hospitals. The commenter requested clarification on
whether using both NPIs in combination would be sufficient for concluding that a claim was
340B-eligible. This commenter strongly opposed identification of 340B-eligiblity based on a
combination of NPIs. One commenter supported CMS’ policy regarding the minimum
manufacturer documentation demonstrating that a claim is 340B-eligible.
Response: CMS appreciates the support and feedback. In response to the commenter who
requested clarification on the sufficiency of certain information for concluding that a claim was
340B-eligible, CMS clarifies that the claim-level data elements included in Table 2 of final
guidance for initial price applicability year 2027, as well as in draft and final guidance for initial
price applicability year 2028, do not include the hospital NPI. CMS believes this commenter may
be referring to the Service Provider ID, which identifies the dispensing entity, and Prescriber ID
claim-level data elements. In this final guidance, CMS has made clarifying revisions in sections
40.4.5 and 90.2 of this final guidance to align the language used in such sections with the data
elements listed in Table 2. CMS affirms that neither the Service Provider ID nor the Prescriber
ID alone will constitute sufficient evidence that a claim was 340B-eligible. The Primary
Manufacturer is responsible for performing appropriate verifications to validate the 340Beligibility of a claim. Absent details on specific analyses that a Primary Manufacturer may use to
implement a 340B nonduplication approach, CMS is unable to confirm whether the Service
Provider ID and Prescriber ID could be used together with other data sources as sufficient
evidence that a claim was 340B-eligible.
