Negotiation Factors (Section 50)
Comment: One commenter stated that CMS’ interpretation that CMS can only consider section
1194(e)(1) factors submitted by manufacturers is incorrect. The commenter stated that the IRA
directs CMS to consider information “submitted by the manufacturer” in relation to the factors
listed in section 1194(e)(1) of the Act but the statute does not dictate how CMS should weigh or
consider that information.
Response: CMS respectfully disagrees with this comment. Section 1194(e)(1) of the Act
specifically refers to the list of section 1194(e)(1) factors as, “The following data, with respect to
such selected drug, as submitted by the manufacturer.” CMS believes this indicates that the
information for section 1194(e)(1) factors must come from the manufacturer of the selected drug.
Comment: A few commenters expressed concern with the deadline for manufacturer
submissions of manufacturer-specific data (as described in section 1194(e)(1) of the Act), and a
couple of these commenters recommended CMS permit manufacturers to submit the required
information after the March 1, 2026 deadline. One commenter suggested CMS broadly allow a
manufacturer to supplement a timely submission if new information of relevance to the
negotiation process becomes available after the submission deadline or otherwise for good cause
shown. A couple of commenters suggested that interested parties should be provided a longer
deadline to section 1194(e) data, including through the duration of the public engagement
sessions.
Response: CMS thanks the commenters for their input. Pursuant to sections 1194(b)(2)(A) and
1193(a)(4)(B) of the Act, Primary Manufacturers must submit the manufacturer-specific data
described in sections 1193(a)(4)(A) and 1194(e) of the Act to CMS by March 1, 2026 for initial
price applicability year 2028. Consistent with CMS’ response on page 104 in the final guidance
for initial price applicability year 2027, CMS will use data submitted by the Primary
Manufacturer and other interested parties when developing the initial offer for a selected drug
along with CMS analyses and assessments of evidence as described in section 60.3 of this final
guidance. Further, due to the statutory timeline of the negotiation period, including the
requirement under section 1194(b)(2)(B) of the Act for CMS to issue an initial offer by June 1,
2026, it is not feasible to extend the timeframe for the submission of information under section
1194(e)(2) of the Act. CMS is abiding by the statutory deadlines in this final guidance. As
described in section 60.4.1 of this final guidance, interested parties will have several
opportunities to provide additional section 1194(e)(2) information after the March 1, 2026
deadline.
Comment: A few commenters encouraged CMS to gather input from a variety of types of
stakeholders. A couple of these stakeholders suggested CMS prioritize input from certain
interested parties, including clinicians. A couple of these stakeholders also raised concerns that
the current written submission process was challenging for certain interested parties and that
CMS should provide multiple pathways to provide feedback that are tailored to specific groups
of stakeholders, including those with audio-visual or physical challenges. One of these
commenters also suggested modifying the information collection so that it required no greater
than an eighth grade reading level and recommended making the information collection available

74
in languages other than English. Additionally, this commenter suggested CMS collect voluntary
demographic information to better understand who is using the written submission process.
Response: CMS thanks commenters for their feedback. The initial price applicability year 2028
negotiation process provides multiple opportunities for any interested party to share their
feedback, including clinicians. The Drug Price Negotiation ICR collects written information on
the factors that are described in section 1194(e)(2) of the Act and is divided into sets of questions
that may be applicable to different types of stakeholders, such as those with clinical-focused
experience, patients and caregivers, those with research-focused backgrounds, and
manufacturers. CMS encourages commenters to provide feedback on revisions to the Drug Price
Negotiation ICR for initial price applicability year 2028, and notes that the proposed optional
form for the public does include a request for submitters to identify their respondent type and for
patients and caregivers to optionally provide certain demographic information. CMS continues to
take suggestions regarding translations and alternative collection methods into consideration for
future initial price applicability years. As discussed in section 60.4.1 of this final guidance and in
response to other comments about opportunities for public input above, interested parties will
also have opportunities to provide input orally to CMS through public engagement events.
Comment: Many commenters requested CMS provide additional information regarding how
CMS uses the information submitted in the negotiation process. A few commenters suggested
such information would improve efficiency in the manufacturer’s process to collect and submit
the required data because the manufacturer could better identify the relevant data. A few other
commenters requested CMS clarify its use of written versus oral information shared about the
section 1194(e)(2) factors.
Response: CMS directs commenters to section 60.3 of this final guidance and responses to
comments about this section, which concern how CMS uses the section 1194(e) data in
developing an initial offer and, if any, counteroffers.
Comment: One commenter suggested that CMS streamline the information by not requesting a
manufacturer to submit data available publicly or via other federal agencies.
Response: Consistent with CMS’ response to similar comments received in relation to the
collection of section 1194(e)(1) data for initial price applicability years 2026 and 2027, CMS
maintains that although some of the information may be available through other sources, CMS
may not be able to ensure that such data are complete or up to date, and, ultimately, CMS
believes that the Primary Manufacturer is best positioned to provide the requested data.
Furthermore, CMS section 1194(e)(1) of the Act requires that manufacturers submit information
required under this section to CMS for purposes of the Negotiation Program.
Comment: One commenter requested that CMS clarify whether Primary Manufacturers are
obligated to continually update their data submissions or only if it becomes clear to the
manufacturer that the information submitted was incorrect based on information available at the
time of submission or if the data changes (e.g., a Medicaid best price restatement). The
commenter raised concerns about the interplay of the requirement to update data with the
reporting of data for renegotiation.

75

Response: As stated in section 50.1 of this final guidance, a Primary Manufacturer must submit
updates to the Primary Manufacturer’s data submitted under sections 1193(a)(4)(A) and
1194(e)(1) of the Act to CMS if the data was restated due to requirements of the government
entity that initially receives and oversees processing of such data, which as the commenter
provides, includes revisions to Medicaid best price under 42 C.F.R. § 447.510. This ongoing
obligation to update the Primary Manufacturer’s original data submissions is separate both from
any voluntary submission of data from a Primary Manufacturer of a selected drug to inform
renegotiation eligibility and selection (see section 130.3.1 of this final guidance) and the required
submission of section 1194(e)(1) data to CMS for drugs selected for renegotiation (see section
130.3.2 of this final guidance), which cover different reporting periods. The reporting
requirements in section 50.1 of this final guidance apply to data submitted for negotiation and
renegotiation.
Comment: Some commenters urged CMS not to use any metrics of cost-effectiveness or “cost
per generic health metric” because the metric and/or the underlying data or assumptions used to
develop the metric may be discriminatory. One commenter requested clarification as to whether
CMS would use any cost effectiveness metrics. A few commenters supported CMS’ decision not
to use Quality-Adjusted Life Years (QALYs) when assessing section 1194(e)(2) factors. One
commenter supported CMS’ consideration of studies that have content relevant to the negotiation
process even if the study uses QALYs. One commenter urged CMS to consider the effects that
indirectly using metrics like the QALY could have on patients. One commenter urged CMS not
to use cost-effectiveness assessments when reviewing a selected drug. One commenter supported
the use of health measures that do not violate the prohibition of discriminatory measures in
section 1194(e)(2) of the Act, noting studies that include such metrics may provide valuable
information on the selected drug.
Response: CMS appreciates these commenters’ feedback on cost effectiveness measures.
Consistent with our response on page 85-86 of the final guidance for initial price applicability
year 2027, CMS reaffirms that QALYs will not be used in the Negotiation Program. CMS will
consider studies that use QALYs only when they contain other content that is relevant and
permitted under applicable law, including section 1194(e)(2) of the Act and section 1182(e) of
Title XI of the Act and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act. In response to feedback received
on whether any measures may be permissible under section 1194(e)(2) of the Act and section
1182(e) of Title XI of the Act, CMS states in section 50.2 of this final guidance that CMS will
review cost-effectiveness measures and studies that use such measures to determine whether the
measure may be considered in accordance with section 1194(e)(2) of the Act. However, while
such measures may be reviewed, they will not be used to adjust the initial offer if the measures
do not provide information related to the negotiation factors described in section 1194(e) of the
Act or are prohibited under section 1194(e)(2) or under section 1182(e) of the Act.
Comment: Some commenters disagreed with CMS’ decision to remove the requirement for
respondents to the Drug Price Negotiation ICR for initial price applicability year 2028 to indicate
whether their submission contains information from studies that use measures or methods that
treat extending the life of an individual who is elderly, disabled, or terminally ill as of lower
value than extending the life of an individual who is younger, nondisabled, or not terminally ill

76
and the request that respondents provide a short description of any cost-effectiveness measures
included in the research they are submitting, and how they believe the data avoids treating
extending the life of an individual who is elderly, disabled, or terminally ill as of lower value
than extending the life of an individual who is younger, nondisabled, or not terminally ill. A few
of these commenters stated without this requirement, the submitter would not need to disclose if
the evidence submitted included discriminatory measures. A few other commenters stated that
removal of this requirement jeopardizes transparency in the information shared with CMS and
used by CMS in the negotiation process. One commenter supported the decision to remove this
requirement because the commenter said it may provide a barrier to submission for respondents
unfamiliar with the concept(s).
Response: CMS thanks commenters for their feedback. Consistent with the response to the
comments about the use of cost-effectiveness measures provided immediately above and in
accordance with section 50.2 of this final guidance, CMS reiterates that QALYs will not be used
in the Negotiation Program. Nonetheless, CMS reviews, and will continue to review, measures
included in studies submitted by respondents through the Drug Price Negotiation and Drug
Selection ICRs. CMS determines, and will continue to determine, if it is appropriate under
section 1194(e)(2) of the Act for CMS to consider the information submitted. Section 50.2 of this
final guidance discusses the criteria CMS will follow when considering the validity and rigor of
the section 1194(e)(2) evidence submitted by interested parties in response to the Drug Price
Negotiation and Drug Selection ICRs. Further, CMS directs commenters to section 60.6.1 of this
final guidance where CMS discusses publication of the explanation of the MFP, which will
include an explanation of CMS’ use of the section 1194(e)(2) factors submitted and redacted
copies of the section 1194(e)(2) factors submitted by interested parties for initial price
applicability year 2028.
Comment: A few commenters requested that CMS provide further detail on study design and
evidence prioritization in the Negotiation Program, including but not limited to details related to
acceptable modes of data collection, whether outcome adjudication is required for all endpoints
in all studies, and approaches to stratifying subgroups of interest. A few commenters suggested
that CMS prioritize real-world evidence. One commenter suggested that CMS balance
manufacturer-submitted evidence with unpublished data. One commenter suggested that CMS
prioritize data submitted by sources other than the Primary Manufacturer. One commenter
requested that CMS indicate that Artificial Intelligence (AI)/Machine Learning (ML)- and Large
Language Model (LLM)-derived real-world data is acceptable as part of the submission of data
under section 1194(e)(2) of the Act.
Response: CMS appreciates commenters’ feedback. Section 50.2 of this final guidance describes
how CMS will consider evidence and how CMS will prioritize such evidence. Specifically,
section 50.2 of this final guidance states that CMS will review existing literature and real-world
evidence, conduct internal analytics, and consult subject matter and clinical experts on these
topics (described in section 60.3.1 of this final guidance) when considering available evidence
about alternative treatments to the selected drug. When reviewing the data submissions from the
public and manufacturer (including the examples of data above) as well as literature from CMS’
review, CMS intends to consider the source, rigor of the study methodology, current relevance to
the selected drug and its therapeutic alternative(s), whether the study has been through peer

77
review, study limitations, degree of certainty of conclusions, risk of bias, study time horizons,
generalizability, study population, and relevance to the negotiation factors listed in section
1194(e)(2) of the Act to ensure the integrity of the contributing data within the negotiation
process. CMS will prioritize research, including both observational research and research based
on randomized samples, that is methodologically rigorous, appropriately powered (i.e., has
sufficient sample size) to answer the primary question of the research, and structured to avoid
potential false positive findings due to multiple subgroup analyses. CMS believes the above
approach will ensure the integrity of the contributing data within the negotiation process.

Comment Solicitation on “Forward-looking” Market Data
Comment: Many comments responded to CMS’ request for comments on the collection of
“forward-looking” market data for the selected drug. Many commenters expressed concern with
the type of data suggested in the draft guidance for initial price applicability year 2028.
Specifically, these commenters stated that data capturing future projections of costs and/or
revenue is not permissible under or consistent with the statute at section 1194(e)(1)(E) of the Act.
One commenter stated that CMS’ proposal to include forward-looking data in the scope of the
factor described at section 1194(e)(1)(E) of the Act is to skew the manufacturer-data towards a
lower initial offer. Additionally, some of these commenters stated the data is variable, dynamic,
and that the evolving nature of the data would not be consistent with the Primary Manufacturer’s
requirement to certify that the data submission is “complete and accurate.” Additionally, one
commenter stated that given the speculative nature of the data, the data is considered highly
confidential by manufacturers and CMS should not take on the risk of needing to protect this
type of data. A few commenters also stated that additional data will increase manufacturer
burden, may require manufacturers to establish new processes to obtain the information, and is
inconsistent with CMS’ otherwise stated intention to streamline the ICRs. A few commenters
also observed that it may be challenging to provide appropriate directions to collect the data
intended by CMS. Other commenters supported collection of forward-looking market data but
cautioned CMS that the data may be manipulated and less reliable because it is speculative.
Some of these commenters suggested CMS require and/or consider third-party sources, such as
SEC disclosures, to support the data. One of these commenters also suggested CMS consider
data and best practices used by other health authorities. One commenter suggested that if CMS
collects this type of data to specify the data is associated with only the selected product because
costs are not static and may increase with investments.
Response: CMS thanks commenters for their suggestions related to additional data to be
collected and considered under section 1194(e)(1)(E) of the Act. CMS will consider these
comments in CMS’ policy development for this issue in future rulemaking.
Establishment of a Single MFP for Negotiation and Renegotiation Purposes (Section 60.1)
Comment: Many commenters responded to CMS’ request for comments on whether it should
take an alternative approach to negotiating the single price for the selected drug—for example,
on a per-unit basis rather than a 30-day equivalent supply basis, or on the basis of a days’ supply
less than 30 days—for drugs for which a 30-days’ supply is not representative of the typical use
of such drug (for example, drugs that have only one formulation and are indicated for
administration once in a course of treatment, or drugs that are typically administered daily for a
short period such as two weeks). Some of the commenters opposed the use of a 30-day
equivalent supply, especially if it were to be applied to drugs payable under Part B. One
commenter opposed using a per unit approach to replace an approach based on 30-day equivalent

79
supply and suggested an alternative approach of using price per course of treatment. A few other
commenters expressed concern with CMS’ approach using a 30-day equivalent supply to apply
MFP across dosage forms and strengths, particularly with drugs with dosing variation across
indications or dosing that involves titration, loading, weight-based, and severity-based variation.
One of these commenters stated that any methodology should be flexible to accommodate the
clinical disease state and treatment landscape, and account for differences in titration and
onboarding versus maintenance dosing, as well as to account for treatment-free intervals. One
separate commenter suggested that instead of using an approach based on 30-day equivalent
supply, that CMS should adopt a lowest unit of measure-based approach (that is the same or
common across all prices, volumes, dosage forms and strengths) for selected drugs. The
commenter suggested that this approach reduces burden and facilitates easy conversion to
package size or billing unit type (e.g., mg for Part B or mL for Part D) and that once a common
billing unit conversion is established (e.g., mL), the prices can be appropriately weighted to
derive at a combined single MFP ceiling for both Part B and Part D (e.g., both ceilings converted
to price per mL). A few commenters requested that CMS consult with Primary Manufacturers on
the methodology to be used for a selected drug, and if feasible, prior to the initial offer so any
limitations are appropriately addressed and accounted for in the initial offer. A couple of the
commenters supported the calculation of one MFP that would apply to all dosage forms and
strengths and appreciated the clarity and transparency provided by CMS in section 60.1 of the
draft guidance for initial price applicability year 2028. A couple of the other commenters
suggested that CMS should divide all amounts of days between service by 30, not just those
where days between service is greater than 34 because Part B products have dosing schedules
that can have much more variability than in Part D.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their thorough and extensive feedback and
suggestions to CMS’ request for comments. CMS will continue to use the 30-day equivalent
supply methodology as it allows CMS to calculate a price for a standardized treatment duration
for all dosage forms and strengths of a given drug, as well as across drugs, and CMS appreciates
the support from the commenters stating there is more clarity and transparency provided in this
final guidance. As stated in section 60.2.1.1 of this final guidance, to calculate the 30-day
equivalent supply for each PDE record associated with a selected drug that is a drug covered
under Part D, CMS will use the methodology as described at 42 C.F.R.
§ 423.104(d)(2)(iv)(A)(2). This methodology relies on the “days’ supply” field in PDE records.
The methodology for a selected drug covered under Part D will remain the same because there is
a “day supply” field in the PDE to calculate total 30-day equivalent supply for a selected drug, or
therapeutic alternative(s), making it easier to apply this methodology.
To calculate the 30-day equivalent supply for Part B data associated with selected drugs that are
payable under Part B, CMS must use an alternative methodology because Part B data does not
contain a “days’ supply” field. CMS appreciates the suggestions from commenters and has taken
into consideration the commenters’ input and updated the methodology for the calculation of 30day equivalent supply methodology in section 60.2.1.1 of this final guidance for selected drugs
payable under Part B. For selected drugs payable under Part B, CMS will use the “days between
service” amount calculated for each Part B claim to calculate the 30-day equivalent supply. For
each Part B claim, the number of 30-day equivalent supplies is equal to the ‘days between
service’ divided by 30. This updated methodology will also prevent overvaluing drugs with less

80
than 30 days between administration because under this methodology, they will have a 30-day
supply equivalent less than 1. CMS understands that drugs payable under Part B often have
recurrent administrations and variable dosing depending on body weight, indication, treatment
phase, or response to treatment, and the “days between services” methodology addresses these
concerns by using observed data from individual patients, which can be captured if providers are
following patient-specific dosing regimens. CMS appreciates the commenters’ suggestion of
working with the Primary Manufacturers on the methodology to be used for a selected drug, but
this would be time and resource intensive and potentially not lead to a standardized approach and
methodology that could be used for selected drugs and their therapeutic alternative(s). For these
reasons listed above (e.g., the suggested approach is time and resource intensive and may not
lead to a standardized approach and methodology that could be used for selected drugs and their
therapeutic alternative(s)), CMS does not believe that a price per course of treatment approach is
feasible. CMS does not believe that a per unit price for Part B drugs would work as well as the
30-day equivalent supply methodology because unit type may differ both across HCPCS within a
Part B selected drug and also across therapeutic alternative(s) for a selected drug, especially if it
includes drugs payable under Part B and covered under Part D. The 30-day equivalent supply
methodology provides a standardized methodology for CMS to calculate a price for a
standardized treatment duration for all dosage forms and strengths of selected drugs and
therapeutic alternatives and also allows for easier comparison across the selected drug and the
respective therapeutic alternative(s).
Determination of the Ceiling for the MFP (Section 60.2.1)
Comment: A few commenters expressed concern for CMS’ approach when determining a
ceiling when a selected drug is payable under Part B and covered under Part D. One of the
commenters stated that the combination of Part B and Part D prices in a qualified single source
drug can lead to a ceiling for a drug payable under Part B calculated based on the price of a drug
covered under Part D (or vice versa) and that it would lead to incongruous results. One of the
commenters requested that CMS state whether the ceiling calculation methodology will differ
between Part B and Part D products, and if so, how those differences will be reflected in the
negotiation process. One of the commenters requested that CMS establish the MFP at the
statutory ceiling for multi-indication drugs which could help ensure that the negotiation process
rewards manufacturers’ innovation. One of the commenters suggested that, with respect to a
selected drug that is payable as a DCAPS drug under Part B and covered as a Part D drug, CMS
should not include the Part B DCAPS utilization when calculating the ceiling.
Response: CMS appreciates the feedback and suggestions from the commenters. As described in
section 60.2.1 of this final guidance, in accordance with section 1194(c) of the Act, for initial
price applicability year 2028, when CMS is determining the ceiling for the MFP for selected
drugs, it shall not exceed:
• As described in section 60.2.2 of this final guidance and section 1194(c)(1)(B) of the Act,
an amount equal to one of the following, as applicable to the selected drug:
o For a selected drug that is covered under Part D but is not payable under Part B,
the sum of the plan-specific enrollment weighted amounts, as described in section
60.2.2.1 of this final guidance; or

81

•

o For a selected drug that is payable under Part B and paid according to section
1847A(b)(4), but is not covered under Part D, the payment amount under section
1847A(b)(4) of the Act for the year prior to the year of that selected drug’s
publication date with respect to the initial price applicability year for that selected
drug, as described in section 60.2.2.2 of this final guidance; or
o For a selected drug that is payable under Part B and paid according to section
1847A(b)(4) of the Act, and covered under Part D, an amount equal to the
weighted average of the payment amount under section 1847A(b)(4) of the Act
and the sum of the plan-specific enrollment weighted amount (hereinafter the
“combined Part B and Part D amount”), as described in section 60.2.2.3 of this
final guidance. CMS interprets the language in section 1194(c)(1)(B) of the Act to
mean that it should calculate a single ceiling incorporating both of these amounts
for selected drugs payable under Part B and covered under Part D.
o For a selected drug that is payable under Part B but not paid according to section
1847A(b)(4) of the Act (for example, selected drugs which are paid on the basis
of 95 percent of Average Wholesale Price (AWP)), but is not covered under Part
D, an amount based on the applicable percent of average non-FAMP, as outlined
in section 60.2.3 of this final guidance; or
o For a selected drug that is payable under Part B but is not paid according to
section 1847A(b)(4) of the Act, and covered under Part D, an amount based on the
lower of the applicable percent of average non-FAMP, as outlined in section
60.2.3 of this final guidance or the sum of the plan-specific enrollment weighted
amounts, as outlined in section 60.2.2.1 of this final guidance.
As described in section 60.2.3 of this final guidance and section 1194(c)(1)(C) of the Act,
an amount equal to the applicable percent, as applicable to the selected drug, of the lower
of:
o The average non-FAMP as defined in section 1194(c)(6) of the Act for such drug
for calendar year 2021 (or in the case that there is not an average non-FAMP for
such drug for calendar year 2021, for the first full year following the market entry
for such drug), increased by the percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index
for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) from September 2021 (or December of such
first full year following the market entry), as applicable, to September 2025; 38 or
o The average non-FAMP as defined in section 1194(c)(6) of the Act for such drug
for the calendar year prior to the selected drug publication date, February 1, 2026,
which for initial price applicability year 2028 is 2025.

CMS interprets the language in section 1194(c)(1)(A) of the Act to mean that it should calculate
a single amount across all dosage forms and strengths of the selected drug for the sum of the
plan-specific enrollment weighted amounts under Part D, the payment amount under section
1847A(b)(4) of the Act under Part B, the combined Part B and Part D amount, and the applicable
percent of the average non-FAMP in order to determine which one is lower and will serve as the
ceiling for the MFP. To determine which of these will be used to calculate the ceiling for the
MFP, CMS will aggregate the amounts determined for each NDC-11 for the selected drug to
calculate a single amount—separately for each methodology—across dosage forms, strengths,
and package sizes of the selected drug. These amounts can then be directly compared, and the
