Determination of the 30-Day Equivalent Supply for a Selected Drug (Section 60.2.1.1)
Comment: Some commenters provided feedback on CMS’ determination and calculation
method of the 30-day equivalent supply for a selected drug. A couple of the commenters stated
that they appreciate the complexity of the issues CMS is seeking to address with the 30-day
equivalent supply calculation. One of these commenters stated practical limitations of
standardizing pricing around a 30-day equivalent supply, particularly for topically applied drugs
as the quantity used can vary significantly from patient-to-patient, and prescribers do not
typically determine usage based on a fixed monthly amount, making the 30-day pricing model
ill-suited for this route of administration and dosage regimen. They recommended that CMS
describe how they would calculate the 30-day equivalent supply for these types of drugs and
ensure that the methodology accounts for variable dosing patterns and real-world clinical use.
The other commenter expressed concern that CMS’ current approach may create calculated
prices that are inconsistent with clinical use. This commenter also expressed concern with the use
of claims data to determine the dose intervals for negotiated drugs, especially for Part B
therapies, to include oncology products, and recommended that treatment intervals be based on
FDA label, rather than claims data. One commenter suggested that CMS should also consider
methods to exclude any outlier Part B claims in which the days between service exceeds the
maximum days between service contemplated in the dosing schedules in the product’s FDAapproved label. One commenter suggested for CMS to use accurate and consistent 30-day
equivalent supply price calculations to calculate price of selected drugs and therapeutic
alternative(s).
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their feedback and suggestions. As stated in
section 60.2.1.1 of this final guidance, CMS will calculate a single ceiling per 30-day equivalent
supply across all dosage forms and strengths of the selected drug. Using the price per 30-day
equivalent supply to calculate this amount facilitates aggregation across dosage forms and
strengths of a selected drug where units (e.g., mg versus mL) and treatment regimens (e.g., daily
consumption of tablets versus monthly injections of solutions) differ. In response to the
commenter regarding topically applied drugs, CMS will use the methodologies described in
section 60.2.1.1 of this final guidance depending on whether it is a drug covered under Part D or
a drug that is payable under Part B. By using a 30-day equivalent supply methodology for both
selected drugs covered under Part D and selected drugs payable under Part B, CMS is using a
consistent approach but understands that there may be some outliers to this methodology. CMS

83
considered using treatment intervals based on FDA label but decided against doing so because
the “days between services” methodology uses observed data from individual patients, which
would capture patient-specific dosing regimens. CMS believes that the finalized methodology for
30-day equivalent supply for selected drugs payable under Part B and covered under Part D
provides accurate and consistent calculations that can be used for most selected drugs and
therapeutic alternative(s). CMS is considering a different methodology for future rulemaking to
calculate the 30-day equivalent supply for drugs that have only one administration (e.g., CAR TCell, vaccines, gene therapies and cancer therapies), as well as an outlier policy.
Comment: A few commenters recommended for CMS to take this opportunity to re-assess the
30-day supply approach and substantially simplify and increase transparency in its approach to
including drugs payable under Part B for initial price applicability year 2028 and subsequent
years by adopting a unit-based approach rather than relying on calculation of a 30-day equivalent
supply of the selected drug.
Response: CMS thanks this commenter for their suggestions and information. As stated in
section 60.1 of this final guidance, once the MFP has been agreed upon, section 1196(a)(2) of the
Act directs CMS to establish procedures to compute and apply the MFP across different dosage
forms and strengths of a selected drug and a 30-day equivalent supply creates a more direct
comparison for drugs that have different dosage form, strength, and treatment regimens than a
unit-based approach. CMS believes that a 30-day equivalent supply methodology also gives a
more complete picture of beneficiary utilization. A unit-based approach may have unit types that
differ across HCPCS within a Part B selected drug and across therapeutic alternative(s) for a
selected drug, especially if the selected drug and/or a therapeutic alternative has both Part B and
Part D utilization. CMS will continue to use the 30-day equivalent supply methodology and for
drugs payable under Part B, CMS has updated the methodology for calculation of 30-day
equivalent supply in section 60.2.1.1 of this final guidance. For drugs payable under Part B,
CMS plans to divide “days between services” by 30 instead of using the methodology described
at 42 C.F.R. § 423.104(d)(2)(iv)(A)(2) for PDE records. This updated methodology should lessen
the possibility of undervaluing the costs of Part B drugs when attempting to determine their cost
per 30-day equivalent supply.
The Sum of the Plan-Specific Enrollment Weighted Amounts (Section 60.2.2.1)
Comment: One commenter recommended CMS incorporate all price concessions from
manufacturers to Part D plans, including those required under the Manufacturer Discount
Program and discounts provided to Part D plans under the redesign, when calculating the ceiling
for the MFP. This commenter believed that including these discounts would meet the definition
of a price concession and should be incorporated into the ceiling.
Response: CMS thanks this commenter for their suggestion. CMS disagrees with this
commenter’s suggestion of including the Manufacturer Discount Program discounts as they are
not a price concession based on current regulation at 42 C.F.R. § 423.100; CMS will continue to
use the C.F.R. definition of direct and indirect remuneration (DIR) and incorporate the
CGDP/MDP discounts in the ceiling calculation.

84
Payment Amount Under Section 1847A(b)(4) of the Act (Section 60.2.2.2)
Comment: A couple of commenters responded to CMS’ request for comments on the approach,
described in section 60.2.2.2 of the draft guidance for initial price applicability year 2028, and on
other options to calculate the ceiling for MFP for selected drugs payable under Part B that are not
paid based on section 1847A(b)(4) of the Act. One of these commenters supported CMS’
proposal to default the ceiling amount calculated via the average non-FAMP methodology for the
Part B drugs not paid under 1847A(b)(4) of the Act (e.g., those paid at 95 percent of the average
wholesale price) but cautioned to ensure that the ceiling amount does not disrupt patient access
due to misalignment with provider acquisition costs. The other commenter stated that CMS
should not substitute an alternative payment amount to calculate the ceiling stating that CMS has
no authority to substitute an alternative payment amount for purposes of calculating the single
ceiling and setting the MFP. A few commenters recommended that CMS exclude Part B
preventive vaccines from the Negotiation Program, as vaccines are paid under section
1842(o)(1)(A)(iv) of the Act, whereas statute refers to section 1847A(b) of the Act as the basis
for determining key implementation provisions of the Negotiation Program in Part B.
Response: CMS thanks the commenters that gave feedback and suggestions to CMS’ request for
comments. For single-source drugs and biological products payable under Part B for which
Medicare does not pay based on section 1847A(b)(4) of the Act (for example, single-source
drugs and biological products which are paid on the basis of 95 percent of AWP but are not
covered under Part D, CMS will use the amount determined under section 1194(c)(1)(C)(ii) of
the Act as the ceiling. That is, for selected drugs payable under Part B but not paid based on
section 1847A(b)(4) of the Act, CMS will calculate the ceiling based on the applicable percent of
average non-FAMP. CMS is not substituting an alternative payment amount to calculate the
ceiling for these drugs because drugs that are not paid under section 1847A of the Act (for
example, single-source drugs and biological products which are paid on the basis of 95 percent
of AWP) do not have a “payment amount under 1847A,” and so CMS is interpreting the statute
as directing it to use the applicable percentage of the average non-FAMP amount to calculate
ceiling and thus not having a comparison to the “lesser of” as is done for single-source drugs and
biological products payable under Part B for which the payment amount is under section
1847A(b)(4) of the Act. As stated in section 60.2.2.3 of this final guidance, for single-source
drugs and biological products payable under Part B for which Medicare does not pay based on
section 1847A(b)(4) of the Act (for example, single-source drugs and biological products which
are paid on the basis of 95 percent of AWP), and covered under Part D, CMS will calculate the
ceiling amount based on the lower of the applicable percent of average non-FAMP, as outlined in
section 60.2.3 of this final guidance and the sum of the plan-specific enrollment weighted
amounts, as outlined in section 60.2.2.1 of this final guidance.
In response to recommendations that CMS exclude Part B preventive vaccines from the
Negotiation Program because they are paid under section 1842(o)(1)(A)(iv) of the Act, as CMS
notes in section 30.1 of this final guidance comment and response section, nothing in the statute
indicates that CMS should exclude vaccines or products with complex and time intensive
production processes from being potential qualifying single source drugs nor from the
Negotiation Program more broadly. In fact, section 1194(c)(3)(A) of the Act makes clear that
vaccines are not categorically excluded from the Negotiation Program. Section 1194(c)(3)(A) of
the Act specifies the same applicable percent, for purposes of calculating the ceiling under

85
section 1194(c)(1)(C) of the Act, for vaccines as it does short-monopoly drugs. By expressly
specifying an applicable percent for establishing a ceiling for the MFP of vaccines as it does for
short-monopoly drugs, the statute contemplates the selection of vaccines under the Negotiation
Program.
Determination of Payment Amount for Selected Drugs Payable Under Part B and Covered
Under Part D (Section 60.2.2.3)
Comment: One commenter recommended for CMS to negotiate and effectuate an MFP under
either Part B or Part D separately rather than calculate a single MFP across Part B and Part D
formulations of the selected drug. This commenter had significant concerns with the proposed
methods discussed in this section such as using Part B claims data to calculate “days between
service” as a proxy for days’ supply as being inappropriate.
Response: CMS thanks this commenter for their input but disagrees with the recommendation.
As stated in section 60.2.2.3 of this final guidance, CMS interprets the language in section
1194(c)(1)(B) of the Act to mean it should calculate a single amount across the payment amount
under section 1847A(b)(4) of the Act and the sum of the plan-specific enrollment weighted
amounts for all dosage forms and strengths of a selected drug that is payable under Part B and
covered under Part D. Section 1194(c)(1)(B) of the Act provides for the calculation of “an
amount,” in the singular, for each selected drug. It then specifies the payment amount under
section 1847A(b)(4) of the Act as the amount to be used for selected drugs for which payment
may be made under Part B and the sum of the plan-specific enrollment weighted amounts as the
amount to be used for selected drugs covered under Part D. It does not specify that CMS should
select only one when calculating the amount for a drug that fits into both categories. For such
selected drugs, section 1194(c)(1)(B) of the Act’s direction to calculate a single amount for each
selected drug therefore means that CMS should calculate a single amount that captures both the
payment amount under section 1847A(b)(4) of the Act and the sum of the plan-specific
enrollment weighted amounts. CMS clarifies that for single-source drugs and biological products
payable under Part B for which Medicare does not pay based on section 1847A(b)(4) of the Act
(for example, single-source drugs and biological products which are paid on the basis of 95
percent of AWP) which do not have a payment amount under section 1847A(b)(4) of the Act, and
covered under Part D, CMS will calculate the ceiling amount based on the lower of the
applicable percent of average non-FAMP, as outlined in section 60.2.3 of this final guidance or
the sum of the plan-specific enrollment weighted amounts, as outlined in section 60.2.2.1 of this
final guidance. As described in section 60.2.4 of this final guidance, CMS will compare the
lower amount of the applicable percent of the average non-FAMP as determined in section 60.2.3
of this final guidance to the amount calculated in section 60.2.2 of this final guidance (sum of the
plan-specific enrollment weighted amounts, the payment amount under section 1847A(b)(4) of
the Act, or the combined Part B and Part D amount, as applicable) to determine the lower
amount, which will be the ceiling for the selected drug. If an agreement on the MFP for a
selected drug is reached, once CMS has determined the ceiling for the selected drug, CMS will
ensure that the MFP per 30-day equivalent supply, as negotiated through the process described in
sections 60.3 and 60.4 of this final guidance, is not greater than the ceiling.
Methodology for Developing an Initial Offer (Section 60.3)

86
Comment: A couple of commenters supported consideration of off-label use when determining
the indications for a selected drug and the therapeutic alternatives, particularly in oncology,
while a few commenters opposed the consideration of off-label use. One commenter asked CMS
to clarify how manufacturers can provide evidence related to off-label use that may not be
included in evidence-based guidelines.
Response: CMS appreciates commenters’ feedback on the consideration of off-label use when
reviewing the indications for a selected drug and determining its therapeutic alternatives, if any.
In response to the request for clarification on evidence related to off-label use, consistent with
the response provided on page 90 of the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027,
CMS encourages members of the public, including manufacturers, Medicare beneficiaries,
researchers, clinicians, caregivers, and other interested parties to provide information about offlabel use(s) through the Drug Price Negotiation ICR. CMS will consider information submitted
through the Drug Price Negotiation ICR when developing the initial offer and throughout the
negotiation process. CMS’ policy includes the criteria that must be met for CMS to consider an
off-label use of a selected drug. Per section 60.3.1 of this final guidance, CMS may consider offlabel use when identifying indications if such use is included in evidence-based clinical practice
guidelines and the off-label use is a medically-accepted indication payable under Part B or
covered under Part D, taking into consideration the major drug compendia, authoritative medical
literature, and/or accepted standards of medical practice.
In section 60.4 of this final guidance, CMS sets forth negotiation process policies including an
opportunity for the Primary Manufacturer to meet with CMS regarding the 1194(e) data
submission prior to CMS sending the initial offer. This initial meeting, as well as the negotiation
process, including offer and counteroffer exchanges and negotiation meetings, provide additional
opportunities for the Primary Manufacturer to discuss off-label use(s) with CMS.
Comment: A few commenters stated that selection of a therapeutic alternative(s) should be
based on only clinical factors and that CMS should not consider the cost of the therapeutic
alternative(s). A couple of commenters urged CMS to limit the selection of therapeutic
alternatives to the same pharmacologic class and a few commenters asked CMS to limit the
selection of therapeutic alternatives to drugs with the same mechanism of action. One commenter
stated that therapeutic alternatives should be chosen if they represent the standard of care for
treatment of a given indication. One commenter suggested that CMS adopt best practices from
the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality’s (AHRQ) Effective Health Care Program
guidance for therapeutic alternative selection. Another commenter recommended that CMS
leverage several resources when reviewing evidence related to therapeutic alternatives, including
the National Pharmaceutical Council’s Guiding Practices for Patient-Centered Value Assessment;
The Myth of Average: Why Individual Patient Differences Matter, published by the National
Pharmaceutical Council; ISPOR – The Professional Society for Health Economics and Outcomes
Research and the International Society for Pharmacoepidemiology (ISPE) practices for real-word
data studies of comparative effectiveness; and National Health Council (NHC) resources on
patient-centeredness in value assessment. One commenter suggested that CMS consider the use
of comparative effectiveness studies and real-world evidence to support the selection of
therapeutic alternatives.

87
Response: CMS appreciates commenters’ feedback regarding the identification of a therapeutic
alternative(s) for the selected drug. Consistent with the response provided on pages 91-92 of the
final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027 and as described in section 60.3.1 of this
final guidance, CMS will identify the therapeutic alternative(s) for the indications of a selected
drug by using data submitted by the Primary Manufacturer and the public, prescribing
information approved by the FDA, drug classification systems commonly used in the public and
private sector for formulary development, major drug compendia, widely accepted clinical
guidelines, evidence identified through the CMS-led literature review, published drug or drug
class reviews, peer-reviewed studies, and Medicare claims or other data sets. CMS believes the
framework described in section 60.3.1 of this final guidance allows CMS to select appropriate
therapeutic alternatives for the indications of current and future selected drugs, if such
alternatives exist. CMS may consult with FDA to obtain information regarding other therapies
with FDA-approved indications for the same indication. CMS may also consult with clinicians,
patients or patient organizations, and/or researchers, to ensure that appropriate therapeutic
alternatives are identified. CMS appreciates the suggested resources for best practices in
observational comparative effectiveness research, real-world data studies of comparative
effectiveness, and patient-centeredness in value assessments and intends to consider how these
resources may be used in the Negotiation Program, consistent with section 1194(e) of the Act, for
initial price applicability year 2028.
Comment: In the draft guidance for initial price applicability year 2028, CMS requested input
on the possibility and feasibility of considering health care services payable under Medicare Part
A or Part B as potential therapeutic alternatives to the selected drug for future rulemaking. One
commenter supported the possibility of considering nonpharmacologic therapeutic alternatives
that are included in clinical guidelines and another commenter supported the approach but
advised CMS to consider ways to ensure that a comparison between a health service and a drug
is fair and appropriate. Some commenters opposed the use of health services as a potential
therapeutic alternative. Among these commenters, one cautioned that expanding comparisons to
including health services is not appropriate because such services do not reflect the risk,
development cost, or patient impact of biopharmaceutical innovation; another commenter noted
that comparing a drug to a health service is difficult because they are reimbursed using different
methodologies; and a couple of commenters indicated that distinguishing between the impact of
drugs and services would be difficult because health services may act as a complementary
therapy to drugs or are part of a sequential order of treatments, such as in oncology (e.g., a health
care service is considered a first or second line treatment, followed by a drug as a third line
treatment). A few commenters indicated that CMS should provide a more detailed policy
approach that includes which Part A and Part B services would be considered as therapeutic
alternatives.
Response: CMS appreciates the feedback provided on this comment solicitation and may
consider commenter feedback on using health care services as therapeutic alternatives for future
rulemaking. CMS reiterates that for initial price applicability year 2028, only drugs or biological
products payable under Part B and/or covered under Part D will be considered therapeutic
alternatives to a selected drug. As stated in section 60.3.1 of this final guidance, at this time,
CMS believes that pharmaceutical therapeutic alternatives will be the most analogous
alternatives to the selected drug when considering treatment effect and price differentials.

88

Comment: A few commenters requested that CMS prioritize clinical appropriateness when
determining the therapeutic alternative(s) to a selected drug. A few commenters requested greater
transparency into the methodology for identifying a therapeutic alternative and the evidence used
for such identification. One commenter asked that CMS adopt a specific definition for “clinically
comparable” and one commenter asked CMS to define “clinical benefit” to specifically prioritize
evaluations around endpoints, patient reported outcomes, patient experience data, and patient
preferences. One commenter suggested that therapeutic alternatives should have comparable
real-world patient use to the selected drug. One commenter urged CMS to limit therapeutic
alternatives to selected drugs that treat HIV to antiretrovirals, account for dosing requirements,
and account for last-line antiretrovirals with no therapeutic alternative. One commenter
cautioned that the use of claims to identify utilization and spend for oncology drugs lacks
specificity and may introduce a large margin of error but did not suggest an alternate data source.
One commenter asked that CMS revert to using the “most” clinically comparable therapeutic
alternative(s) as was described in the revised guidance for initial price applicability year 2026.
One commenter stated that therapeutic alternatives should be considered at the time of approval
rather than the time of negotiation to credit innovation, particularly first-in-class drugs.
Response: CMS appreciates commenters’ feedback regarding the selection of a therapeutic
alternative(s) for a selected drug. As indicated in CMS’ response on page 91 of the final guidance
for initial price applicability year 2027, CMS believes the framework described in this final
guidance will allow CMS to identify appropriate therapeutic alternative(s) for the indications of
current and future selected drugs, if such alternatives exist, including those used in cancer and
HIV treatment. Consistent with the response provided on page 94 of the final guidance for initial
price applicability year 2027 and as described in section 60.3.1 of this final guidance, CMS will
identify the therapeutic alternative(s) for the indication of the selected drug by using data
submitted by the Primary Manufacturer and the public, prescribing information approved by the
FDA, drug classification systems commonly used in the public and private sector for formulary
development, major drug compendia, widely accepted clinical guidelines, evidence identified
through the CMS-led literature review, published drug or drug class reviews, peer-reviewed
studies, and Medicare claims or other data sets. CMS believes that the current framework
provides sufficient detail on how CMS will determine therapeutic alternatives to a selected drug
and notes that both the Primary Manufacturer and other interested parties are able to provide
input on therapeutic alternatives through the Drug Price Negotiation ICR. CMS also provides the
option for a Primary Manufacturer to meet with CMS after the Drug Price Negotiation ICR
information is submitted but before CMS provides the initial offer, which serves an opportunity
for the Primary Manufacturer to provide additional context or information on possible
therapeutic alternatives. Additionally, CMS will evaluate therapeutic alternative(s) for the
indications of a selected drug, as described in this final guidance section 60.3.1, as of the time
the section 1194(e)(2) data is submitted, which CMS believes is consistent with section 1194(e)
of the Act. This also aligns with CMS’ approach to reviewing the extent to which a selected drug
addresses an unmet medical need, the extent to which a selected drug represents a therapeutic
advance, manufacturer-submitted data, and other considerations related to the section 1194(e)
negotiation factors. As such, CMS does not think it is necessary to adopt definitions for
“clinically comparable” and “clinical benefit”.

89
Comment: One commenter stated that defining an indication as condition or disease state for the
purpose of determining a therapeutic alternative is inconsistent with statute, noting that the IRA
uses the word “indication” twice, first in reference to orphan drug indications in section
1192(e)(3)(A) and then in reference to renegotiation in section 1194(f)(2)(A) of the Act. This
commenter also stated that defining an indication as a condition or disease state for the purpose
of determining a therapeutic alternative is inconsistent with other portions of guidance, including
identifying FDA-approved indications of the selected drug and in the context of what factors
CMS will consider when identifying therapeutic alternatives.
Response: CMS appreciates this commenters’ feedback. CMS notes that title XI of Act
specifically references section 526 of the FD&C Act when directing CMS to provide an
exclusion for certain orphan drugs with an “approved indication” in section 1192(e)(3)(A) of the
Act but does not do so in section 1194(f)(2)(A) of the Act when discussing renegotiation. CMS
similarly differentiates the use of the term “FDA-approved indication” and “indication” to clarify
when CMS is specifically referring to information included in drug labeling per 21 C.F.R. §
201.57(c)(2) or other applicable FDA regulations and when CMS is referring to the more
common use of the word “indication” as the condition or disease state for which the selected
drug is used. Further, the term “indication” as defined in section 60.3.1 and section 130.1.3 of
this final guidance provides CMS with the ability to consider relevant clinical evidence for the
selected drug, for example, related to off-label use.
Comment: Some commenters requested that clinicians, manufacturers, and patients be involved
in the selection of the therapeutic alternative(s), and the initial offer more broadly, for a selected
drug to ensure patient preferences and experiences are included and to leverage the expertise of
practicing clinicians and manufacturers. A few commenters requested that CMS publish the
potential therapeutic alternatives for a selected drug when the selected drugs are announced.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their input. CMS notes that statute does not
require publication of potential therapeutic alternatives. However, as in past cycles of
negotiation, CMS is committed to gathering and incorporating input from patients, clinicians,
and other interested parties to inform negotiation. Consistent with CMS’ response on page 92 of
the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027, CMS encourages all interested parties,
including but not limited to clinicians, patients, caregivers, manufacturers, and researchers, to
provide information on the selection of a therapeutic alternative(s) through the Drug Price
Negotiation ICR for selected drugs for negotiation and renegotiation. CMS also encourages
members of the public, including manufacturers, Medicare beneficiaries, researchers, clinicians,
caregivers, and other interested parties to provide input through the public engagement events
described in section 60.4 of this final guidance. Additionally, CMS sets forth negotiation process
policies in section 60.4 of this final guidance, including the opportunity for the Primary
Manufacturer to meet with CMS prior to sending the initial offer. This initial meeting, as well as
the negotiation process including offer and counteroffer exchanges and negotiation meetings,
provide Primary Manufacturers with additional opportunities to discuss the therapeutic
alternative(s) with CMS.
Comment: CMS solicited comments on alternative approaches to establishing a starting point
for developing the initial offer. Many commenters recommended that CMS use the ceiling as the

90
starting point for all or a subset of selected drugs; for example, drugs that provide a therapeutic
advance, fill an unmet medical need, or otherwise demonstrated significant patient benefit; small
molecule drugs; and HIV drugs. Many commenters opposed using the unit cost of production
and distribution or other section 1194(e)(1) factors to establish the starting point; among these
commenters, some stated doing so would stifle innovation and does not reflect value to patients.
A few commenters opposed the use of a range of therapeutic alternative prices to establish a
starting point and some commenters opposed the use of a domestic reference price to establish a
starting point; one commenter also opposed the use of an international reference price. One
commenter suggested that CMS weigh indications relative to patient utilization data. A few
commenters suggested alternative approaches, including using a “Fair Market Price calculation,”
using a cost-effectiveness approach, or weighing biosimilars more when determining the starting
point than Medicare utilization reflects to account for delays in formulary uptake. A few
commenters supported continuing CMS’ existing approach to determining a starting point. One
commenter opposed using the price of a therapeutic alternative to determine the starting point.
Response: CMS thanks commenters for their feedback on this comment solicitation. Consistent
with CMS’ response on page 54 of the revised guidance for initial price applicability year 2026,
CMS notes that some of the proposed alternatives for determining a starting point would limit
CMS’ ability to consider the benefit provided by the selected drug relative to its therapeutic
alternative(s). Suggestions to use a starting point based on specific section 1194(e)(2) factors
could also limit CMS’ ability to adjust the starting point when developing the initial offer to
incorporate these factors. Upon consideration of these comments, CMS declines to adopt these
alternative approaches to establishing a starting point for developing the initial offer to preserve
agency flexibility in making adjustments to the price based on section 1194(e) factors.
CMS will maintain the overall approach in this final guidance to determining a starting point
consistent with initial price applicability year 2027 and has added that CMS will consider the
WAC of a therapeutic alternative for both drugs covered under Part D and drugs payable under
Part B. This allows CMS to account for certain circumstances where other prices are misaligned
with the WAC set by the manufacturer.
Comment: Some commenters opposed the removal of MDP and/or CGDP payments from Total
Gross Covered Drug Cost (TGCDC) when determining the Net Part D Plan Payment and
Beneficiary Liability during the process of determining a starting point for developing the initial
offer. A couple of commenters also opposed using the MFP as the starting point for initial offer
development in cases where the therapeutic alternative(s) is itself a selected drug where it is
lower than the Net Part D Plan Payment and Beneficiary Liability or ASP, with one of these
commenters stating that there is no statutory basis for doing so.
Response: CMS thanks commenters for their feedback. Consistent with CMS’ response on page
97 of the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027 and as discussed in section 60.3.2
of this final guidance, removing MDP and/or CGDP payments and DIR from TGCDC to
determine the Net Part D Plan Payment and Beneficiary Liability of the therapeutic alternative(s)
appropriately accounts for the price paid by the plan and the beneficiary for therapeutic
alternative(s) to determine a starting point, which can then be adjusted based on the negotiation
factors described in section 1194(e) of the Act. Further, removing MDP and/or CGDP payments

91
is appropriate because under the Manufacturer Discount Program, a selected drug during its price
applicability period is not an applicable drug for which manufacturer discounts are required.
Similarly, the policy to use the MFP as the starting point in cases where the therapeutic
alternative was itself a selected drug from initial price applicability year 2026 or 2027 and the
MFP is lower than the Net Part D Payment and Beneficiary Liability is aligned with the statutory
directive in section 1194(e)(2)(A) of the Act to consider the costs of therapeutic alternatives,
which may include selected drugs with an agreed-upon MFP. The negotiation process outlined in
sections 60.3 and 60.4 of this final guidance results in an MFP for a selected drug that reflects
each selected drug’s circumstances and is based on the negotiation factors that CMS is required
to consider under section 1194(e) of the Act, regardless of whether the starting point is another
selected drug’s MFP (in cases where there is one therapeutic alternative) or includes an MFP (in
cases where there are multiple therapeutic alternatives and only one or some of the therapeutic
alternatives were selected drugs).
Comment: One commenter urged CMS to establish an MFP at the ceiling for selected drugs that
provide a therapeutic advance and/or treat an unmet medical need. The commenter suggested
that if a selected drug does not meet at least one of these criteria, CMS should consider
comparative effectiveness evidence to determine whether the selected drug provides benefit
compared to therapeutic alternatives.
Response: Consistent with CMS’ response on page 53 of the revised guidance for initial price
applicability year 2026, CMS notes that section 1194(b)(1) of the Act instructs CMS to develop
and use a consistent methodology and process for negotiations that aims to achieve agreement on
the lowest MFP for each selected drug and in doing so, to consider the nine factors described in
sections 1194(e)(1) and 1194(e)(2) of the Act. Offering the ceiling without a more thorough
review of those statutory factors, including manufacturer-submitted data, may not achieve that
objective and is inconsistent with the statutory directive.
Comment: One commenter asked CMS to clarify how, whether quantitatively or qualitatively,
the cost of a therapeutic alternative will impact the assessment of the extent to which a selected
drug provides a therapeutic advance.
Response: CMS appreciates this commenters’ request for clarification. As described in section
60.3.3 of this final guidance, CMS uses a qualitative approach to develop the initial offer,
including for the consideration of the extent to which a selected drug represents a therapeutic
advance.
Comment: CMS requested input on whether certain section 1194(e) factors should be
emphasized over others when adjusting the starting point to determine the preliminary price.
Many commenters supported emphasizing section 1194(e)(2) factors when developing the initial
offer, stating that CMS should prioritize factors that are important to patient health and
outcomes, as well as societal impact and other non-clinical benefits of a selected drug. A couple
of commenters recommended that CMS apply an upward adjustment to the starting point for
pending and approved patent applications, exclusivities, and pending or approved marketing
applications as these indicate clinical benefit, innovation, manufacturer investment, and a lack of

92
therapeutic alternatives. A couple of commenters cautioned against applying a downward
adjustment based on prior Federal financial support as this may discourage future innovation.
One commenter asked that section 1194(e)(1) factors only be considered when a selected drug
provides fewer benefits than its therapeutic alternative(s). One commenter supported the existing
methodology and cautioned against using a formulaic approach; one commenter suggested
applying an upward adjustment for a selected drug that advances the standard of care. One
commenter opposed weighting section 1194(e) factors, stating that doing so is not in statute. One
commenter stated that giving greater weight to some section 1194(e) factors over others without
providing specific information on which factors would be given greater weight undermines
transparency and due process.
Response: CMS appreciates commenters’ feedback. After consideration of the comments
received regarding whether CMS should place greater emphasis on certain section 1194(e)
factors, CMS declines to change its methodology and process for negotiation in initial price
applicability year 2028. Section 1196(a)(4) of the Act provides the Secretary with the authority to
establish a negotiation and renegotiation process in accordance with section 1194 of the Act. This
section directs the Secretary to establish a consistent methodology and process for negotiation
(section 1194(b)(1) of the Act) and to consider the section 1194(e) factors as the basis for
determining the initial offer and counteroffers (section 1194(e) of the Act) but does not dictate
the manner in which those factors must be considered. As such, CMS believes that flexibility in
determining which section 1194(e) factors to emphasize over others will depend on the unique
considerations related to each selected drug.
Comment: Some commenters requested more information on how section 1194(e) factors are
weighted or otherwise used to adjust the starting point to determine the initial offer. Among these
commenters, one requested more information on how health economic outcomes research is
considered, one requested that CMS confirm that section 1194(e)(1) data will not be used to
reduce prices, and a few specifically requested more clarity on how patents and exclusivities will
be considered. Similarly, a few commenters asked CMS to provide more information on the
methodology used to develop the initial offer and the process of negotiating the MFP. One
commenter stated that the methodology described in draft guidance for initial price applicability
year 2028 could not be standardized. One commenter suggested that CMS use a costeffectiveness threshold to develop the initial offer. A few commenters suggested that CMS
implement a framework or rubric to provide transparency and ensure consistency in the
methodology used to review selected drugs.
Some commenters urged CMS to provide more detailed information to Primary Manufacturers
and other interested parties on the framework, data, calculations, and other information so that a
manufacturer can provide an informed counteroffer and patients and other stakeholders have
more transparency into how the information they provide is used in the development of the initial
offer. Suggestions of what CMS should share publicly included how patient input is used in the
negotiation process, what types of evidence inform the assessment of unmet medical need and
therapeutic advance, any decision-making framework CMS uses, and details of calculations
related to the initial offer. A few commenters asked that CMS detail similar information in the
MFP explanations. Some commenters urged CMS to provide more transparency on the types of
evidence that would be prioritized during initial offer development, including during the

93
determination of therapeutic alternatives, adjusting the starting point, and determining the extent
to which a selected drug fulfills an unmet medical need or represents a therapeutic advance. A
few commenters supported CMS’ consideration of real-world evidence in the development of the
initial offer.
Response: CMS appreciates commenters’ feedback and recognizes the importance of balancing
transparency and confidentiality in the negotiation process. Consistent with CMS’ response on
page 99 of the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027, CMS believes it is
important to maintain flexibility when considering how each negotiation factor contributes to the
initial offer and subsequent offers and counteroffers, as applicable, which may be impacted by
the unique characteristics of each selected drug, the populations each selected drug is intended to
treat, and information that may emerge from meaningful discussions with manufacturers,
patients, and patient representatives.
Considerations for how evidence will be prioritized are described in section 50.2 of this final
guidance. This final guidance also describes the approach CMS will use to identify indications
for a selected drug, identify a therapeutic alternative(s) for such indications, determine a starting
point for the initial offer, and the factors CMS will consider when adjusting the starting point in
section 60.3 of this final guidance. All applicable negotiation factors will be considered in
totality for each selected drug. CMS directs interested parties to the comment summaries and
responses for section 60.6 of this final guidance for a response to the comments received on the
MFP explanations.
Comment: Some commenters requested that CMS consider factors not mentioned in the draft
guidance for initial price applicability year 2028, including equity, the impact of a selected drug
on the health system, the societal and public health value of a selected drug, the value of
prevention, cost of care outcomes, the future value of a selected drug, adherence, and a
manufacturer’s global pricing strategy. A few commenters encouraged CMS to consider the full
range of patient outcomes including but not limited to patient preferences, caregiver burden, and
quality of life. One commenter supported CMS’ inclusion of patient and caregiver input.
Response: CMS thanks commenters for their suggestions. Consistent with the response provided
on pages 87 and 102 of the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027, CMS agrees
that considerations related to the patient and caregiver experience are important and relevant for
CMS’ consideration of the section 1194(e)(2) factors. Outcomes such as changes to productivity,
independence, and quality of life will be considered to the extent that these outcomes correspond
with a direct impact on individuals taking the drug and are permitted in accordance with section
1194(e)(2) of the Act. In addition to patient and caregiver experience, CMS outlines in section
60.3.3.1 of this final guidance a variety of outcomes that CMS may consider when developing
the initial offer. CMS encourages patients and other interested parties to submit their perspective
on outcomes that CMS should consider for each selected drug through the Drug Price
Negotiation ICR submission and in the public engagement events, per section 60.4 of this final
guidance.
Comment: Some commenters suggested changes to the definition of unmet medical need,
including expanding the definition to include non-clinical benefits such as patient and caregiver

94
mental and social wellbeing, patient and caregiver quality of life, improvement in health
outcomes, sustainable costs for patients, value to society, and meeting public health needs;
expanding the definition to account for subpopulations with disparate access or outcomes;
expanding the definition to account for adherence and preventing resistance; accounting for
characteristics, such as alternative dosing regimens, route of administration, reduction of side
effects, shorter treatment periods, and diagnostic strategies.
One commenter recommended that CMS consider unmet medical need from initial approval of
the selected drug through the time of assessment. One commenter requested that CMS align
FDA's definition of unmet medical need with orphan and pediatric exclusivities codified in other
federal statutes (the commenter did not suggest specific statutes). One commenter stated that
CMS should review unmet medical needs specifically within the scope of FDA prescribing
information.
Response: CMS appreciates commenters’ feedback. Consistent with CMS’ response on pages
100-101 of the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027, CMS will consider any
updates concerning unmet medical need that may be issued by FDA. The definition of unmet
medical need included in section 60.3.3.1 of this final guidance was developed after
consideration of public comments submitted for the initial price applicability year 2026 revised
guidance and with reference to section 1194(e)(2)(D) of the Act and FDA’s “Guidance for
Industry Expedited Programs for Serious Conditions – Drugs and Biologics.” Many of the
considerations commenters raised, such as patient quality of life, are considered as part of other
factors listed at section 1194(e)(2) of the Act. CMS will evaluate the extent to which a selected
drug addresses an unmet medical need as of the time the section 1194(e)(2) data is submitted,
which aligns with CMS’ approach to identifying indications for a selected drug, reviewing
manufacturer costs and data, selecting a therapeutic alternative(s), and considering other
negotiation factors.
Comment: One commenter stated that the definition of “therapeutic advance” should include
additional detail such as whether the definition includes both safety and efficacy of a drug. A
couple of commenters recommended that the definition of therapeutic advance include factors
such as how the drug impacts patient experience, mode of administration, adherence, and quality
of life; whether the drug significantly impacts a socially or economically vulnerable population;
whether the drug provides improvements in the symptoms or health outcomes associated with a
disease (e.g., reduction of symptoms, ability to perform daily functions); and whether the drug
offers improvement on a validated clinical outcome or a validated clinical measure.
Response: CMS thanks commenters for their input on the definition of therapeutic advance.
CMS will determine whether a selected drug represents a therapeutic advance by examining
improvements in outcomes for the selected drug compared to its therapeutic alternative(s) as
described in section 60.3.3.1 of this final guidance. Many of the other factors mentioned by
commenters are considered during the development of the initial offer as outlined in sections
50.2 and 60.3.3 of this final guidance.

95
Negotiation Process (Section 60.4)
Comment: One commenter stated that CMS’ decisions on the format and content of meetings,
including meeting materials, meeting length, and meeting attendance, impose arbitrary
limitations on manufacturers in the negotiation process. A couple of commenters stated that
limiting negotiation meetings to a maximum of three meetings is restrictive, and one commenter
recommended that CMS allow for more exchanges throughout the negotiation period. One
commenter recommended CMS continue to hold at least three negotiation meetings. Another
commenter indicated their support for an open and transparent dialogue with CMS earlier in the
negotiation process that includes discussion of therapeutic alternatives.
Response: CMS recognizes commenters’ interest in having meetings throughout the negotiation
period. Consistent with CMS’ response on pages 122-123 of the final guidance for initial price
applicability year 2027, CMS will continue to hold one optional meeting with the Primary
Manufacturer of each selected drug prior to CMS’ initial offer to allow the Primary Manufacturer
to provide context for and any new information about the section 1194(e) data submission as
CMS reviews the submitted data and develops its initial offer for initial price applicability year
2028. Additionally, as described in section 60.4.2 of this final guidance, the first negotiation
meeting may occur after CMS issues the initial offer and prior to the deadline for the Primary
Manufacturer’s response to CMS’ initial offer, and up to two additional negotiation meetings, if
applicable, may occur after the deadline for the Primary Manufacturer’s response. This will
enable CMS and Primary Manufacturers to engage in negotiation discussions at different
intervals throughout the negotiation period and totals up to four optional meetings per selected
drug. CMS believes that the duration, format, and number of the negotiation meetings continue
to be sufficient for engagement and that additional meetings during the negotiation period are not
feasible due to time constraints.
Additionally, consistent with CMS’ response on page 123 of the final guidance for initial price
applicability year 2027 and as described in section 60.4.5 of this final guidance, CMS is offering
an additional price exchange functionality in which CMS and Primary Manufacturers can initiate
additional, written offers and counteroffers via the CMS HPMS during the period between CMS’
rejection of the Primary Manufacturer’s statutory written counteroffer, if applicable, and the
parties reaching an agreement on MFP, or by September 18, 2026, whichever is earlier. CMS
believes this functionality will provide additional opportunities for exchanges between CMS and
Primary Manufacturers throughout the negotiation period.
Comment: A couple of commenters asked that CMS’ concise justification of its initial offer be
meaningful and explain how CMS arrived at the offer. A couple of commenters recommended
CMS provide manufacturers with the opportunity to comment on CMS’ justification. One
commenter suggested manufacturers should be able to submit additional data or other
information to support their response to an offer. Another commenter stated that without a
meaningful justification from CMS in the initial offer, manufacturers cannot provide a
meaningful justification in a statutory written counteroffer. A few commenters suggested that the
justification should detail specific information, such as the sources CMS referenced, section
1194(e) data considered and how they were weighted, therapeutic alternatives considered,
interested parties consulted, and benefits and impacts of the drugs considered.

96

Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their feedback. Consistent with CMS’ response on
page 107 of the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027, section 1194(b)(2)(B) of
the Act directs CMS to provide a concise justification to the Primary Manufacturer when the
initial offer is made. CMS will include information regarding the range of evidence and other
information submitted pursuant to section 1194(e) of the Act that CMS found compelling in
developing its initial offer, which includes the identification of therapeutic alternatives. Because
this information will be shared with the Primary Manufacturer, CMS believes the concise
justification will be meaningful and will provide the Primary Manufacturer with information to
build a statutory written counteroffer if the Primary Manufacturer decides to reject the initial
offer. While any statutory written counteroffer should respond to the justification provided in
CMS’ written initial offer, a Primary Manufacturer is not limited by the information provided in
CMS’ written initial offer when developing a statutory written counteroffer. As described in
section 60.4.3 of this final guidance, a Primary Manufacturer making a statutory written
counteroffer should provide a justification for such counteroffer based on the data described in
section 50 of this final guidance.
As described in section 60.4.2 of this final guidance, CMS will offer to schedule an optional
negotiation meeting after CMS provides the initial offer to the Primary Manufacturer and before
the Primary Manufacturer’s statutory written counteroffer is due. The purpose of this meeting is
to allow both parties to begin discussion related to negotiating an MFP for the selected drug,
including with respect to CMS’ initial offer for the MFP. CMS anticipates that such discussion
might focus on CMS’ initial offer and the evidence CMS used to develop the initial offer;
nevertheless, as applicable, both CMS and the Primary Manufacturer could discuss other
potential offers or counteroffers during this meeting, including discussion of the Primary
Manufacturer’s forthcoming statutory written counteroffer, as applicable. CMS will not revise
the initial offer in this negotiation meeting. Consistent with the statutory framework, CMS
anticipates that any oral potential counteroffers discussed during this meeting might be provided
later in writing consistent with section 1194(b)(2)(C) of the Act. Accordingly, while CMS may
engage in discussion about an oral potential counteroffer, CMS does not intend to accept or reject
any such oral potential counteroffer in this first meeting and intends to respond to any later
statutory written counteroffer consistent with the agency’s obligations to respond in writing
under section 1194(b)(2)(D) of the Act. Additional details around this first optional negotiation
meeting can be found in section 60.4.2 of this final guidance.
Comment: One commenter stated that CMS should provide a confidential report to
manufacturers alongside the initial offer and concise justification. This confidential report would
include information on how CMS evaluated a selected drug based on section 1194(e)(2) data
submitted by other interested parties and allow manufacturers to use this information in
developing a statutory written counteroffer.
Response: Consistent with CMS’ response on page 106 of the final guidance for initial price
applicability year 2027, CMS understands that Primary Manufacturers may benefit from
awareness of section 1194(e)(2) data submitted by other interested parties during the negotiation
period. CMS maintains in this final guidance that CMS will aim to share with the Primary
Manufacturer of a selected drug the section 1194(e)(2) data received from other interested parties

97
during the negotiation period when feasible. These data will be appropriately redacted and will
not include proprietary information, PHI / PII, or information that is protected from disclosure
under other applicable law. CMS does not plan on issuing a confidential report or other summary
document in addition to the agency’s provision of these redacted section 1194(e)(2) submissions.
If agreement on an MFP is reached during the negotiation period, CMS will issue the MFP
explanation no later than March 1, 2027. As part of this MFP explanation, CMS will share
redacted information regarding the section 1194(e) data received, exchange of offers and
counteroffers, and the negotiation meetings, if applicable. This redacted information will not
contain any proprietary data, as described in section 40.2.1 of this final guidance, PHI / PII, or
other information that is protected from disclosure under other applicable law. However, as
described in section 40.2.1 of this final guidance, if a Primary Manufacturer chooses to disclose
any material that is made public that CMS has previously deemed to be proprietary information
of that Primary Manufacturer, CMS will no longer consider that material proprietary and will not
redact it in the MFP explanation.
Comment: A couple of commenters suggested that CMS provide justifications for all offer and
counteroffer responses and not just initial offers. One commenter recommended CMS update its
latest offer after each negotiation meeting.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their feedback. Section 1194(b)(2)(D) of the Act
requires that CMS provide the Primary Manufacturer with a written response to the Primary
Manufacturer’s statutory written counteroffer. Consistent with our response on page 122 of final
guidance for initial price applicability year 2027, CMS believes that if CMS declines the Primary
Manufacturer’s statutory written counteroffer and conducts a subsequent negotiation meeting
with the Primary Manufacturer, this meeting will provide an opportunity for CMS to explain its
rationale for not accepting the manufacturer’s statutory written counteroffer, and this meeting or
any subsequent meeting would provide further opportunities for both parties to discuss their
rationales for making and responding to offers and counteroffers. Additionally, as described in
section 60.4.5 of this final guidance, CMS is offering additional price exchange opportunities in
which CMS and Primary Manufacturers can initiate additional, written offers and counteroffers
via the CMS HPMS during the period between CMS’ rejection of the Primary Manufacturer’s
statutory written counteroffer, if applicable, and the parties reaching an agreement on MFP, or by
September 18, 2026, whichever is earlier. CMS believes that if a Primary Manufacturer or CMS
makes an offer or counteroffer via the additional price exchange functionality, the negotiation
meetings will provide an opportunity for both parties to discuss their justifications for the offer
or counteroffer and rationale for determinations with respect to the offer or counteroffer. The
additional price exchange functionality in the CMS HPMS will include an optional text field to
enable either party to include additional contextual information for the offer or counteroffer.
Only one offer or counteroffer per selected drug may be active at a time in the CMS HPMS as
part of the additional price exchange functionality. An offering/counteroffering party may revise
its offer/counteroffer in the period before the other party accepts or rejects it, but not afterwards,
which has the effect of nullifying the previously submitted offer or counteroffer before it has
been accepted or rejected. Parties do not need to alternate making offers and counteroffers.
Comment: One commenter suggested CMS broadly allow a manufacturer to supplement a
timely submission of 1194(e) data if new information of relevance to the negotiation process

98
becomes available after the submission deadline or otherwise for good cause shown. Another
commenter suggested CMS should allow manufacturers to submit comparative effectiveness data
after the submission deadline, such as when CMS has identified therapeutic alternatives.
Response: CMS thanks the commenters for their input. Pursuant to sections 1194(b)(2)(A) and
1193(a)(4)(B) of the Act, Primary Manufacturers must submit the manufacturer-specific data
described in sections 1193(a)(4)(A) and 1194(e) of the Act to CMS by March 1, 2026 for initial
price applicability year 2028. Consistent with CMS’ response on page 104 of the final guidance
for initial price applicability year 2027, CMS will use data submitted by the Primary
Manufacturer and other interested parties when developing the initial offer for a selected drug
along with CMS analyses and assessments of evidence as described in section 60.3 of this final
guidance. Due to the statutory timeline of the negotiation period, including the requirement
under section 1194(b)(2)(B) of the Act for CMS to issue an initial offer by June 1, 2026, it is not
feasible to extend the timeframe for the submission of information under section 1194(e)(2) of
the Act. CMS is abiding by the statutory deadlines in this final guidance.
As described in section 60.4.1 of this final guidance, interested parties will have several
opportunities to provide additional section 1194(e)(2) information after the March 1, 2026
deadline.
First, CMS will invite the Primary Manufacturer of each selected drug to a meeting after the
March 1, 2026 deadline and before CMS makes an initial offer to allow the manufacturer an
opportunity to present its section 1194(e) data submission and share its perspective. These
meetings will occur in Spring 2026. Primary Manufacturers may bring materials to facilitate
discussion, and CMS may request any materials presented in the meeting afterwards. Primary
Manufacturers are limited to sharing 50 pages (or a combination of pages, slides, and/or charts
totaling 50 pages) of material to focus the discussion on issues that can reasonably be discussed
within the scope of the meeting, anticipating that these materials may contain cross-references to
other material, particularly other material already submitted to CMS. This material is meant to
provide context on the Primary Manufacturer’s 1194(e) submission and may also be used to
share any new information regarding the section 1194(e)(2) data that has been identified
following the March 1, 2026 data submission.
Second, CMS will host public engagement events to gather patient-focused feedback on the
selected drugs as well as feedback from the larger community of interested stakeholders. CMS
will host patient-focused roundtable events for patients, patient advocacy organizations, and
caregivers. Selected participants for the roundtables will be invited to share feedback on patient
experiences with the conditions or diseases treated by the selected drugs, as well as with the
selected drugs and therapeutic alternatives to the selected drugs, and other information. CMS
will also host a town hall meeting for clinicians and other interested parties, such as researchers,
manufacturers, and members of the public. Selected speakers for the town hall meeting will be
invited to share additional input on therapeutic alternatives and other section 1194(e)(2) data
regarding selected drugs. Interested parties may also use these events to share new information
regarding the section 1194(e)(2) factors that has been identified since the March 1, 2026
deadline. These events will occur in Spring 2026 after the section 1194(e) data submission

99
deadline, which will give patients and other interested parties additional time to prepare their
input. Additional information about these events will be shared in the future.
Primary Manufacturers are required to provide information on the non-FAMP and information
required to carry out negotiations (including manufacturer-specific data described in section
1194(e)(1) of the Act) by March 1, 2026 for initial price applicability year 2028. CMS expects
Primary Manufacturers to submit information that is complete and accurate by this deadline. As
noted above, while Primary Manufacturers may share new information on section 1194(e)(2)
data during meetings before the initial offer, new manufacturer-specific data (described in section
1194(e)(1) of the Act) will not be considered; rather, any information shared during these
meetings and materials shared afterwards should only contextualize the Primary Manufacturer’s
March 1, 2026 submission of manufacturer-specific data.
As described in section 50.1 of this final guidance, the Primary Manufacturer has an ongoing
obligation to timely report certain updates to data submissions required of Primary
Manufacturers under sections 1193(a)(4)(A) and 1194(e)(1) of the Act and previously submitted
to CMS through the initial response to the Negotiation Data Elements ICR Form. 39 Primary
Manufacturers must submit updates to the Primary Manufacturer’s data submitted under sections
1193(a)(4)(A) and 1194(e)(1) to CMS if the data was restated due to requirements of the
government entity that initially receives and oversees processing of such data.

Comment: Many commenters expressed appreciation for CMS’ efforts to improve the public

drugs selected for renegotiation, if applicable. CMS believes the private, discussion-based
roundtable events—facilitated by a moderator—elicited valuable patient-focused input from

this approach will continue to foster meaningful engagement and input. Additionally, CMS

IRARebateandNegotiation@cms.hhs.gov.

into how public engagement event are selected. Finally, one commenter expressed concern that

Response: CMS appreciates these commenters sharing their concerns but disagrees with
commenters that the roundtable events did not provide opportunities for meaningful engagement.
For initial price applicability year 2027, CMS established a discussion-based format for patientfocused roundtable events. CMS also engaged a moderator to facilitate discussion among
participants during roundtable events and to facilitate follow-up questions from CMS during the
town hall meeting. CMS engaged a moderator rather than having CMS staff facilitate discussions
during public engagement events to mitigate the risk of bias. CMS implemented these changes
based on commenter feedback received on draft guidance for initial price applicability year 2027.

60.4.1 of this final guidance, CMS will host up to 15 patient-focused roundtable events, which
will be open to patients, patient advocacy organizations, and caregivers and will allow for

CMS also will continue to engage a moderator to facilitate discussions for the roundtable events
and CMS will have the opportunity to ask follow-up questions of participants during the town
hall meeting. Additionally, CMS appreciates that commenters want CMS to post redacted
transcripts more quickly. However, the process CMS uses to ensure that event transcripts are
complete and accurate and that they de-identify all health information as required by the Health
Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) Privacy Rule 41 is thorough and takes
time. Therefore, CMS will post redacted transcripts as soon as practicable after all public
engagement events have concluded. Further, as with public engagement events held for initial
price applicability year 2027, CMS will select speakers through an intentional process—rather
than random selection—to help ensure diverse representation of viewpoints. Finally, with regards
to participation among health care providers, CMS expressly included practicing clinicians in the
town hall meeting for initial price applicability year 2027 and will continue to encourage their
participation in the town hall meeting for initial price applicability year 2028.

Application of the MFP Across Dosage Forms and Strengths (Section 60.5)
Comment: A few commenters expressed concerns or opposition regarding the application of the
MFP across dosage forms and strengths. One commenter stated that section 60 of the draft
guidance for initial price applicability year 2028 purports to require Primary Manufacturers to
offer the MFP for every package size or type of a product dosage form and strength and that such
a requirement is not consistent with statute as the statute requires only that the manufacturer offer
the MFP across different dosage forms and strengths of a selected drug and not across every
formulation, package size, or configuration ever derived from the original active ingredient. A
couple of the commenters stated that CMS’ application of a single MFP across all formulations
with the same active ingredient, regardless of regulatory pathway, instead of applying a single
MFP only across the dosage forms and strengths within the selected product’s NDA / BLA
conflicts with FDA standards which could create disincentives for label expansion, lifecycle
development, investment in therapies serving underserved populations, or even force market exit
of products by manufacturers. The commenter suggested that CMS only apply the MFP across
dosage forms and strengths within the selected product’s NDA / BLA. One commenter suggested
for CMS to negotiate and apply an MFP for a selected drug payable under Part B only with
respect to Part B, and that CMS should negotiate and apply an MFP for a selected drug covered
under Part D only with respect to Part D, following the IRA’s statutory language and removing a
significant amount of confusion and complexity that would be created by attempting to develop
and apply a single MFP to both Part B and Part D. One of the commenters suggested that if
pricing varies by indication, CMS should clarify how those prices will be applied at the point of
sale, especially when utilization management tools cannot verify diagnosis, to ensure accurate
MFP application. This commenter also requested that CMS clarify how the MFP will apply to
MA enrollees for a Part B drug, particularly for drugs with multiple indications or indication‐
specific pricing.
Response: Consistent with CMS’ response on page 124 of the final guidance for initial price
applicability year 2027, section 1192(d)(3)(B) of the Act directs CMS to “use data that is
aggregated across dosage forms and strengths of the drug, including new formulations of the
drug, such as an extended-release formulation, and not based on the specific formulation or
package size or package type of the drug” for purposes of determining whether a qualifying
single source drug is a negotiation-eligible drug. In addition, section 1194(e)(1)(D) of the Act
instructs CMS, for purposes of the negotiation process, to consider, among other information,
“applications and approvals under section 505(c) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act or
section 351(a) of the Public Health Service Act,” in the plural, for the “drug,” in the singular.
Similarly, section 1196(a)(2) of the Act directs CMS to establish procedures “to compute and
apply the maximum fair price across different strengths and dosage forms of a selected drug and

108
not based on the specific formulation or package size or package type of such drug.” The
aggregation rules under sections 1192(d)(3)(B), 1194(e)(1)(D), and 1196(a)(2) of the Act require
a Primary Manufacturer of a selected drug that continues to participate in the Negotiation
Program and reaches agreement upon an MFP to provide access to the MFP for all dosage forms,
strengths, and package sizes of the selected drug included on the list of NDC-9s and NDC-11s
for the selected drug maintained on the CMS HPMS and published in accordance with sections
30.4 and 60.6 of this final guidance. A Primary Manufacturer may not selectively apply the MFP
to certain dosage forms and strengths or package sizes of the selected drug, nor may the MFP
vary based on indication of the selected drug. As stated in section 60.5 of this final guidance, an
MFP that is agreed upon, as described in section 60.4 of this final guidance, establishes one price
for the selected drug. In accordance with section 1196(a)(2) of the Act, CMS has the
administrative duty to establish procedures to compute and apply the MFP across different
dosage forms and strengths of the selected drug and not based on the specific formulation or
package size or package type of such drug. Regardless of whether a selected drug is payable
under Part B only, covered under Part D only, or is payable under Part B and covered under Part
D, the MFP will apply to all dosage forms and strengths of that selected drug. For the commenter
requesting information on how the MFP will apply to MA enrollees for a selected drug payable
under Part B, CMS intends to address Part B MFP effectuation in the future.
Publication of the MFP (Section 60.6)
Comment: A few commenters asked that CMS detail specific information in the explanations of
MFP. These elements include information on how therapeutic alternatives were selected, specific
data and evidence used, benefits and impacts considered, stakeholders consulted and how their
input was used, sources for information used in negotiation, and details on how information
influenced the MFP. Another commenter suggested CMS publish justifications for how MFPs are
determined. One commenter stated that a lack of transparency regarding how the public
engagement events and data submitted by the public are used in negotiations may deter the
public from participating in the events or from submitting data. The same commenter said the
explanations of the MFP for initial price applicability year 2026 largely restated information in
prior guidance rather than providing more detail on the negotiation process or how CMS used
submitted data. Some commenters requested CMS discuss in the MFP explanations how
stakeholder input was used in negotiations.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their suggestions to include specific information in
the MFP explanations. Consistent with our response on page 126 of the final guidance for initial
price applicability year 2027, as required under section 1195(a)(1) of the Act, CMS will publish
the explanation of the MFP for all selected drugs where there is an agreed-upon MFP for initial
price applicability year 2028 no later than March 1, 2027. The MFP explanation, as described in
section 60.6.1 of this final guidance, will include a narrative explanation of the negotiation
process that occurred with that manufacturer and redacted information regarding the section
1194(e) data received, exchange of offers and counteroffers, and the negotiation meetings, if
applicable, in alignment with the confidentiality policy described in section 40.2 of this final
guidance. CMS will also strive to share the section 1194(e)(2) data submitted by the public with
the Primary Manufacturer of a selected drug during the negotiation period. This data will be
redacted as per the confidentiality standards described in section 40.2 of this final guidance and

during negotiations.
