MFP-Eligible Individuals in 2026, 2027, and 2028 (Section 80)
Comment: One commenter recommended CMS require MA plans to ensure access to the MFP.
Another commenter stated that CMS should not broaden the scope of MFP-eligible individuals
to include individuals enrolled in MA plans.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their input. As CMS stated in section 80 of this
final guidance, for 2026, 2027, and 2028, in accordance with section 1191(c)(2)(A) of the Act,
the term “maximum fair price eligible individual” or “MFP-eligible individual” means, with
respect to a selected drug, the following: in the case such drug is dispensed to the individual at a
pharmacy, by a mail order service, or by another dispensing entity, an individual who is enrolled
in a prescription drug plan under Medicare Part D or an MA–PD plan under Medicare Part C
(including an Employer Group Waiver Plan), if Part D coverage is provided under such plan for
such selected drug. For 2028, in accordance with section 1191(c)(2)(B) of the Act, the term
“maximum fair price eligible individual” or “MFP-eligible individual” also means, with respect
to a selected drug, the following: in the case such drug is furnished or administered to the
individual by a hospital, physician, or other provider of services or supplier, an individual who is
enrolled under Medicare Part B or in an MA plan under Medicare Part C, if payment may be
made under Part B for such selected drug. For 2028, for drugs selected for initial price
applicability year 2028 or with a renegotiated MFP for initial price applicability year 2028, CMS
expects Primary Manufacturers to provide access to the MFP of a selected drug to hospitals,
physicians and other providers of services and suppliers with respect to a drug furnished or
administered to MFP-eligible individuals enrolled under Part B, including an individual who is
enrolled in a Medicare Advantage plan under Part C.

111
Comment Solicitation on Monitoring MA Plans’ Step Therapy Practices
Comment: Many commenters raised concerns about step therapy practices and recommended
CMS take action to ensure that there is appropriate oversight over MA plans so that enrollees do
not face undue barriers to selected drugs payable under Part B in initial price applicability year
2028. Some commenters stated opposition to MA plans’ use of step therapy for drugs payable
under Part B and recommended CMS prohibit MA plans from applying step therapy
requirements for selected drugs or all drugs payable under Part B. One commenter stated that
MA plans’ use of step therapy violates section 1852(a) of the Act because they permit MA plans
to impose restrictions that do not exist in Original Medicare. Some commenters cited studies to
support that MA plans’ use of step therapy for drugs payable under Part B has been linked to
significant burdens for physicians attempting to prescribe, and patients attempting to access,
clinically appropriate treatments. A couple of commenters recommended that if CMS continues
to allow MA plans to use step therapy, that CMS should develop policies to protect access to
drugs payable under Part B, including by implementing strong coverage determination and
appeals processes with short adjudication timelines. One of these commenters also recommended
CMS implement policies to maintain lengthy lookback periods to reflect complex therapy
intervals and protect stability in patient treatments, require that plan documents identify which
drugs are subject to step therapy, and prohibit mid-year step therapy additions.
Many commenters recommended that CMS monitor MA plans’ (and their contractors’)
implementation of the MFP effectuation process for selected drugs payable under Part B to
ensure enrollees can access medically necessary care. One commenter recommended CMS
leverage any lessons learned from selected drugs covered under Part D in initial price
applicability years 2026 and 2027 and issue policy to conduct rigorous formulary and coverage
policy review to assess instances in which MA plans impose more restrictive step therapy and
other utilization management practices for certain drugs payable under Part B compared to
another drug in the same class.
A few commenters stated that CMS can monitor MA plans’ use of step therapy practices under
existing program rules and stated that no additional requirements or clarifications are needed at
this time. A couple of commenters stated that step therapy is used to ensure appropriate use of
drug therapies and to prevent fraud, waste, and abuse. A couple of other commenters cited the
regulations at 42 C.F.R. § 422.136 to support their assertion that additional policy is not needed
related to MA plan’s step therapy practices and noted that CMS can monitor issues and conduct
audits related to step therapy. A few commenters stated that given the President’s directive to
reduce regulatory burdens, CMS should rely on existing processes unless and until there is an
indication that process changes may be needed. One of these commenters stated that increased
regulatory burdens acutely impact regional and not-for-profit organizations compared to forprofit national organizations and smaller health plans are less able to absorb administrative costs.
Another commenter stated that CMS should not place higher standards of review for selected
drugs.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their input related to the comment solicitation on
monitoring MA plans’ use of step therapy practices. As CMS stated in section 80 of this final
guidance, for 2028, in accordance with section 1191(c)(2)(B) of the Act, the term “maximum fair
price eligible individual” or “MFP-eligible individual” also means, with respect to a selected

112
drug, the following: in the case such drug is furnished or administered to the individual by a
hospital, physician, or other provider of services or supplier, an individual who is enrolled under
Medicare Part B or in a Medicare Advantage plan under Medicare Part C, if payment may be
made under Part B for such selected drug.
CMS anticipates that Medicare Advantage plan requirements under 42 C.F.R. Part 422 will apply
to selected drugs. CMS notes that 42 C.F.R. § 422.136 requires MA plans that implement a step
therapy program for Part B-covered drugs to: apply step therapy only to new administrations of
drugs payable under Part B, using at least a 365 day lookback period; establish policies and
procedures to educate and inform health care providers and enrollees concerning its step therapy
policies; and ensure that the step therapy program has been reviewed and approved by the MA
organization's pharmacy and therapeutic (P&T) committee. CMS conducts audits that target preservice organization determination and appeal cases related to requests for drugs payable under
Part B, monitors the Complaints Tracking Module (CTM) for access concerns, and monitors MA
plans’ use of Part B step therapy practices through MA reporting requirements that cover
organization determinations and reconsiderations. Requests for drugs payable under Part B,
including drugs payable under Part B subject to step therapy, are processed under the same
adjudication timeframes as used in the Part D drug program. Under the standard timeframe, an
MA plan must provide notice of its decision as expeditiously as the enrollee’s health condition
requires, but no later than 72 hours after receipt of the request, while notice of an expedited
decision must be provided as expeditiously as the enrollee’s health condition requires, but no
later than 24 hours after receipt of the request.
Direct Member Reimbursements and Access to the MFP for Selected Drugs in 2026, 2027,
and 2028 (Section 80.1)
Comment: A few commenters recommended that CMS create a process for manufacturers to
reimburse Part D plans for any difference between the cash price paid by beneficiaries and MFP
for direct member reimbursement (DMR) claims for selected drugs paid by the Part D plan. One
commenter asserted that if there is not one standardized process for manufacturers to reimburse
plans, it would result in inefficiencies and make oversight challenging for CMS. A couple of
commenters recommended CMS leverage the MTF or develop a new process like the MDP and
work to develop guidance on a PDE submission field to indicate the amount the manufacturer
owes to the plan. A couple of commenters recommended CMS align the DMR process for
selected drugs with the existing framework for other Part D drugs to avoid additional complexity
for plan sponsors. A few commenters stated that manufacturers are unlikely to reimburse Part D
plans if they are not required to do so.
A few commenters requested additional clarifications in the guidance, including more detailed
examples on how to facilitate implementation of the DMR process for situations involving innetwork and out-of-network claims and for the different phases of plan benefits. A few
commenters requested more information on how a plan should process DMR requests if it does
not know the associated dispensing fees. One commenter requested that CMS define a standard
dispensing fee in this process. One commenter requested that CMS provide more detailed
information no later than the end of July 2025 to provide time for plans and their PBMs to make
any changes to adjudication and PDE systems. This commenter stated that DMR requests are

113
more common in the first quarter of the year due to enrollment and eligibility issues that
individuals encounter at the point of sale. Another commenter requested that CMS provide more
information on how the DMR process interacts with the Executive Order on Delivering MostFavored-Nation Prescription Drug Pricing to American Patients.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their input and recommendations. At this time,
CMS declines to leverage the MTF or detail a standardized process for manufacturers to
reimburse plan sponsors in a specific method. CMS does not believe that creating a standard
process for this purpose is critical to the efficient administration or oversight of the Negotiation
Program. Plans and manufacturers negotiate prices and contracts directly. Therefore, plans and
manufacturers can negotiate for resolution of DMR requests for MFP-eligible claims as they are
best positioned to determine payment of owed amounts, frequency of reimbursement, and other
elements related to reimbursement. As CMS stated in section 80.1 of this final guidance, Primary
Manufacturers and Part D plan sponsors may establish a reimbursement process related to DMR
requests for MFP-eligible claims as necessary to ensure MFP effectuation for these MFP-eligible
individuals.
In response to the comments requesting more information on how a plan should process DMR
requests if it does not know the associated dispensing fees, CMS notes that in instances where
the plan does not know the dispensing fee charged by the pharmacy and paid by the enrollee for
the out-of-network claim, it may reimburse the enrollee based on the MFP and the plan’s
customary dispensing fee, if any, paid on an out-of-network point-of-sale electronic claim. CMS
recommends that plans populate PDE records for these claims with the MFP and the dispensing
fee paid, if any.
Lastly, CMS notes that comments related to the Executive Order on Delivering Most-FavoredNation Prescription Drug Pricing to American Patients are outside the scope of this guidance.
Comment: A couple of commenters thanked CMS and expressed support for the process CMS
outlined for DMR requests. One commenter agreed that in the process for DMR requests,
dispensing entities have already received the cash payment at the point of sale and are not
involved in the submission of the claim to the Part D plan or the transaction to reimburse the
MFP-eligible individual.
A couple of commenters objected to plan sponsors being held responsible for reimbursement to
members and stated that manufacturers should be required to provide access to the MFP to MFPeligible individuals through MTF-enrolled dispensing entities. One commenter stated that the
actual number of DMR requests for selected drugs is not insignificant and noted that these must
be handled manually by the plan sponsor within a specified timeframe.
A couple of commenters requested that CMS consider potential incentives for increased out-ofnetwork pharmacy use under the DMR process outlined in the draft guidance for initial price
applicability year 2028 and requested that CMS ensure that the new process not disrupt existing
plan utilization management practices. One of these commenters also noted that this policy
would incentivize pharmacies not to submit claims through beneficiaries’ Part D plans, even

114
though pharmacy contracts include language requiring in-network pharmacies to process claims
through the Part D benefit when they have the beneficiary’s Part D insurance information.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their support and input. CMS does not believe that
pharmacies would change procedures to avoid submitting claims to enrollees’ Part D plans
because, as one commenter noted, under 42 C.F.R. § 423.120(c)(3), a Part D sponsor must
require its network pharmacies to submit claims to the Part D plan or its intermediary whenever
the beneficiary’s Part D insurance card is presented or on file at the pharmacy, unless the enrollee
expressly requests the claim not be submitted.
As CMS details in section 80.1 of this final guidance, sections 1196(a)(1) and (a)(3)(A) of the
Act direct the Secretary to establish procedures to ensure that the MFP for a selected drug is
applied before any coverage or financial assistance under other health benefit plans or programs
or other discounts, as well as to establish procedures to carry out the provisions of the IRA with
respect to MFP-eligible individuals who are enrolled in a Part D plan. DMR requests are unique
from typical claims for selected drugs and, therefore, warrant procedures to facilitate access to
the MFP for MFP-eligible individuals that differ from how the MFP is normally effectuated for
selected drugs. For example, when an eligible individual submits a DMR request, the Part D
benefit is not used at the point of sale, the dispensing entity does not bill the individual’s Part D
plan but rather charges the individual the cash price established by the dispensing entity, and the
individual’s status as an MFP-eligible individual is not determined until after the point of sale
when the individual submits the DMR request to their Part D plan. While a Primary
Manufacturer of a selected drug that is participating in the Negotiation Program and reaches
agreement upon an MFP remains responsible for providing access to the MFP to MFP-eligible
individuals who are dispensed that selected drug during a price applicability period, CMS
believes that, in light of these unique aspects of DMRs, it is necessary to establish a procedure
that leverages existing Part D plan sponsor procedures for DMRs to help ensure that the MFP is
available to an MFP-eligible individual that submits a covered DMR request. For 2026, 2027,
and 2028, access to the MFP for an MFP-eligible individual that submits a covered DMR request
for a selected drug will be facilitated by the Part D plan sponsor. Primary Manufacturers and Part
D plan sponsors may establish a reimbursement process related to DMR requests for MFPeligible claims as necessary to ensure MFP effectuation for these MFP-eligible individuals.

involvement from CMS.

Comment: A few commenters provided feedback on CMS’ plan to bifurcate the due date for the
MFP Effectuation Plan starting with initial price applicability year 2027, such that the Primary
Manufacturer’s election whether or not to use the MTF PM, the Primary Manufacturer’s
communication plan, the Primary Manufacturer’s approach to dispensing entities who indicate
they anticipate having material cashflow concerns at the start of the initial price applicability
year, and information about the Primary Manufacturer’s plan if they do not intend to use the
MTF PM will be required to be submitted via the MTF DM by June 1 of the calendar year before
the MFP goes into effect, and the remainder of the information in the MFP Effectuation Plan will
be due September 1 of the calendar year before the MFP goes into effect. A few commenters
opposed CMS’ proposed bifurcation and urged CMS to maintain a single September 1 deadline
for all information, with one commenter expressing that it would be incredibly challenging for
manufacturers to submit any aspect of their plans by June 1st given the many operational
complexities. A couple of commenters supported the earlier date and requested that CMS move
the deadline for the entire MFP Effectuation Plan to June 1, to provide pharmacies and CMS
more time to review the MFP Effectuation Plans.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their feedback. In this final guidance, CMS
confirms that, starting with initial price applicability year 2027, the Primary Manufacturer’s
election whether or not to use the MTF PM, the Primary Manufacturer’s communication plan,
the Primary Manufacturer’s approach to dispensing entities who indicate they anticipate having
material cashflow concerns at the start of the initial price applicability year, and information
about the Primary Manufacturer’s plan if they do not intend to use the MTF PM must be
submitted via the MTF DM by June 1 of the calendar year before the MFP goes into effect, and
the remainder of the information in the MFP Effectuation Plan is due September 1 of the
calendar year before the MFP goes into effect. CMS believes this is the best way to balance the
interests of dispensing entities, who need information about how MFP access will be effectuated
and the interests of Primary Manufacturers, who need time to develop appropriate processes and
procedures. This will also allow CMS earlier insight into the MFP Effectuation Plans for the
purpose of undertaking a risk assessment of the plans. CMS notes that the MTF functionality will
allow Primary Manufacturers to submit required information by the June 1 deadline, with the rest
of the information submitted by September 1.

116
Comment: A few commenters requested, if the due date for the entire MFP Effectuation Plan
was not moved up to June 1, then CMS should require manufacturers to submit information
about whether they will use the SDRA, or another mechanism to determine a pharmacy’s cost
when providing retrospective reimbursements by the earlier June 1 deadline. One commenter
reinforced their concern that the manufacturers use of SDRA must be mandatory, unless a
different amount is agreed upon by both the dispensing entity and the Primary Manufacturer.
Response: CMS thanks these comments for their input. At this time, CMS declines to require
additional sections of the MFP Effectuation Plan be due by June 1. The sections due by June 1
include the entirety of the sections of the MFP Effectuation Plan that contain information that is
directed towards dispensing entities: specifically, the Primary Manufacturer’s election whether or
not to use the MTF PM, the Primary Manufacturer’s communication plan, the Primary
Manufacturer’s approach to dispensing entities who indicate they anticipate having material
cashflow concerns at the start of the initial price applicability year, and information about the
Primary Manufacturer’s plan if they do not intend to use the MTF PM.
CMS interpreted the concern about Primary Manufacturer use of the SDRA as a concern that
Section 3, Question 8, where the Primary Manufacturer indicates the Primary Manufacturer’s
general plan for calculating the MFP refund amount if using a retrospective reimbursement
model, will not be due by June 1 and will not be shared with dispensing entities or other
stakeholders. As described in section 40.4.3.1 of this final guidance, the obligation to calculate
and pay an appropriate amount to ensure the dispensing entity has access to the MFP rests with
the Primary Manufacturer. A Primary Manufacturer can choose to refund an amount different
than the SDRA if the Primary Manufacturer determines some other amount is appropriate and
sufficient to make the MFP available. That is, regardless of the response that a Primary
Manufacturer provides in the MFP Effectuation Plan, it is the Primary Manufacturer’s
responsibility to make the MFP available for every claim, and the Primary Manufacturer may
elect to use the SDRA or may refund a different amount if the Primary Manufacturer determines
some other amount is appropriate to make MFP available on that claim. For this reason, on the
Drug Price Negotiation Program MTF DM Primary Manufacturer MFP Effectuation Plan Form 46
CMS indicated that any responses to Section 4, MFP Effectuation are for CMS use only and will
not be made public. CMS is collecting this information for oversight purposes only and believes
receiving it by September 1 allows CMS enough time to review and complete a risk assessment.

described in MFP Effectuation Plans and the impact on dispensing entities. CMS appreciates the

concerns, but maintains that a Primary Manufacturer, in the MFP Effectuation Plan, is
responsible for describing their approach to mitigating material cashflow concerns, including
establishing qualifying criteria for dispensing entities to participate in their approach. Dispensing
entities may update whether or not they anticipate experiencing potential material cashflow
concerns at any time via the MTF DM.
CMS acknowledges that Primary Manufacturers have limited ability to address potential cash
flow concerns, but as stated above, hopes that the questions related to material cashflow concerns
are the start of a collaborative process between the Primary Manufacturer and the dispensing
entity. CMS will consider the information provided by a Primary Manufacturer in its mitigation
process when conducting a risk assessment of the Primary Manufacturer’s MFP Effectuation
Plan. CMS affirms that a Primary Manufacturer’s mitigation approaches may vary across
different selected drugs, and that a Primary Manufacturer’s plans for addressing such concerns
will have flexibility to evolve over time. A Primary Manufacturer may update its mitigation
approach by submitting an updated MFP Effectuation Plan, as soon as practicable, and in any
event, within 90 days of the change.
Comment: CMS also received a couple of comments about the burden placed on dispensing
entities regarding MFP effectuation. One commenter urged CMS to consider the operational
realities faced by providers in implementing MFP-related processes. Another commenter
encouraged CMS to consider alternatives to reduce the burden on pharmacies in future years,
including looking at ways that that pharmacies could be made whole at the point of sale.
Response: CMS appreciates these comments. By creating clear timelines and expectations for
MFP effectuation and options like the ability of dispensing entities to identify themselves as
anticipating material cashflow concerns at the start of a price applicability period with respect to
a selected drug as a result of potential delays created by reliance on retrospective MFP refunds
within the 14-day prompt MFP payment window, CMS has adopted policy positions to address
dispensing entity burden. CMS will continue to consider dispensing entity burden for future
years of the Negotiation Program but otherwise retains the approach described in draft guidance
for initial price applicability year 2028.
Comment: A couple of commenters requested that dispensing entities be required to use the
MTF PM.
Response: CMS seeks to clarify dispensing entity interaction with the MTF DM and the MTF
PM. Consistent with CMS’ previous response on page 134 of the final guidance for initial price
applicability year 2027, during a dispensing entity’s enrollment process into the MTF DM, a
dispensing entity will have the option to select whether it prefers to receive MFP refund
payments through electronic transfer of funds, which will be the default election for dispensing

120
entities at the time of enrollment, or paper check. If the Primary Manufacturer participates in the
MTF PM and elects to send an MFP refund payment to the dispensing entity through the MTF
PM, then the MTF PM will pass through the payment to the dispensing entity in accordance with
the dispensing entity’s preferred payment method (i.e., electronic transfer of funds or paper
check). As discussed in section 40.4.3.3 of this final guidance, the MTF PM will not require an
affirmative election of participation by dispensing entities for the MTF PM to pass along MFP
refund payments submitted by the Primary Manufacturer. During dispensing entity enrollment in
the MTF DM, they will provide information that will allow for payment through Primary
Manufacturer utilization of the MTF PM, as well as for payment outside of the MTF PM, for
Primary Manufacturers who decline to participate in the MTF PM.
Comment: One commenter supported CMS’ approach to the MFP Effectuation Plan, namely
requiring manufacturers to describe details of their approach for MFP effectuation outside of the
MTF PM, and for an approach that requires dispensing entities and Primary Manufacturers to
come to an agreement on MFP effectuation outside of the MTF PM.
Response: CMS thanks this commenter for the support of CMS’ approach to the MFP
Effectuation Plan.
Centralized Intake System for Complaints and Disputes Related to MFP Availability and
MTF Functionality (Section 90.2.2)
Comment: CMS received a few comments in response to its comment solicitation on how the
complaints and disputes process for drugs payable under Part B should differ from what is
outlined in section 90.2.2 of this final guidance, in particular the types of documentation CMS
should consider when a complaint or dispute is filed regarding a selected drug payable under Part
B. A couple of commenters emphasized that CMS would need to provide more resources and
support to hospitals and other Part B providers as they access the complaints and disputes
process. Other commenters raised concerns about the timeliness of complaints and disputes
related to Part B. Finally, commenters supported that the complaints and disputes process for Part
B should be as similar to the Part D process as possible.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their input. CMS will consider these suggestions
in CMS’ policy development for the complaints and disputes process for drugs payable under
Part B.
Comment: A few commenters requested more information about the process for assessment of
complaints and disputes, including procedural steps, complaint management methodology and
evaluation criteria.
Response: CMS appreciates this input. To reflect further policy and process development
regarding CMS’ process for assessing complaints and disputes, this final guidance provides more
information about the operational steps CMS will take once an issue is submitted. Upon receipt
of a reported issue, a threshold review will be completed, including a review to ensure, among
other factors, that the issue is timely, contains supporting documentation or an explanation as to
why supporting documentation is not available, and contains enough information on the face of

121
the submission for CMS to move forward with the triage process, and to identify the appropriate
track, either as a complaint or dispute. Once the issue has been identified as either a complaint or
dispute, it will be triaged and prioritized, taking into account market factors, including but not
limited to the monetary value and/or the number of claims at issue; and the extent to which the
price made available to the dispensing entity appears to differ from the MFP, among other
factors. This prioritization is to ensure CMS is reviewing all submissions systematically and in
appropriate order with the potential impact on the dispensing entity, Primary Manufacturer, or
other stakeholder submitting the issue. For example, a complaint that includes substantial
financial ramifications to either the dispensing entity or a Primary Manufacturer will be
prioritized for review, investigation, and resolution compared to complaints with lesser financial
impact. CMS is committed to reviewing all submitted issues in a timely and efficient manner;
prioritization will allow CMS to identify and address the most urgent concerns. After a complaint
or dispute is triaged, as part of the investigation, CMS may reach out to impacted parties, as
appropriate, to request additional information or documentation as needed. CMS intends to
include more information about the operationalization of the complaint and dispute processes in
future technical instruction.
Comment: CMS received a few comments relating to timelines for complaints and disputes,
with one commenter urging CMS to establish timelines for resolving complaints and disputes.
Another commenter suggested 30 days for a response. A couple of commenters suggested that
CMS use the same resolution deadlines as CGDP. One commenter recommended that the
deadline to file a complaint or dispute 120 days from the date of the subject of the complaint or
dispute be shortened to 60 days.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their input. CMS declines to make updates to this
final guidance. Consistent with CMS responses on page 142 of the final guidance for initial price
applicability year 2027, CMS intends to respond as quickly and efficiently as practicable to
address concern(s) raised in a dispute or a complaint (and expects the same from the MTF
Contractor), however, at this time CMS wants to gain more practical experience implementing
the disputes and complaints process before establishing further timelines. CMS has not updated
this approach at this time. CMS has not yet gained the operational experience necessary to set
timelines for the resolution of complaints and disputes, so declines to do so in this final guidance.
Comment: CMS received a few comments regarding an appeal process or dispute arbitration
process for complaints and disputes, including whether there will be an opportunity for an appeal
or further engagement, as well as a couple of suggestions for the creation of an independent
review process. This included recommendations for neutral decisionmakers who are a dedicated
resource with the appropriate training to be able to handle all issues expeditiously.
Response: CMS thanks commenters for their input. Consistent with our responses on pages 137138 of the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027, CMS reiterates that anytime
CMS seeks to impose a CMP on a manufacturer for noncompliance relating to MFP availability,
manufacturers will be able to appeal the CMP through an administrative appeals process. CMS
intends for the dispute process to be a fact-finding exercise with the goal of resolving a potential
error in the MTF process identified by a Primary Manufacturer or a dispensing entity (e.g., two
claims that were identified as MFP-eligible appear to be duplicates). CMS will perform a fact-

122
based analysis to determine if there is indeed an error, and either correct the issue or provide
information to the dispensing entity or Primary Manufacturer affirming that the information in
the MTF DM is correct. If a stakeholder submits a complaint, CMS will assess the complaint to
determine if further investigation is appropriate to determine whether there is noncompliance. If,
after providing an opportunity for corrective action, CMS determines that it is appropriate to
move forward with the imposition of a CMP, as established in section 100.4 of this final
guidance, CMS is adopting the existing procedures as codified in 42 C.F.R. § 423 Subpart T:
Appeal Procedures for Civil Money Penalties (see § 423.1000 through § 423.1094) which
provide an opportunity for an administrative appeal, if requested by the manufacturer. CMS has
not changed its position on an appeals process for complaints and disputes. CMS will consider
the recommendations made as the operational approach to disputes is developed.
CMS also highlights, as described in section 90.2.2 of this final guidance, that for both
complaints and disputes, as part of the investigation, CMS will reach out to impacted parties, as
appropriate, to request additional information or documentation as needed.
Comment: One commenter recommended that CMS establish an online portal for submitting
and tracking complaints.
Response: CMS thanks this commenter for this suggestion. As described in section 90.2.2 of this
final guidance, Primary Manufacturers, dispensing entities, and other stakeholders will have
access to a web-based portal for submitting complaints and disputes.
Comment: CMS received a few comments regarding beneficiary complaints, urging CMS to
provide clear direction to beneficiaries on the system and what types of complaints to send. One
commenter also urged CMS to establish a maximum allotted time for resolution of complaints
brought by beneficiaries, and to publish an annual report with information on beneficiary
complaints. Two commenters also recommended a patient-facing error and correction appeals
process.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their input. As described in section 90.2.2 of this
final guidance, beneficiaries are able to submit a complaint to CMS that the MFP was not made
available. Complaints will be captured through a public-facing online portal and phone number,
supported by the MTF platform, which are already live. CMS is also providing scripts to 1-800
MEDICARE to direct beneficiaries to these pathways if they call with complaints related to the
MFP. When a beneficiary submits a complaint, the complaint will be triaged and if the issue is
more appropriately handled by the beneficiary contacting their plan or following up with their
pharmacy, information on how to pursue those options will be provided. If it is an appropriate
complaint about MFP availability, CMS will review the complaint and any supporting
documentation to determine if the Primary Manufacturer failed to make the MFP available and is
therefore potentially subject to a CMP. As stated in the previous comment response, CMS intends
to respond as quickly and efficiently as practicable to address concern(s) raised in a dispute or a
complaint (and expects the same from the MTF Contractor), including a beneficiary complaint,
however, is declining to set specific timeframes for resolution in this final guidance, as CMS
wants to gain more practical experience implementing the disputes and complaints process
before establishing further timelines. Finally, as stated in a previous comment response, if a

123
stakeholder, including a beneficiary, submits a complaint, CMS will assess the complaint to
determine if further investigation is appropriate to determine whether there is noncompliance. If,
after providing an opportunity for corrective action, CMS determines that it is appropriate to
move forward with the imposition of a CMP, as established in section 100.4 of this final
guidance, CMS is adopting the existing procedures as codified in 42 C.F.R. § 423 Subpart T:
Appeal Procedures for Civil Money Penalties (see § 423.1000 through § 423.1094) which
provide an opportunity for an administrative appeal, if requested by the manufacturer. This is
why an appeals process is not contemplated directly as part of the complaints process; anytime
CMS seeks to impose a CMP on a manufacturer for noncompliance relating to MFP availability,
manufacturers will be able to appeal the CMP through an already-established administrative
appeals process.
Comment: CMS received a few comments about how the MFP will be provided at the point of
sale. One commenter stated that CMS should “clearly articulate how beneficiaries will be
notified if they are charged more than the MFP,” and that CMS should require that “point-of-sale
systems generate standardized alerts for overcharges.” Another commenter also questioned how
the MFP will be operationalized at the point of sale.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for this input and points commenters to section 40.4
of this final guidance, “[I]n accordance with section 1860D-2(d)(1)(D) of the Act, as amended by
section 11001(b) of the IRA, the negotiated prices used in payment by each Part D plan sponsor
for each selected drug must not exceed the applicable MFP plus any dispensing fees for such
drug. 49 In Part D, the negotiated price of a drug is the basis for determining beneficiary costsharing and for benefit administration at the point-of-sale. That is, in the case of a selected drug
for which an MFP is in effect, the MFP-eligible individual’s Part D cost-sharing is based on a
negotiated price that cannot exceed the MFP plus any dispensing fees for such drug. Therefore,
the requirement that the price used for MFP-eligible individual cost-sharing and benefit
administration cannot exceed the applicable MFP (plus dispensing fees) helps to ensure that
MFP-eligible individuals will have access to the MFP at the point-of-sale for selected drugs
covered under Part D.”

process, specifically, “how such refunds are initiated, how patients will receive them (e.g., direct
deposit, mailed check, or copay credit), or how long processing will take.”
Response: CMS wishes to clarify that the “retrospective refunds” discussed throughout this final
guidance reference refund payments that a Primary Manufacturer may use to provide access to
the MFP for the selected drug to pharmacies, mail order services, and other dispensing entities
with respect to MFP-eligible individuals who are dispensed such drugs. The MFP refunds
discussed in this guidance are not intended to be directed to, or received by, beneficiaries. As
discussed in the prior comment response, the requirement that the price used for MFP-eligible

individual cost-sharing and benefit administration cannot exceed the applicable MFP (plus

Comment: CMS received a few comments regarding the intersection between the 14-day
prompt payment window and disputed claims. One commenter asked CMS to clarify if it will
“pause” the 14-day prompt MFP payment window while disputes are reviewed and addressed.
One commenter recommended that manufacturers not pause payments to dispensing entities
during disputes, as the credit/debit ledger system exists as a mechanism to address MFP refund
payments that are later adjusted.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their input. Consistent with CMS’ response on
page 140 of the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027, CMS disagrees with the
recommendation to suspend or toll the 14-day prompt MFP payment window for disputed
amounts. It is essential that Primary Manufacturers make timely payments to make the MFP
available to pharmacies, mail order services, and other dispensing entities that dispense the
selected drug with respect to MFP-eligible individuals pursuant to the requirements of section
1193(a)(3)(A) of the Act. If the resolution of a dispute results in a claim adjustment or reversal
that entitles a Primary Manufacturer to a credit towards a future MFP refund payment, the MTF
PM system will provide this credit to the Primary Manufacturer (if that Primary Manufacturer
participates in the MTF PM and payment was passed through the MTF PM). CMS has not
changed this position in this final guidance. The initiation of a dispute on a claim does not negate
the Primary Manufacturer’s statutory responsibility to make the MFP available to the dispensing
entity for an MFP-eligible claim subject to a dispute. Nor does initiating a dispute affect the
Primary Manufacturer’s obligation to transmit the claim-level payment elements for such claim
within the 14-day prompt MFP payment window, including the manufacturer-determined MFP
refund amount (if any) and the appropriate transaction code. As is the case for any claim,
whether it is under dispute or not, Primary Manufacturers may make individual determinations
about whether an MFP refund is appropriate, and, if so, the amount of the MFP refund, to
effectuate the MFP. If the Primary Manufacturer provides an MFP refund on a claim for which
there is a dispute and the dispute results in an updated amount required to make the MFP
available, the Primary Manufacturer utilizing the MTF PM can use the adjustment processes
described in sections 40.4.3.2 of this final guidance. Primary Manufacturers who elect not to use
the MTF PM can utilize the method they have established for handling changes to payment
amounts, as discussed in section 40.4.4.4 of this final guidance.
Comment: One commenter requested that CMS confirm that manufacturers have an unspecified
amount of time to resolve, submit evidence, and adjust payments where required.
Response: CMS assumes that this commenter is referring to responses from manufacturers once
a complaint has been received by CMS. CMS confirms that manufacturers, and all interested
parties, will have the ability to submit evidence, and are free to resolve issues and adjust
payments while CMS is investigating a complaint, which would likely have an impact on CMS’
decision to move forward with any enforcement action. When requesting evidence, CMS plans to

125
set reasonable timelines within which evidence must be produced to be considered while CMS is
investigating the complaint. CMS plans to provide more information about the complaint process
in future technical instruction and other outreach and education efforts.
Comment: CMS received a few comments about public reporting of compliance data, including
complaints and disputes, including recommendations about reporting related to complaint and
dispute volumes, types of complaints and disputes, outcomes, and the timeframes for resolution.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their input. As stated in section 90.2.2 of this final
guidance, CMS intends to track complaints and disputes over time to monitor overall trends and
emerging compliance issues, and to make process improvements in the implementation of the
complaint and dispute process, as applicable. CMS will consider the extent to which CMS will
share these findings publicly and in what format.
Comment: CMS also received a couple of comments regarding the publication of MFP
effectuation data including data related to complaints and disputes, specifically regarding
beneficiaries. One commenter recommended that CMS should publish annually a report detailing
the number of beneficiary complaints and outcomes. Another commenter urged CMS to
“carefully monitor whether beneficiary cost-sharing does indeed reflect the negotiated price, and
that savings actually accrue to beneficiaries.”
Response: CMS appreciates these suggestions. As stated in this final guidance, CMS intends to
track complaints and disputes over time to monitor overall trends, which will include beneficiary
complaints. As part of CMS’ oversight responsibilities, CMS intends to monitor MFP
effectuation and market impact, including metrics related to drug access and costs during MFP
effectuation from a beneficiary perspective. CMS will consider to the extent to which CMS will
share these findings publicly and in what format.
Comment: One commenter requested that CMS clarify that Part D plans may avail themselves
of the “first track” of the complaint and dispute process described in the draft guidance for initial
price applicability year 2028.
Response: CMS understood this comment as a request to clarify in guidance that Part D plans
may avail themselves of the dispute process outlined in section 90.2.2 of this final guidance.
CMS thanks this commenter for their comment. Consistent with CMS’ response on page 140 of
the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027, the dispute process is intended to
allow manufacturers and dispensing entities to raise a specific, identifiable challenge with a
technical aspect of the MTF. As Part D plans are not directly interacting with the MTF, the
dispute process is not an appropriate mechanism for Part D plans to raise concerns. Part D plans
will have access to the complaint process established in section 90.2.2 of this final guidance, as
will all interested stakeholders.

claim number, and that parties to a dispute identify a singular point of contact for all disputes.

Response: CMS refers the commenter to the Drug Price Negotiation Complaint and Dispute

entity or Primary Manufacturer is filing a dispute.

Comment: One commenter requested that CMS further clarify who can be an appropriate party
to a dispute or a complaint and requested further information on how a scenario where a Part D
plan sponsor submitted the wrong claims level data would be handled.
Response: CMS thanks this commenter for this input. CMS declines to make any policy changes
at this time. As described in section 90.2.2 of this final guidance, “This system is intended to
address complaints and disputes related to MFP availability and MTF functionality and is not
intended to receive general comments or feedback related to the implementation of the
Negotiation Program as a whole. Any issues unrelated to MFP availability and MTF

are outside the above scope will be referred to the appropriate channels for assistance.
Additionally, CMS describes the verification of data that will take place prior to the claim

elements will be derived from claims that have been verified…by both the Part D plan and
DDPS[.]”
Comment: CMS received a couple of comments regarding a good faith effort on the part of

before using CMS’ complaints process.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their input. CMS declines to make further updates
to final guidance at this time. As described in section 90.2.2 of this final guidance, CMS
encourages dispensing entities and Primary Manufacturers to work together in good faith to
resolve any issues regarding MFP availability. Proof of any efforts to resolve the issue should be
submitted once the complaint is filed and will be considered by CMS as part of the investigation
into the complaint.
Civil Monetary Penalties (Section 100)
Comment: One commenter noted that CMS added an additional example to Table 10, titled
“Violations of the Agreement,” specifically the “[f]ailure to submit data requested by CMS in
accordance with its oversight responsibilities under section 1196(b) of the Act.” The commenter
requested this example be struck or specified further.

OMB approved the ICR titled “Medicare Transaction Facilitator for 2026 and 2027 under Sections 11001 and
11002 of the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) Information Collection Request” (0938-1483), which includes details on
information that dispensing entities, Primary Manufacturers and other stakeholders will be required to provide when
submitting a complaint or dispute. See: https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAViewICR?ref_nbr=202503-0938001.
50

127
Response: CMS thanks this commenter for their feedback. The example added to Table 10 is
consistent with the requirements outlined in the revised guidance for initial price applicability
year 2026 and the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027. This example refers to
the Primary Manufacturer’s responsibility to submit information requested by CMS to support
CMS’ compliance monitoring responsibilities described in section 1196(b) of the Act. CMS
revised the language in this example in Table 10 to clarify that a manufacturer must provide any
information requested by the agency in the course of executing its compliance monitoring
responsibility including data and failure to do so may be a violation of the Negotiation Program
agreement. CMS declines to adopt the commenter’s suggestion to strike or narrow this language
which is consistent with the compliance monitoring authority provided to CMS through statute
and CMS’ corresponding need to collect a variety of materials related to such authority.
Comment: Some commenters requested that CMS create a safe harbor for “good faith efforts” to
effectuate the MFP. In particular, commenters expressed concerns about Primary Manufacturers
being subject to CMPs for technical issues with the MTF PM or MTF DM that were beyond the
control of the manufacturer.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their feedback. Consistent with our response on
page 135 of the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027, CMS declines to
designate a safe harbor in this final guidance. Section 1193(a) of the Act places the obligation on
the Primary Manufacturer to ensure that the MFP is made available to dispensing entities that
dispense the selected drug to MFP-eligible individuals. CMS stresses that a Primary
Manufacturer’s decision to participate in the voluntary MTF PM alone is not sufficient to negate
its responsibilities set forth in section 40.4.3 of this final guidance (e.g., returning their claimlevel payment elements to the MTF DM to effectuate payment), nor does it absolve a Primary
Manufacturer of its statutory responsibility to provide access to the MFP to dispensing entities.
Additionally, if the Primary Manufacturer uses the MTF PM to pass through an MFP refund
payment, the receipt of such payment by the dispensing entity (either electronically or via paper
check issued by the MTF PM) does not constitute the dispensing entity’s agreement that access
to the MFP has been provided by the Primary Manufacturer. CMS will take into consideration a
Primary Manufacturer’s choice to participate in the MTF PM, a system that CMS has designed
with safeguards and procedures it has deemed sufficient to facilitate manufacturer effectuation of
the MFP, when conducting the risk assessment procedures set forth in section 90.2.1 of this final
guidance. CMS has not updated this approach and will not explicitly create a safe harbor from
CMPs in this final guidance. As stated in section 100 of this final guidance, CMS intends to
exercise the authority to impose CMPs for instances of noncompliance that substantively
obstruct Negotiation Program processes and/or availability of the MFP. CMS is establishing a
structure for enforcement actions that, among other things, is not punitive in response to
immaterial noncompliance or other instances of noncompliance that are not substantive. Further,
section 100.1 of this final guidance, related to potential imposition of CMPs for failure to make
the MFP available, states that, upon discovery and confirmation of a Primary Manufacturer’s
failure to make MFP available, CMS intends to send the Primary Manufacturer a Notification of
Potential Noncompliance that will include information on the potential violation and an
opportunity for corrective action. CMS intends to establish a process in which the Primary
Manufacturer will have 10 business days to respond to the Notice of Potential Noncompliance to
provide additional context, evidence refuting the violation, proof of mitigation of

128
noncompliance, and/or other factors for CMS’ consideration. CMS intends to consider the
materials provided by the Primary Manufacturer when determining the Primary Manufacturer’s
CMP liability, including any technical failures outside the control of the Primary Manufacturer
related to the transmission of payment.
Comment: One commenter urged CMS to establish an escalation and remediation pathway for
enforcement actions to include informal correction opportunities, formal notices, and CMPs with
well-defined criteria. The commenter suggested the compliance program within the Medicare
Shared Savings Program as a model. A couple of commenters requested that CMS provide a
dispute resolution or appeals process for manufacturers facing an enforcement action. One
commenter requested that manufacturers have 30 days to cure a compliance issue.
Response: CMS appreciates commenters’ feedback. CMS provides opportunities, described in
sections 100.1 and 100.2 of this final guidance, for the Primary Manufacturer to engage in
corrective action in applicable circumstances, including examples of substantive violations in
section 100 that would warrant the issuance of a CMP based on agency discretion. Consistent
with CMS’ response on page 143-144 of the final guidance for initial price applicability year
2027, CMS believes the timeframes outlined in sections 100.1 and 40.2.3 of this final guidance
provide sufficient time for the Primary Manufacturer to address correction of any compliance
issue while also ensuring program operations are not impacted by manufacturer non-compliance.
Comment: CMS received a comment stating that the commenter was concerned that the 10
business days does not provide enough time for manufacturers to investigate, gather required
information and provide it to the MTF, particularly in light of the broad scale of the program, and
high volume of claims, including for Secondary Manufacturers. This commenter recommended
that the 10 days be extended to 60 days.
Response: CMS assumes the 10-business-day time period mentioned in the comment is a
reference to the 10 business days for response triggered by the Notification of Potential
Noncompliance, discussed in section 100.1 of this final guidance. CMS appreciates this feedback
but declines to change the 10 business days for response triggered by the Notification of
Potential Noncompliance. In circumstances where the Notification of Potential Noncompliance
is the result of an investigation related to a complaint, CMS will likely have engaged the Primary
Manufacturer to provide evidence and information during the complaint investigation. Even
where the Notification of Potential Noncompliance is the result of an audit or other investigation,
CMS envisions engaging with the Primary Manufacturer during the audit or investigation. The
Notification of Potential Noncompliance merely represents the final opportunity a Primary
Manufacturer has to provide evidence or take corrective action before CMS makes a decision
regarding potential enforcement action.
Comment: CMS received a comment requesting that manufacturers be given the opportunity to
correct potentially incorrect refund amounts without fear of incurring CMPs.
Response: CMS thanks this commenter for this comment. CMS refers the commenter to the
Medicare Transaction Facilitator Data Module User Agreement for Manufacturers which
includes a responsibility for Primary Manufacturers to submit revised claim-level payment

129
elements if the Primary Manufacturer knows or has reason to know that previously returned
claim-level payment elements do not accurately reflect the amount needed to make the MFP
available to dispensing entities. Primary Manufacturers can do so following the process
described in sections 40.4.3.2 and 40.4.4.4 of this final guidance. Primary Manufacturers can
follow this process if they determine that a refund amount is “incorrect.” Additionally, once CMS
has sent a Primary Manufacturer the Notice of Potential Noncompliance described in section
100.1 of this final guidance, Primary Manufacturers can follow the above process to update the
rebate amount paid to the dispensing entity, and CMS will take that action into account when
deciding whether to move forward with a decision to assess CMPs.
Part D Formulary Inclusion of Selected Drugs (Section 110)
Comment: A few commenters stated that research is showing that Part D plan sponsors are
already making changes to steer beneficiaries away from selected drugs. A couple of
commenters cited an analysis evaluating changes in formulary coverage for the 25 medicines
selected for negotiation in initial price applicability years 2026 and 2027, which found that fewer
medicines are available on formulary in 2025 relative to 2024, and that Part D plan sponsors are
combining utilization management and tiering strategies to restrict access to selected drugs.
Another commenter acknowledged CMS’ statement in the draft guidance for initial price
applicability year 2028 that it is aware of concerns that Part D plan sponsors could broadly shift
access with respect to a selected drug after the drug has been announced as a selected drug. This
commenter expressed support for CMS’ statement that it will continue to monitor trends in
formulary placement for selected drugs beginning after drugs are selected for an initial price
applicability year.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their feedback. CMS is aware of concerns that Part
D plan sponsors could broadly shift access with respect to a drug selected for negotiation after
the drug has been announced as a selected drug, i.e., in the contract year prior to the selected
drug’s MFP taking effect. While CMS did not see this occur in contract year 2025 with respect to
selected drugs for initial price applicability year 2026, CMS will continue to monitor trends in
formulary placement for selected drugs beginning after drugs are selected for an initial price
applicability year (e.g., contract years 2026, 2027, 2028, and each additional year in the selected
drug’s price applicability period, if an MFP is in place with respect to that year).
CMS expects Part D sponsors to provide their enrollees with meaningful access to selected drugs
and will use its comprehensive formulary review process to assess any practices that may
undermine beneficiary access to selected drugs, as discussed in section 110 of this final
guidance. To help ensure that beneficiaries have meaningful access to selected drugs and
consistent with the agency’s statutory obligation to monitor plan compliance with all applicable
formulary requirements, CMS will use its formulary review process to assess any instances
where Part D sponsors place selected drugs on non-preferred tiers or where a selected drug is
placed on a higher tier than non-selected drugs in the same class. As discussed in section 110 of
this final guidance, as part of the annual bid review process, CMS will expect Part D sponsors to
provide CMS with a reasonable justification to support the submitted plan design that includes
any such practices. This justification should address applicable clinical factors, such as clinical
superiority, non-inferiority, or equivalence of the selected and non-selected drugs, as well as the
plan design’s compliance with applicable statutory and regulatory requirements (e.g., the

130
requirement to have a cost-effective drug utilization management program that bases decisions
on the strength of the clinical evidence and standards of practice). As CMS reviews Part D plan
formularies to ensure they comply with statutory and regulatory requirements, pursuant to
section 1860D-11(e)(2)(D)(i) of the Act, CMS will only approve a Part D plan bid submitted by
a Part D plan sponsor if CMS does not find that the design of the plan and its benefits (including
any formulary and tiered formulary structure) are likely to substantially discourage enrollment by
certain Part D eligible individuals under the plan. CMS believes this approach will provide Part
D sponsors with the flexibility to continue to manage costs through tier placement in a clinically
appropriate manner, while allowing CMS to monitor practices that may undermine beneficiary
access to selected drugs and inform new requirements for future contract years.
Comment: A couple of commenters expressed support for CMS maintaining the existing Part D
formulary review standards and not implementing explicit tier placement or utilization
management requirements that apply uniformly across selected drugs in all formularies for initial
price applicability year 2028. Some commenters disagreed that CMS does not have sufficient
information to determine whether to change its formulary inclusion policies and expressed
concerns with what they referred to as CMS’ “wait and see” or “passive” approach to monitoring
Part D plans’ compliance with existing formulary requirements. Many commenters expressed
concern that plans may hinder beneficiary access to selected drugs or non-selected drugs (e.g., by
applying utilization management requirements that are not based on medical appropriateness or
placing selected drugs on less favorable tiers compared to non-selected drugs). These
commenters recommended CMS take additional steps to ensure broad beneficiary access under
Part D by, for example, providing additional specificity around the requirements for coverage of
both selected and non-selected drugs and establishing a mechanism for patients to provide
feedback directly to CMS on any access issues they experience and publicizing such feedback. A
few commenters recommended changes to CMS’ formulary review processes, including that
CMS strengthen its current formulary review standards, collect additional information, and
increase transparency by making public the results of its formulary reviews. A couple of
commenters opposed the oversight of formularies described in section 110 of the draft guidance
for initial price applicability year 2028 and stated that the steps CMS is taking lack statutory
basis and restrict Part D plan sponsors.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for both their support and feedback. CMS agrees with
commenters about the importance of ensuring meaningful beneficiary access to selected drugs
and their MFPs and ensuring that plans do not engage in behavior that hinders access to selected
drugs or non-selected drugs when medically appropriate.
As stated in CMS’ response on pages 146 and 147 of the final guidance for initial price
applicability year 2027, CMS shares concerns that Part D sponsors may be incentivized in
certain circumstances to disadvantage selected drugs by placing selected drugs on less favorable
tiers compared to non-selected drugs, or by applying utilization management that is not based on
medical appropriateness to steer Part D beneficiaries away from selected drugs in favor of nonselected drugs. CMS understands that sponsors could also be incentivized in certain
circumstances to steer Part D beneficiaries away from non-selected drugs in favor of selected
drugs. CMS reiterates that CMS expects Part D sponsors to provide their enrollees with
meaningful access to selected drugs and will use its comprehensive formulary review process to

131
assess any practices that may undermine beneficiary access to selected drugs, as discussed in
section 110 of this final guidance.
Consistent with CMS’ response on page 147 of the final guidance for initial price applicability
year 2027, CMS appreciates commenters’ suggestions for changes to CMS’ formulary review
processes. Plan sponsors must submit their drug formularies to CMS for approval each contract
year, and CMS maintains, and will continue to maintain, a robust, clinical formulary review
process to ensure that all Part D plan formularies comply with statutory and regulatory
requirements. This includes the requirement under section 1860D-11(e)(2)(D)(i) of the Act that
CMS may only approve a Part D plan if it “does not find that the design of the plan and its
benefits (including any formulary and tiered formulary structure) are likely to substantially
discourage enrollment by certain Part D eligible individuals under the plan.” Further, if CMS
identifies that Part D sponsors are not providing beneficiaries with meaningful access to selected
drugs, CMS may consider implementing new requirements for future contract years. CMS
believes this approach will provide Part D sponsors with the flexibility to continue to manage
costs when clinically appropriate while allowing CMS to monitor practices that may undermine
enrollee access to selected drugs and inform further action, as necessary. CMS does not publish
the results of its formulary reviews, or the clinical justifications submitted by Part D plan
sponsors, or publicly share such clinical justifications with any external stakeholders, including
manufacturers. Coverage information is available when beneficiaries search for plans by
inputting their drugs into the Medicare Plan Finder and is also required to be available on the
plan’s printed formulary, on the formulary on the plan’s website, and by calling the plan.
As explained in section 110 of this final guidance, CMS does not have sufficient information at
this time to determine whether changes to formulary inclusion policies are warranted. The
formulary inclusion requirement in section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I) of the Act has not taken effect yet,
and plan sponsors did not submit their formularies for the first contract year in which MFPs are
in effect (i.e., contract year 2026) until June 2, 2025. In light of the substantial time required for
CMS to complete the formulary review process and analyze the impacts of the formulary
inclusion requirement, information is not yet available to inform whether changes to formulary
inclusion policies are warranted. For these reasons, CMS will continue monitoring Part D plans’
compliance with all applicable formulary requirements and treatment of drugs and may further
address formulary inclusion policies in the future.
Beneficiaries may report any issues or concerns regarding access to their prescribed medications,
including selected drugs, to their plan first, and also to CMS by utilizing the public-facing online
portal for the Negotiation Program, supported by the MTF platform, or by contacting
1-800-MEDICARE, which has scripts to direct beneficiaries to one of the above pathways if they
call with a complaint related to the MFP. In addition, as described in section 90.2.2 of this final
guidance, CMS will establish a centralized intake system for receiving reports related to access
to the MFP with respect to MFP-eligible individuals, including complaints from the public
related to MFP availability.
Comment: A commenter recommended CMS only require the formulary inclusion of dosage
forms and strengths of selected drugs that are necessary to meet the needs of the Part D plan’s
patient population.

an MFP is in effect with respect to the year. Accordingly, all dosage forms and strengths of the
selected drug that constitute a covered Part D drug and for which the MFP is in effect must be
included on formulary.
Comment: A few commenters asked that CMS consider a selected drug’s protected class status

Formulary Inclusion Exception Successor Regulation for 2027 and 2028 (Section 110.1)
Comment: One commenter opposed CMS’ identification in the Final CY 2026 Part D Redesign
Program Instructions of a successor regulation that permits immediate substitution of selected
drugs for interchangeable biological products. This commenter remarked broadly on policies
beyond those finalized in the Final CY 2026 Part D Redesign Program Instructions, asserting that
allowing substitutions of biological products, whether an interchangeable biological product or a
biosimilar biological product other than an interchangeable biological product, and whether via
immediate substitution or maintenance changes, undercuts the IRA’s explicit requirement that
Part D sponsors include selected drugs on their formularies, and that allowing biosimilar
biological product substitution (including interchangeable biological product substitution)
exceeds CMS’ authority because the plain language of the statute applies only to generic drugs.
In contradiction to these statements, this same commenter also requested that CMS maintain its
formulary inclusion exception for 2027 and 2028 as described in section 110.1 of the draft
guidance for initial price applicability year 2028 for selected drugs covered under Part D and
extend the exception for all future initial price applicability years. One commenter supported the
policy to allow Part D sponsors to replace selected drugs on formulary through immediate

133
substitution when a generic or interchangeable biological product comes to market, stating that
this proposal provides appropriate flexibility for plan sponsors to develop formularies that drive
the lowest net costs to the plan, the Medicare program, and Medicare beneficiaries.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their perspectives and support. Comments on the
Final CY 2026 Part D Redesign Program Instructions are outside the scope of this guidance.
With regard to the incorporation of section 90 of the Final CY 2026 Part D Redesign Program
Instructions with respect to the successor regulation exception and extension of the policies
therein to 2027 and 2028, CMS reiterates its response on pages 11 through 14 of the Final CY
2026 Part D Redesign Program Instructions. The statutory exception to the selected drug
formulary inclusion requirement in section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(ii) of the Act allows for a Part D
plan sponsor to remove a selected drug from its formulary if such removal would be permitted
under 42 C.F.R. § 423.120(b)(5)(iv) (or any successor regulation). Because 42 C.F.R. §
423.120(b)(5)(iv) no longer exists in the Part D regulations, CMS was required to name a
successor regulation.
The statute does not explicitly limit the exception to 42 C.F.R. § 423.120(b)(5)(iv) at the time of
enactment. We believe it is significant that the statute did not establish a static exception (e.g., by
indicating that the exception was limited to 42 C.F.R. § 423.120(b)(5)(iv) at the time of
enactment), but rather expressly indicated that the exception would include “any successor
regulation.” The statute could have limited the meaning or scope of “any successor regulation” to
apply only to the scope of 42 C.F.R. § 423.120(b)(5)(iv) at the time of enactment (i.e., brand
name drugs and their therapeutically equivalent generic drugs), but it did not do so. Other
provisions of the Part D statute make clear that when the statute limits a provision that crossreferences an existing regulation to the terms of such regulation at a particular point of time, the
statute expressly states that this is the case. For example, section 1860D-14A(g)(6) of the Act
defines “negotiated price” to have “the meaning given such term in [42 C.F.R. 423.100] (as in
effect on March 23, 2010)” (emphasis added). However, section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(ii) of the Act
does not state that the exception is limited to 42 C.F.R. § 423.120(b)(5)(iv) as codified at a
specific time, but instead expressly includes the words “or any successor regulation,” leaving it
to CMS to identify any such successor regulation as necessary.
Furthermore, the statute does not explicitly limit the exception to brand name drugs and their
therapeutically equivalent generic drugs. When CMS codified 42 C.F.R. § 423.120(b)(5)(iv),
there were no Part D drugs that were interchangeable biological products. At the time the IRA
was enacted, there were no codified requirements for immediate substitutions with
interchangeable biological products, nor were there codified requirements for maintenance
changes with interchangeable biological products or biosimilar biological products other than
interchangeable biological products. As a result, at the time of enactment, it would not have been
possible for the statute to point to specific regulations permitting formulary changes other than
those related to therapeutically equivalent generic drugs.
Consistent with the text of section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(ii) of the Act, in this final guidance CMS is
maintaining the policy described in the draft guidance for initial price applicability year 2028 to
incorporate section 90 of the Final CY 2026 Part D Redesign Program Instructions with respect
to the successor regulation exception and extension of the policies therein to 2027 and 2028.

134

Comment: A few commenters took the view that the successor regulation identified for 2027
and 2028 takes an overly narrow interpretation of the underlying statute and regulations and will
limit generic and biosimilar biological product uptake. These commenters stated that the
proposed implementation is confusing and raised concerns that plans will be restricted in their
formulary decisions based solely on when during a year a generic or interchangeable biological
product comes to market. To address this concern, a couple of commenters recommended that
CMS interpret the successor regulation to include maintenance changes, which would give Part
D plans flexibility to remove a selected drug when there is a generic or interchangeable
biological product being marketed, but because of the timing of formulary submissions, the
immediate substitution conditions for removal could not be met. A couple of commenters
recommended that CMS revise the immediate substitution requirements as applied to selected
drugs to allow their removal as soon as a generic or interchangeable biological product becomes
available, and irrespective of whether this is before or after the initial formulary submission. One
of these commenters stated that the immediate substitution rationale (namely, that plans should
not have the option to replace a brand with a generic after the formulary is submitted if they
could have done so before) does not apply with respect to a selected drug, since plans must
include the selected drug as part of their initial formulary submission, even if a generic or
interchangeable biological product has become available by then, and even if that generic or
interchangeable biological product is included on the formulary as part of the initial formulary
submission. One commenter expressed concern with the policy in the draft guidance for initial
price applicability year 2028 to not allow plans to continue similar formulary treatment from
year-to-year after a selected drug has been removed via immediate substitution, stating that this
policy is not aligned with Congressional intent, and urged CMS to expand the successor
regulation to include maintenance changes.
Response: In response to the requests that CMS expand the successor regulation to include
maintenance changes, CMS reiterates its response on pages 12 and 13 of the Final CY 2026 Part
D Redesign Program Instructions. CMS understands that permitting the removal of a selected
drug via maintenance changes (which allow for substitution with a generic drug, interchangeable
biological product, or a biosimilar biological product other than an interchangeable biological
product) would provide Part D sponsors with greater flexibility to design their benefits and
further promote access to potentially lower cost alternatives to the selected drugs. While we
maintain that section 1860D4(b)(3)(I)(ii) of the Act gives CMS the authority to identify such
maintenance changes as part of the successor regulation for purposes of section 1860D4(b)(3)(I)(ii) of the Act, CMS declines to do so at this time. In the future, however, CMS may
identify new regulations that constitute the successor regulation (e.g., as the biosimilar market
matures or as additional changes are made to the underlying regulations). CMS also reminds Part
D plan sponsors that they can add new generic drugs and biosimilar products to their formularies
at any time during the plan year. Part D plan sponsors may also make maintenance changes with
respect to selected drugs other than removing them from the formulary, in accordance with 42
C.F.R. § 423.120(e) and the notice requirements of 42 C.F.R. § 423.120(f). Comments with
requests for revisions to the immediate substitution requirements in the Part D regulations,
including with respect to timing, are outside the scope of this guidance.

135
CMS thanks the commenter for their feedback on the policy in the draft guidance to not allow
plans to carry over similar formulary treatment from year-to-year within the price applicability
period after a selected drug has been removed in a preceding year via immediate substitution.
This policy is consistent with CMS’ longstanding policy to consider each plan year’s formulary
to be separate and distinct from the prior year. CMS maintains in this final guidance that a
removal could only apply to multiple plan years in a price applicability period if it independently
meets the immediate substitution requirements for each applicable plan year.
Comment: One commenter requested clarity on the formulary inclusion requirements for a
selected drug for which multiple generics or interchangeable biological products come to market.
Specifically, the commenter presented a scenario where one interchangeable biological product
for a drug selected for initial price applicability year 2026 came to market prior to the CY 2026
formulary submission deadline and another interchangeable biological product for that selected
drug came to market after the CY 2026 formulary submission deadline. The commenter stated
that they expect, but ask CMS to confirm, that Part D sponsors would be permitted to, in
accordance with the successor regulation, substitute the selected drug with the interchangeable
biological product that came to market after the CY 2026 formulary submission deadline.
Response: For questions about the successor regulation exception to the formulary inclusion
requirement for selected drugs in 2026, CMS refers the commenter to section 90 of the Final CY
2026 Part D Redesign Program Instructions. If the scenario described by the commenter were to
occur with respect to plan years 2027 or 2028, CMS affirms that Part D sponsors would be
permitted to substitute the selected drug with the interchangeable biological product that came to
market after the 2027 or 2028 formulary submission deadline, if such removal meets the
requirements specified in 42 C.F.R. § 423.120(e)(2)(i) and the notice requirements specified in
42 C.F.R. § 423.120(f)(2), (3), and (4), and irrespective of whether a different interchangeable
biological product came to market prior to the such formulary submission deadline.
Application of Medicare Part B and Part D Drug Inflation Rebate Programs to Selected
Drugs (Section 120)
Comment: Two commenters opposed CMS’ application of the Medicare Part B and Part D Drug
Inflation Rebate Programs to selected drugs. These commenters contended that manufacturers
should not be obligated to pay an inflation rebate on a selected drug in both Part B and Part D
because Medicare expenditures on a selected drug are already constrained by the MFP. The
commenter further expressed that Medicare does not need to be made whole on account of such a
price increase, and, therefore, no inflation rebate should be due. These commenters pointed to the
Part B inflation rebate calculation in statute to assert that Congress did not intend for rebates to
apply to selected drugs. One of these commenters urged CMS to clarify that a selected drug is
not subject to inflation rebates.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their feedback. Consistent with CMS’ response on
page 85 of the revised guidance for initial price applicability year 2026, the statute provides that
the inflation rebates apply to selected drugs. 51 Specifically, the rebate calculation specified in
section 1847A(i)(3)(A)(ii)(l) of the Act references section 1847A(b)(1)(B) of the Act, which
50F

includes payment for selected drugs. That is, there is no statutory exemption from inflation
rebates for selected drugs.

Schedule final rule, in which CMS codified with modification and additional clarification in
parts 427 and 428 of title 42, Chapter IV of the Code of Federal Regulations 52 the policies set
forth in the revised Medicare Part B Drug Inflation Rebate Guidance and the revised Medicare
