Renegotiation of a Maximum Fair Price for Initial Price Applicability Year 2028 (Section
130)
Comment: A few commenters requested additional clarity on the timeline for renegotiation.
Among these commenters, a couple of commenters also requested clarification as to whether
renegotiation would be assessed on a set schedule or an ad-hoc basis. One commenter asked that
CMS restrict renegotiation to no more than once annually and provide 120-day advance notice to
MA plans of any changes to the MFP of a selected drug.

CMS, Final Rule, “Medicare and Medicaid Programs: CY 2025 Payment Policies Under the Physician Fee

Response: CMS thanks commenters for their inquiry. As described in section 130 of this final
guidance and section 1194(f) of the Act, CMS will review selected drugs with an agreed-upon
MFP from initial price applicability years 2026 and 2027 for renegotiation eligibility. If any of
these selected drugs are renegotiation-eligible based on the criteria described in section 130.1 of
this final guidance, CMS will then determine whether to select those renegotiation-eligible drugs
based on the criteria described in section 130.2 of this final guidance. Any drugs that are
renegotiation-eligible and selected for renegotiation will be renegotiated for initial price
applicability year 2028. Per section 1194(f) of the Act this process will occur annually thereafter.
CMS notes that this guidance applies only to initial price applicability year 2028.
Regarding the request for notice to MA plans of changes to the MFP of a selected drug, CMS
notes that renegotiation will occur at the same cadence (per section 1194(f) of the Act, that is
annually beginning for initial price applicability year 2028) and on the same timeline (i.e.,
adhering to the same statutory deadlines provided in section 1194(b) of the Act) as negotiation.
As such, a renegotiated MFP will be publicly available no later than November 30 two years
prior to the relevant initial price applicability year when the MFP becomes effective in
accordance with section 1195(a)(1) of the Act and as described in section 60.6 of this final
guidance. Additionally, per section 60.6 of this final guidance, CMS will publish an updated
MFP no later than November 30 of the year that is two years prior to such subsequent year.
Given this timeline, the renegotiated MFP will be publicly available (including for MA plans)
more than 120 days before a renegotiated MFP takes effect.
Comment: One commenter said that CMS should only consider selected drugs to be
renegotiation-eligible if the MFP is likely to be reduced during renegotiation. One commenter
supported the notion that renegotiation would not always result in a lower negotiated price.
Response: Section 1194(f)(2) of the Act defines a “renegotiation-eligible” drug as a selected
drug that has a new indication, a change of status to an extended-monopoly drug, a change in
status to a long-monopoly drug, or a material change to a section 1194(e) factor. Section 130.1 of
this final guidance aligns with this statutory definition and provides additional detail on how
CMS will determine renegotiation eligibility. CMS declines to only consider selected drugs as
renegotiation-eligible if the MFP is likely to be reduced during renegotiation as this is not part of
the definition of a renegotiation-eligible drug per section 1194(f)(2) of the Act.
Section 1194(b)(1) of the Act directs CMS to develop a methodology and process for
negotiations that “aims to achieve the lowest maximum fair price for each selected drug.” CMS
notes that the lowest MFP that may be achieved through renegotiation of a selected drug may
increase or decrease based on the emergence of new information about the drug related to section
1194(e) factors. For example, new data could emerge after an MFP is negotiated for a selected
drug indicating a significant improvement in outcomes not previously reported that may warrant
an increase in the MFP should that selected drug be eligible and selected for renegotiation. As
such, CMS will strive to negotiate the lowest MFP for each selected drug based on the evidence
available at the time of negotiation and renegotiation, as applicable.

138
Comment: A couple of commenters suggested that CMS should issue a public notice of the
agency’s intent to renegotiate a selected drug followed by a public comment period for interested
parties to submit updated information. Another commenter requested clarification on whether
CMS would notify a Primary Manufacturer if its selected drug is eligible for renegotiation, and if
so, when that notification would be provided.
Response: Section 1194(f)(4)(B) of the Act requires the methodology and process for
renegotiation to be consistent with the methodology and process for negotiation established
under 1194(b) of the Act to the extent practicable. As such, CMS intends to follow the same
process and timeline for publishing the selected drug list for renegotiation as this is both
practicable and follows a similar process and methodology to align with statute. As for notice to
the manufacturer, CMS indicated in section 30.1 of the draft guidance for initial price
applicability year 2028 and now in this final guidance that CMS will publish the list of selected
drugs selected for renegotiation, if any, no later than February 1, 2026. CMS added this
information to section 130.2 of this final guidance for additional clarity. CMS appreciates the
commenter’s request for public notice and comment, but CMS does not believe this is
operationally feasible on this timeline.
Identification of Renegotiation-Eligible Drugs for Initial Price Applicability Year 2028
(Section 130.1)
Comment: One commenter requested that CMS delay eligibility for renegotiation for two years
following a selected drug’s initial price applicability year because CMS will not be able to
understand if there has been a material change without seeing the financial impact of MFP. One
commenter noted a drug could be subject to multiple rounds of renegotiation in a short period of
time if a drug with an agreed-upon MFP had multiple new indications and a change in monopoly
status. Some commenters suggested that CMS restrict renegotiation-eligible drugs to those with a
change in monopoly status for initial price applicability year 2028. These commenters noted the
short timeframe between MFP agreements signed for initial price applicability years 2026 and
2027 and potential renegotiation, the need for simplification and specificity, and the need to
follow the statute more closely as concerns warranting this policy change. One commenter
suggested restricting renegotiation eligibility to selected drugs with a new indication, a change in
safety, or a patent expiration.
Response: CMS appreciates the perspective offered by these commenters and acknowledges that
it is possible under the statute that a selected drug with an agreed-upon MFP could be
renegotiated relatively shortly after the conclusion of a prior negotiation. However, as discussed
in section 130.1 of the draft guidance for initial price applicability year 2028 and this final
guidance, CMS interprets section 1194(f)(1) of the Act to mean that the Secretary must provide
for a process of renegotiation for years during the selected drug’s price applicability period.
Because calendar year 2028 will be a year within the price applicability period for drugs selected
for initial price applicability years 2026 and 2027, such selected drugs may be eligible for
renegotiation in calendar year 2026 (i.e., for initial price applicability year 2028) and may be
selected for renegotiation if certain criteria are met (as discussed in sections 130.1 and 130.2 of
this final guidance). Section 1194(f)(2) of the Act also establishes that the definition of a
“renegotiation-eligible drug” includes not only drugs with certain changes in monopoly status

139
but also selected drugs for which a new indication is added or for which the Secretary determines
there has been a material change to a section 1194(e) factor. Section 1194(f)(3) of the Act then
describes the circumstances under which CMS shall select a renegotiation-eligible drug for
renegotiation. The statute does not provide for exceptions or delay in selection for renegotiation
for any specific category of renegotiation-eligible drugs.
Comment: One commenter urged CMS to work with Congress to remove new indications as a
trigger for renegotiation eligibility. A couple of commenters expressed concern that using new
indications as a trigger for renegotiation eligibility might disincentivize post-approval label
expansion, particularly for rare and ultra-rare diseases.
Response: CMS will continue to implement the Negotiation Program, including renegotiation, in
accordance with current law.
Comment: One commenter stated that the requirement for a new indication to be for a new
disease or condition outlined in draft guidance for initial price applicability year 2028 departs
from the statutory definition of new indication in section 1192(e)(3)(A) of the Act and from the
FDA definition of new indication.
Response: As discussed in section 60.3.1 of this final guidance, for purposes of the Negotiation
Program, CMS distinguishes between use of the word “indication” and “FDA-approved
indication.” As specified in sections 60.3.1 and 130.1.3 of this final guidance, CMS will consider
an “indication” to be the condition or disease state that the selected drug treats. “FDA-approved
indication” refers to the information included in drug labeling per 21 C.F.R. § 201.57(c)(2) or
other applicable FDA regulation(s). CMS also notes that the statutory text at section
1192(e)(3)(A) of the Act related to the Orphan Drug Exclusion does not define a “new
indication.” Additionally, the language at section 1192(f)(2)(A) of the Act, where the statute
directs CMS to consider a selected drug “for which a new indication is added” to be
renegotiation-eligible, does not use the same language of “approved indications” as is used in
section 1192(e)(3)(A) of the Act nor does it reference section 526 of the FD&C Act.
Comment: A couple of commenters stated that the draft guidance for initial price applicability
year 2028 did not sufficiently define what constitutes a material change to a section 1194(e)
factor and expressed concern that this could lead to confusion and/or inconsistent application of
CMS’ approach. A few commenters requested additional clarity around the process that CMS
will use to assess a material change to a section 1194(e) factor, including the suggestion to
publish examples or specific circumstances to illustrate CMS’ approach.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their feedback. CMS simplified the description of
the criteria for what constitutes a material change(s) to a section 1194(e) factor in this final
guidance to provide additional clarity. Table 11 of this final guidance provides examples to
illustrate CMS’ approach.
Comment: One commenter asked that assessments of caregiver burden and family financial
impact be considered when assessing material change. One commenter recommended that the

140
entry of a new biosimilar or generic that could be considered a therapeutic alternative to a
selected drug be considered as a potential material change.
Response: CMS thanks the commenter for their suggestion to assess caregiver and family
financial burden when considering a material change. In alignment with section 60.3.3.1 of this
final guidance, CMS may consider the caregiver perspective to the extent that it reflects directly
upon the experience or relevant outcomes of the patient taking the selected drug for purposes of
evaluating the factors under section 1194(e)(2). CMS also confirms that the entry of a new
biosimilar or generic that could be considered a therapeutic alternative to a selected drug could
be considered a material change as it would reflect a change in a section 1194(e)(2) factor. In
both cases, the change would have to meet the criteria to be considered “material” as outlined in
section 130.1.2 of this final guidance.
Comment: A couple of commenters stated that Part B utilization for a selected drug that has an
agreed-upon MFP based upon Part D information (i.e., a selected drug negotiated for initial price
applicability year 2026 or 2027) does not constitute a material change to a section 1194(e) factor
and should not trigger renegotiation eligibility.
Response: CMS provided edits to language in section 130.1 of this final guidance to clarify that
the existence of Part B utilization for a selected drug that was negotiated in initial price
applicability year 2026 or 2027 does not automatically result in a selected drug becoming
renegotiation eligible. Rather, for example, CMS notes that Part B utilization could impact the
section 1194(e) factors (e.g., the factor under section 1194(e)(1)(E) of the Act (“market data and
revenue and sales volume data from the drug in the United States”)) and may be renegotiationeligible as a material change to a section 1194(e) factor under section 1194(f)(2)(D) of the Act.
To the extent that CMS determines that there has been a material change in a section 1194(e)
factor after considering the Part B utilization, the drug would be deemed renegotiation-eligible.
Selection of Drugs for Renegotiation for Initial Price Applicability Year 2028 (Section
130.2)
Comment: A few commenters supported CMS’ holistic approach to the selection of
renegotiation-eligible drugs. One commenter expressed support for the general parameters
outlined in draft guidance for initial price applicability year 2028 for the renegotiation process.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their support.
Comment: Many commenters asked that CMS provide additional clarity on the rationale for the
15 percent renegotiation selection criterion concerning the likelihood that a new indication or
material change would result in a renegotiated MFP that represents a 15 percent or greater
change relative to the current MFP as well as more information on what factors CMS would
consider during the holistic evaluation and additional detail on how CMS would consider various
factors, including section 1194(e) factors, during its holistic evaluation. In addition to reviewing
the impact on the Medicare program and beneficiaries, a few commenters recommended that
CMS consider the impact on value to patients when assessing the potential for a significant
change to the MFP. A couple of commenters alleged that the criterion concerning the likelihood

141
that the new indication or material change would result in a renegotiated MFP that represents a
15 percent or greater change relative to the current MFP is a “threshold”, for which there is no
statutory authority or basis, including one based on the change in the non-FAMP ceiling.
Response: CMS thanks commenters for their input. As described in section 130.2.1 of this final
guidance, CMS developed the criteria related to a significant change to the MFP to serve to
support CMS in making a selection determination in alignment with the requirements set forth in
section 1194(f)(3)(C) of the Act for drugs eligible for renegotiation because a new indication is
added or for which the Secretary determines there has been a material change to a section
1194(e) factor. While statute does not explicitly require any specific criterion to select these
drugs for renegotiation in section 1194(f)(3)(C) of the Act, CMS set forth these criteria to
provide transparency for the benefit of interested parties and the public into how the agency
would approach determining what constitutes a significant change to the MFP. As described in
section 130.2.1 of this final guidance, CMS’ review of the two criteria – (1) the likelihood that
the new indication or material change would result in a renegotiated MFP that represents a 15
percent or greater change relative to the current MFP and (2) whether such a change in the MFP
would have a significant impact on the Medicare program – will be a holistic inquiry based on
the totality of the information available and the circumstances of the renegotiation-eligible drug,
including nonfinancial information, such as the expiration of an exclusivity period under the
FD&C Act or the PHS Act. The scope of information considered may include a CMS-led review
of the information sources discussed in section 50 of this final guidance pertaining to section
1194(e)(1) and section 1194(e)(2) factors. CMS notes that no criteria to select drugs for
renegotiation can predict the actual outcome of a renegotiation. A determination by CMS that
renegotiation is likely to result in a significant change in MFP does not restrict the possibilities
for the outcome of renegotiation. Any given renegotiation, informed by data on section 1194(e)
factors available during the renegotiation period, could result in an increase in the MFP, decrease
in the MFP, or no change in the MFP. Further, the magnitude of the change in the MFP could be
higher or lower than 15 percent.
Comment: One commenter supported the criterion regarding assessing the likelihood of a 15
percent or greater change to the current MFP to define what constitutes a significant change in
the MFP. One commenter suggested that CMS revise the approach such that a renegotiationeligible drug must only fulfill one of the two criteria in section 130.2 of the draft guidance for
initial price applicability year 2028 rather than requiring the renegotiation-eligible drug to meet
both criteria in order to be selected for renegotiation. One commenter requested that CMS make
clear that the criteria could reflect potential increases or decreases in the MFP. One commenter
asked CMS to clarify how the agency would analyze a material change that would significantly
impact the Medicare program but the anticipated percent change to the MFP is less than 15
percent.
Response: CMS appreciates these commenters’ feedback. Regarding the suggestion to require a
selected drug with an agreed-upon MFP to meet one of the two criteria describe in this final
guidance for “likely to result in a significant change to the MFP” rather than both criteria, CMS
believes these criteria are complementary and important to consider holistically. There may be
circumstances for a selected drug that is likely to result in a 15 percent or greater change to the
MFP if renegotiated, but that change would have minimal impact on the Medicare program or

142
Medicare beneficiaries (for example, if CMS expects robust generic competition may occur, as
described in section 130.2.1 of this final guidance). In such a case, it may not be prudent to select
such a drug for renegotiation given the resources invested in the negotiation process by both
Primary Manufacturers and CMS. A holistic approach of both criteria is important to consider the
circumstances for each selected drug.
Additionally, to clarify, and as described in section 130.2.1 of this final guidance, in assessing the
likelihood of a 15 percent or greater change to the current MFP, CMS will consider either a
potential increase or decrease to the MFP. The criterion reflects the magnitude of the change that
CMS considers to be significant, not whether that change is an increase or a decrease to the MFP.
Additionally, as discussed in section 130.2.1 of this final guidance, a determination by CMS that
renegotiation is likely to result in a significant change in MFP does not restrict the possibilities
for the outcome of renegotiation. Any given renegotiation, informed by data on section 1194(e)
factors available during the renegotiation period, could result in an increase in MFP, decrease in
MFP, or no change in MFP. Further, the magnitude of the change in MFP could be higher or
lower than 15 percent. Similarly, CMS does not presume that the result of a renegotiation will
reflect these approximations, for example, with respect to the impact of a renegotiated MFP on
the Medicare program. These criteria only serve to support CMS in making a selection
determination in alignment with the requirements set forth in section 1194(f)(3)(C) of the Act.
Comment: Some commenters asked that CMS change the renegotiation selection criterion
concerning the likelihood that renegotiation of a renegotiation-eligible drug due to a new
indication or material change could result in a renegotiated MFP that represents a 15 percent or
greater change relative to the current MFP by instead evaluating the likelihood that renegotiation
could result in at least a 35 percent change to the current MFP. Among these commenters, some
stated that a 35 percent change to the current MFP would be more appropriate because when a
drug moves from short-monopoly to long-monopoly status, there is a 35 percent change applied
to the non-FAMP ceiling.
Response: CMS appreciates commenters’ feedback. CMS considered the option of evaluating
the likelihood that a new indication or material change would result in a 35 percent or greater
change to the MFP. The agency balanced considerations about the resources invested in
renegotiation in determining what constitutes a significant change, and maintains that a 15
percent change is more appropriate than a 35 percent change. As discussed in section 130.2 of
this final guidance, CMS also recognizes that there may be other circumstances related to the
renegotiation-eligible drug that may make selecting the drug for renegotiation less reasonable,
for example the impending entry of a generic or biosimilar to market. As such, CMS added the
complementary criterion of evaluating whether renegotiation would likely have a significant
impact to the Medicare program. As such, CMS declines to revise the criterion.
Data Collection to Inform Renegotiation Drug Eligibility, Selection, and Renegotiation of
the MFP for Initial Price Applicability Year 2028 (Section 130.3)
Comment: Many commenters provided feedback on the manufacturer data submission
processes. Some commenters requested CMS streamline the data submission requirements to
reduce manufacturer burden and provide predictability in the requirements by permitting a

143
manufacturer to update its original ICR submission or to attest that no material or significant
change(s) had occurred in the data of its original ICR submission. Other commenters requested
CMS provide additional flexibility with data submissions, including making the post-selection
data submission optional, accepting data during the renegotiation process, and accepting
information on factors that were not available during the initial negotiation. A couple of other
commenters expressed concerns that the pre-selection data submission is voluntary and
suggested the data submission prior to selection be mandatory so that it would not be biased to
the manufacturer. A few other commenters thanked CMS for making the pre-selection data
submission optional to reduce manufacturer burden.
Response: CMS thanks commenters for their feedback. First, regarding the submission of
information prior to identification of renegotiation-eligible drugs and selection, as specified in
section 130.3.1 of this final guidance, section 1194(f) of the Act does not require CMS to collect
data from Primary Manufacturers to determine if a new indication has been added to the selected
drug or if there has been a material change in any of the section 1194(e) factors. However, CMS
believes that it may be helpful to permit a voluntary submission of new information regarding
the addition of a new indication to the selected drug or new information regarding the section
1194(e) factors, that was not included in the original submission of data from the Primary
Manufacturer, prior to the CMS determination of renegotiation eligibility and selection from
Primary Manufacturers of selected drugs that do not have a change to long-monopoly status.
CMS is aware of the burden an information collection request poses to manufacturers and CMS
has endeavored to provide limited questions to capture critical information a Primary
Manufacturer may choose to share to inform eligibility and selection of a selected drug due to the
addition of a new indication or material change in a section 1194(e) factor.
Additionally, in response to other commenters’ concern that Primary Manufacturers may selfselect the information to be shared in a voluntary submission, CMS directs interested parties to
sections 130.1.3, 130.1.4, and 130.2.1 of this final guidance for the discussion of evidence CMS
will review for identification of and selection of drugs due to a new indication or material change
in a section 1194(e) factor, separate from the voluntary submission of manufacturers. Also, when
submitting a response to the Drug Selection ICR, the Primary Manufacturer must follow the
instructions provided by CMS and must certify that the information provided is accurate.
Second, regarding the mandatory submission of data from Primary Manufacturers of drugs
selected for renegotiation, while post-selection submission of section 1194(e)(1) data is required
of Primary Manufacturers, CMS has also endeavored to streamline the data required in this step.
In keeping with section 1194(f)(4)(B) of the Act to establish a renegotiation process that is
consistent with the negotiation process to “the extent practicable,” as provided in the 60-day
revisions to the Drug Price Negotiation ICR, Primary Manufacturers will use a system, process,
and questions already familiar to them to submit limited, new information for renegotiation. The
data requested covers time periods separate from the original submission of 1194(e) data. With
respect to commenters’ request to accept data during the renegotiation process, Primary
Manufacturers have the flexibility to share additional section 1194(e) information with CMS
during the negotiation meeting process by following the instructions described in section 60.4.4
of this final guidance.

144
Finally, for both submissions, neither a supplementation to the original 1194(e) submission from
the Primary Manufacturer or an attestation of no additional information from the Primary
Manufacturer is sufficient for CMS’ determination of renegotiation eligibility or selection and to
determine an initial offer or, if any, counteroffers. As stated above, CMS has provided a narrow
set of questions to capture new information that is distinct from the original submission,
however, to reduce burden.
Comment: Some commenters requested clarification of the data submission timeline. A couple
of commenters requested additional time to submit manufacturer data.
Response: CMS thanks commenters for their questions. For the voluntary submission of data
from the Primary Manufacturer, as specified in section 130.3.1 of this final guidance, CMS will
provide the date and time by which the information must be submitted to CMS upon approval
from the Office of Management and Budget of the Drug Selection ICR. For the mandatory
submission of data from Primary Manufacturers and the voluntary submission of section
1194(e)(2) data from any interested party, submissions must be provided by March 1, 2026, as
specified in sections 50, 50.2, and 130.3.2 of this final guidance.
The statutory deadline for the Negotiation Program to publish the selected drug list does not
provide enough time to extend the submission window for the voluntary submission of
manufacturer data beyond what is anticipated to be at least a 30-day window similar to the period
of time that has been generally provided in past initial price applicability periods for the small
biotech exception and a request for a biosimilar delay. The submission of data post-selection is
specified in the statute for Primary Manufacturers (sections 1193(a)(4)(B) and 1194(b)(2)(A) of
the Act) and CMS’ intention to require public submission on the same date as manufacturer
submission (i.e., March 1, 2026) serves to enable CMS to consider all submitted evidence in
totality and meet the statutory deadline for the initial offer, pursuant to general program
administration authority. For operational feasibility and for consistency, to the extent practicable,
CMS is adopting for initial price applicability year 2028, the same deadlines for post-selection
data submission to enable the timeline to be identical between renegotiation and negotiation.
Comment: A couple of commenters suggested CMS permit other interested parties to submit
evidence prior to selection of renegotiation-eligible drugs.
Response: CMS thanks commenters for their feedback. As discussed in section 130.3.1 of this
final guidance, CMS is not obligated to collect information from external parties prior to
identification and selection of drugs for renegotiation due to the addition of a new indication or
material change in a section 1194(e) factor. CMS believes that the information that the public
may provide that is critical to identification and selection of such drugs will already be identified
by CMS in the evidence CMS will review, through the reviews specified in sections 130.1.3,
130.1.4, and 130.2.1 of this final guidance. However, CMS recognizes the importance of
ongoing feedback from other interested parties in the renegotiation process and is providing an
opportunity for public feedback on the section 1194(e)(2) factors post-selection for renegotiation,
which is consistent with section 1194(f)(4)(B) of the Act.

145
Comment: A couple of commenters expressed concern that it may be difficult to predict which
drugs would be selected for negotiation. Specifically, one commenter asked how the public
would be aware that renegotiation may be triggered for a selected drug and invited to submit
information about selected drugs. Another commenter stated that this would make preparing for
potential selection challenging for a manufacturer.
Response: CMS thanks commenters for their feedback. CMS has provided a few examples of
scenarios and the potential result in determination of material change in section 130.1.4 of this
final guidance to also aid Primary Manufacturers prior to submission of the voluntary collection
of information prior to identification of renegotiation-eligible drugs and their selection. In
addition, as specified in sections 30.4 and 130.2.2 of this final guidance, CMS will publish the
list of drugs selected for renegotiation for initial price applicability year 2028 prior to the
deadline for the submission of the section 1194(e)(2) information from interested parties (see
additional details on the submission by interested parties for renegotiation in section 130.3.2 of
this final guidance).
Comment: One commenter suggested that a notice and comment process should be used for
consideration of new evidence and that CMS must use an evidence-based approach.
Response: Section 11001(c) and 11002(c) of the IRA direct CMS to implement the Negotiation
Program provisions in sections 11001 and 11002 of the IRA, including amendments made by
such sections, for 2026, 2027, and 2028 through program instruction or another form of program
guidance. When required by law, CMS will develop its policies for 2029 and all future years of
the Negotiation Program through notice-and-comment rulemaking. CMS appreciates the input
received from commenters on this methodology through the voluntary solicitation of comments
in the guidance process.
CMS directs interested parties to sections 130.1.3, 130.1.4, and 130.2.1 of this final guidance for
the discussion of evidence CMS will review for identification of and selection of renegotiationeligible drugs due to a new indication or a material change in a section 1194(e) factor.
Renegotiation Process (Section 130.4)
Comment: A few commenters requested that CMS provide public input opportunities for
renegotiations, such as through public data submissions, public comment periods before
establishing a renegotiated MFP, and public engagement events. A couple of commenters
requested CMS provide additional details regarding how public engagement will be implemented
in the renegotiation process. Another commenter recommended CMS hold additional roundtable
events for drugs selected for renegotiation.
Response: CMS recognizes the importance of ongoing feedback from other interested parties,
including patients, in the renegotiation process. As stated above, CMS is providing an
opportunity for public feedback on the section 1194(e)(2) factors for drugs selected for
renegotiation, consistent with section 1194(f)(4)(B) of the statute. Additionally, CMS directs
commenters to sections 60.4.1 and 130.4.3 of this final guidance, which provide specific steps
for engagement with interested parties prior to the issuance of initial offers. CMS may

146
incorporate drugs selected for renegotiation into the public engagement events for drugs selected
for negotiation or host separate events specifically for drugs selected for renegotiation, as
described in section 130.4.3 of this final guidance.
Comment: One commenter encouraged CMS to publish an MFP explanation for drugs selected
for renegotiation. One commenter recommended CMS provide the public with a summary of the
outcomes of renegotiation. The same commenter recommended CMS provide advance notice
and a justification for the renegotiated MFP. A few commenters asked that CMS detail specific
information to be included in the MFP explanation, such as details on the reason a drug was
selected for renegotiation and how patient-focused considerations were used in renegotiations.
Response: CMS thanks these commenters for their feedback. As described in section 130.4.5 of
this final guidance, CMS will release an MFP explanation for each selected drug with a
renegotiated MFP following the completion of the renegotiation process in accordance with
section 60.6.1 of this final guidance and in accordance with the confidentiality policy described
in sections 40.2.1 and 50.2 of this final guidance. As stated in response to comments above, CMS
notes that renegotiation will occur at the same cadence (per section 1194(f) of the Act that is
annually beginning for initial price applicability year 2028) and on the same timeline (i.e.,
adhering to the same statutory deadlines provided in section 1194(b) of the Act) as negotiation.
As such, a renegotiated MFP will be publicly available no later than November 30 two years
prior to the relevant initial price applicability year when the MFP becomes effective in
accordance with section 1195(a)(1) of the Act and as described in section 60.6 of this final
guidance.
CMS thanks commenters for their recommendation to include more detail regarding the reason
for selection and how patient-focused considerations were used in renegotiations in the MFP
explanations. CMS will further consider these suggestions as CMS develops the renegotiated
MFP explanations.
Comment Solicitation on the Procedures, Structure, and Timing of the Renegotiation Process
Comment: A couple of commenters expressed support for the renegotiation process conforming
to the procedures, structure, and timing of the negotiation process. One commenter asked CMS
to provide flexibility in circumstances where a manufacturer has a drug selected for negotiation
and renegotiation during the same initial price applicability year, such as by extending the
negotiation and renegotiation timeframe. Another commenter suggested aligning the
renegotiation process with the negotiation process is burdensome to manufacturers and other
stakeholders interested in submitting input on the selected drugs and asked CMS to consider
simplifying the renegotiation process where possible.
Response: CMS thanks commenters for their feedback. Due to the statutory timeline of the
negotiation period, including the requirement under section 1194(b)(2)(B) of the Act for CMS to
issue an initial offer by June 1, 2026, and the requirement under section 1194(b)(2)(E) of the Act
that negotiations must end prior to November 1, 2026, it is not feasible to extend the timeframe
for the negotiation period. CMS is abiding by the statutory deadlines for the negotiation period in
this final guidance. As described in section 130.4.3 of this final guidance, and in accordance with
section 1194(f)(4)(B) of the Act, CMS intends, to the extent practicable, for the renegotiation

147
process to conform to the procedures, structure, and timing established under section 1194(b) of
the Act, and in accordance with sections 1194(c), (d), and (e) of the Act as set forth in section
60.4 of this final guidance. Additionally, CMS has endeavored to streamline the renegotiation
process where possible. For example, as noted in response to comments above, for the data
submission process for renegotiations, as provided in the 60-day revisions to the Drug Price
Negotiation ICR, Primary Manufacturers will use a system, process, and questions already
familiar to them to submit limited, new information for renegotiation.
Appendix A
Comment Solicitation on Streamlining the Definitions
Comment: CMS received many comments in response to CMS’ solicitation for suggestions to
streamline the definitions included in Appendix A. Some of these commenters suggested CMS
refine the definitions by reducing the scope of the data collected to items critical to the
Negotiation Program, improving alignment of the data with collection of such information in the
pharmaceutical industry, and restructuring calculations to adhere to U.S. GAAP and SEC
requirements. To do so, some of these commenters suggested removing distinct definitions for
R&D costs (e.g., costs related to the selected drug, costs for failed and abandoned products
related to the selected drug) and permitting the Primary Manufacturer to attest to recoupment of
R&D costs and provide optional supplemental information. A few of these commenters
suggested the delineated terms were difficult for manufacturers to identify in their data and
questioned their relevance to the Negotiation Program. One commenter suggested streamlining
by permitting manufacturers to use reasonable assumptions to determine and submit statutorily
required information. Additionally, some of these commenters requested CMS revise and/or
remove definitions related to data collection of pricing data in the ICRs beyond the collection of
non-FAMP because, the commenters stated, the collection of such data is not required by the
statute and the requested data metrics are not consistent with industry-practices. Specifically, one
commenter disagreed with the aggregation of price concessions from supply chain entities across
the pharmaceutical supply chain in “Manufacturer Net Part D Price.” Another commenter
suggested additional guidance is needed if CMS retains CMS-specific pricing metrics (e.g.,
manufacturer net Medicare Part D average unit price, manufacturer U.S. commercial average net
unit price) because manufacturers needed to rely on assumptions to respond. Some commenters
also included overall feedback on the data submission and information collection process,
including the removal of character limitations on responses, the burden of submitting free
response field explanations, and the requirement to provide certain information on behalf of a
Secondary Manufacturer.
Response: CMS thanks commenters for their suggestions. CMS has included further revisions to
the definitions for R&D costs to clarify which costs should be included for Questions 1 and 2 of
the Drug Price Negotiation ICR. For example, CMS removed the word “indications” from the
terms defined for consistency with the revisions to the definitions of these terms included in the
draft guidance for initial price applicability year 2028, which expanded collection of R&D costs
to include costs for indications that have not been approved by the FDA. CMS does not intend
the language included in this final guidance to substantially change the definitions for the terms
as compared to the language included in the draft guidance. CMS declines to revise the
definitions for R&D costs beyond these changes because CMS believes the information included

148
in the definitions is consistent with the statutory intent to collect “research and development
costs of the manufacturer for the drug” as specified in section 1194(e)(1)(A) of the Act.
Consistent with CMS’ response on page 83 of the final guidance for initial price applicability
year 2027, CMS is not adopting the recommendation that Primary Manufacturers submit a
statement of reasonable assumptions for manufacturer-specific data submissions or otherwise use
reasonable assumptions, except where the use of assumptions is explicitly indicated in the Drug
Selection ICR and Drug Price Negotiation ICR. For example, in the ICR forms, CMS instructs
the Primary Manufacturer of the selected drug to explain the methodology used to calculate
certain costs reported to CMS (e.g., Question 4 related to unit production and distribution cost in
the Drug Selection ICR and Question 7 related to prior Federal financial support in the Drug
Price Negotiation ICR). CMS continues to provide specific terms and instructions to make clear
the information required for the Negotiation Program, and CMS believes Primary Manufacturers
have experience providing similar data and information to other federal and state entities. CMS
included technical corrections to the specific definitions that clarify the items that should or
should not be deducted from the price for: manufacturer U.S. commercial average net unit price,
manufacturer U.S. commercial average net unit price—net of patient assistance, manufacturer
net Medicare Part D average unit price, and manufacturer net Medicare Part D average unit
price—best. CMS declines to further revise the series of terms on manufacturer U.S. commercial
average net price and manufacturer net Medicare Part D price because CMS believes that the
Primary Manufacturer has access to the specific data required to calculate these data elements
included in the related ICRs, CMS provides terms and instructions to clarify which specific data
should be included in this set of metrics, and CMS believes this information is relevant to the
section 1194(e)(1)(E) of the Act “market data” factor for adjusting the preliminary price (see
section 60.3.4 of this final guidance).
Regarding the requirement to provide certain information on behalf of a Secondary
Manufacturer, CMS directs commenters to section 40 of this final guidance regarding the
definition of manufacturer and the requirements of manufacturers of selected drugs. Section
1194(e)(1) of the Act specifically refers to the list of section 1194(e)(1) factors as, “The
following data, with respect to such selected drug, as submitted by the manufacturer.” CMS
believes this indicates that the information for section 1194(e)(1) factors must come from the
manufacturer of the selected drug (which will be the Primary Manufacturer on behalf of the
Secondary Manufacturer, as applicable).
Additionally, CMS directs interested parties to responses provided in response to comments
received about data collection burden, instructions, and questions on the 60-day revisions to the
Drug Selection ICR (as included with the 30-day revisions published concurrently with this final
guidance) and the Drug Price Negotiation ICR (as included in the 30-day revisions, which CMS
expects to publish in late Fall 2025).
Comments About Specific Terms
Comment: A few commenters disagreed with CMS’ removal of acquisition costs from the
definition for R&D costs. These commenters argued that while CMS appears to believe that an
acquisition results in zero R&D costs, these commenters contend that the acquisition is part of

149
the actual costs for developing and marketing a product. One commenter supported the removal
of acquisition costs as an R&D cost to help streamline the data required of manufacturers.
Response: CMS thanks commenters for their feedback. CMS, however, disagrees with the
comments that opposed the removal of acquisition costs. CMS believes the information included
in the definitions is consistent with the statutory intent to collect “research and development
costs of the manufacturer for the drug” as specified in section 1194(e)(1)A) of the Act. As
included in Appendix A of the draft guidance for initial price applicability year 2028, CMS has
removed the separate question regarding acquisition costs because, among other impacts on the
data, CMS understands that acquisition costs are generally driven by the estimated net of the
present value that is assessed based on the future revenue expectations for a drug, and that
acquisition costs are not driven by R&D.
Comment: A few commenters raised concerns about the definitions related to prior Federal
financial support. Specifically, one commenter disagreed with including tax credits for orphan
drugs because the commenters say the tax credit is intended for drug development related to
treatment of rare diseases and reporting of this information may not be known to manufacturers
or at the specificity required. These commenters suggested limiting funding related only to a
patent application containing a Government Interest Statement and/or research where a patent
assignee was a U.S. government entity. Additionally, one commenter raised concerns about the
applicability of early-stage research federal funding because it may not indicate the purpose of
the funding, and the commenter also noted the documentation may not be available to the
manufacturer. Finally, another commenter stated that the definition was overly broad regarding
discovery and development for a selected drug.
Response: CMS thanks the commenters for their feedback. CMS declines to further revise the
series of terms on prior Federal financial support because the information collected is consistent
with section 1194(e)(1)(C) of the Act (and in line with the revisions CMS has incorporated to the
collection of R&D costs) and CMS provides terms and instructions to clarify which specific data
should be included in this set of data elements in the appliable ICRs.
Comment: One commenter raised concerns about the feasibility of manufacturers reporting
abandoned and failed products with the same mechanism of action because the commenter said
drug development investment is not structured at this product level.
Response: CMS thanks the commenter for the feedback. CMS has continued to incorporate
revisions to definitions and collection of information related to R&D costs in response to public
comment. Based on the collection of information from Primary Manufacturers in two cycles of
the Negotiation Program thus far, CMS believes the information included within the definition
for R&D costs for failed and abandoned products related to the selected drug is feasible for
Primary Manufacturers to submit to CMS. Further, CMS believes the term as defined in this final
guidance is consistent with section 1194(e)(1)(A) of the Act and is necessary for the Negotiation
Program, as discussed in further detail in sections 50.1 and 60.3 of this final guidance.
Comment: One commenter provided suggested revisions to the definitions for patents and
exclusivities. Specifically, the commenter suggested removing expired and non-public patents

150
and expired regulatory exclusivities, unless the Primary Manufacturer chooses to share this
information.
Response: CMS thanks the commenter for the feedback. CMS declines to further revise the
series of terms on patents and exclusivities because the information collected is consistent with
section 1194(e)(1)(D) of the Act and CMS provides terms and instructions to clarify which
specific data should be included in this set of data elements in the applicable ICRs.
Comment: One commenter requested CMS clarify the replacement of “related” to “relevant”
within the definitions for patents, exclusivities, and approvals.
Response: CMS included the revision in the draft guidance for initial price applicability year
2028 to align with the structure of questions about patents, exclusivities, and approvals in the
Drug Selection ICR and the Drug Price Negotiation ICR. However, CMS clarifies that the
revisions are not intended by CMS to substantively alter the definitions for patents, exclusivities,
and approvals.
Comment: Some commenters provided suggestions to revise the terms related to the section
1194(e)(2) factors.
Response: CMS directs interested parties to responses to these and similar comments in
comment summary and responses for section 60.3 of this final guidance.

D. Final Guidance on the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program
10. Introduction
Sections 11001 and 11002 of the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (IRA) (P.L. 117-169), signed
into law on August 16, 2022, establish the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program

153
(hereinafter the “Negotiation Program”) to negotiate maximum fair prices (MFPs) 57 for certain
high expenditure, single source drugs and biological products. The requirements for this program
are described in sections 1191 through 1198 of the Social Security Act (hereinafter “the Act”), as
added by sections 11001 and 11002 of the IRA.
56F

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) is committed to actively engaging with
interested parties to consider opportunities to bring greater transparency to the Negotiation
Program. Through the final guidance, CMS gathered input from a broad range of interested
parties regarding the implementation of the Negotiation Program for initial price applicability
year 2028 and manufacturer effectuation of the MFP in 2026, 2027, and 2028. Public feedback
on all aspects of the negotiation process and manufacturer effectuation of the MFP is critical to
achieving the goals of greater value for beneficiaries and taxpayers and continuing to foster
innovation. CMS is committed to learning from, collaborating with, and engaging the public,
including patients, consumer advocates, health and data experts, and pharmaceutical supply
chain entities in the policy-making process.
Sections 11001(c) and 11002(c) of the IRA direct the Secretary of the Department of Health and
Human Services (HHS) (hereinafter “the Secretary”) to implement the Negotiation Program
provisions in sections 11001 and 11002 of the IRA, including amendments made by such
sections, for 2026, 2027, and 2028 by program instruction or other forms of program guidance.
In accordance with the law, CMS is issuing this final guidance for implementation of the
Negotiation Program for initial price applicability year 2028, including for renegotiation, and for
manufacturer effectuation of the MFP in 2026, 2027, and 2028. To improve program
transparency, CMS also voluntarily solicited comments on the topics in the draft guidance,
except section 90.3. 58
57F

This final guidance is not subject to the notice-and-comment requirements of the Administrative
Procedure Act (APA) or the Medicare statute due to the requirement in sections 11001(c) and
11002(c) of the IRA to implement the Negotiation Program provisions in sections 11001 and
11002 of the IRA, including amendments made by such sections, for 2026, 2027, and 2028 by
program instruction or other forms of program guidance. The terms “program instruction” and
“program guidance” are terms of art that Congress routinely uses in Medicare statutes to refer to
agency pronouncements other than notice-and-comment rulemaking. The statutory directive in
sections 11001(c) and 11002(c) thus specifies that CMS shall follow policymaking procedures
In accordance with section 1191(c)(3) of the Social Security Act, MFP means, with respect to a year during a price
applicability period and with respect to a selected drug (as defined in section 1192(c) of the Act) with respect to such
period, the price negotiated pursuant to section 1194 of the Act, and updated pursuant to section 1195(b) of the Act,
as applicable, for such drug and year.
58
CMS did not solicit comments on section 90.3 of the draft guidance for initial price applicability year 2028
because the Department of the Treasury and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) issued regulations that govern the
administration of the excise tax (see Excise Tax on Designated Drugs; Procedural Requirements, 88 Fed. Reg.
67690, available at https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2023/10/02/2023-21586/excise-tax-on-designateddrugs-procedural-requirements and Notice 2023-53; see also, Notice 2023-52, Section 5000D Excise Tax on Sales
of Designated Drugs; Reporting and Payment of the Tax, available at https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/n-23-52.pdf.
Revenue Procedure 2025-9, available at https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/rp-25-09.pdf. Excise Tax on Designated
Drugs; Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, available at https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/01/02/202431462/excise-tax-on-designated-drugs).
57

154
that differ from the notice-and-comment procedures that would otherwise apply under the APA
or the Medicare statute. Congress underscored this directive by placing the Negotiation Program
in the newly enacted Part E of Title XI of the Act.
Moreover, although CMS has endeavored to solicit public comment and to respond to comments
to the extent feasible consistent with the statutory deadlines for implementation of the
Negotiation Program, to the extent this final guidance establishes or changes any substantive
legal standard, CMS finds that notice and public procedure on this final guidance would be
impracticable, unnecessary, and contrary to the public interest in light of the statutory
requirement to implement sections 11001 and 11002 of the IRA for 2026, 2027, and 2028 by
program instruction and in light of the complexity of the preparations that must be undertaken in
advance of the publication by February 1, 2026 of the selected drug list for initial price
applicability year 2028 and to establish the mechanisms necessary for manufacturers to provide
access to any MFP agreed upon for drugs selected for initial price applicability year 2026
starting on January 1, 2026. In particular, manufacturers need to take a number of actions well in
advance of February 1, 2026, to prepare for the possibility that a drug they manufacture might be
included on the selected drug list for initial price applicability year 2028. For example,
manufacturers may need to engage in internal discussions regarding whether the manufacturer
would choose to participate in the Negotiation Program if its drug is included among the selected
drug list published not later than February 1, 2026, review the template Medicare Drug Price
Negotiation Program Agreement and guidance to understand Negotiation Program requirements
for participating manufacturers in advance of the statutory deadline for entering agreements of
February 28, 2026, and gather information for potential submission to CMS by the statutory
deadline of March 1, 2026. In addition, for the reasons explained below, interested
manufacturers will need to submit a request for a Small Biotech Exception under section
1192(d)(2) of the Act or a request for a Biosimilar Delay under section 1192(f) of the Act in
advance of selection for initial price applicability year 2028 and by the date to be specified by
CMS. Similarly, both CMS and manufacturers must prepare for and take various actions on an
accelerated timeline to ensure manufacturers are able to effectuate any agreed-upon MFPs
starting on January 1, 2026 for drugs selected for initial price applicability year 2026.
CMS could not have proceeded through notice-and-comment rulemaking and still provided
interested parties with guidance sufficiently far in advance of these statutory deadlines to allow
them adequate time to complete these complex preparations. For the same reasons, CMS also
concludes that there is good cause to issue this guidance as final without a delayed effective date,
in order to meet the statutory deadlines of the Negotiation Program and consistent with the
authority provided to CMS in sections 11001(c) and 11002(c) of the IRA. See 5 U.S.C. §
553(b)(B) & (d)(3); see also section 1871(b)(2)(C) of the Act.
This final guidance describes how CMS will implement the Negotiation Program for initial price
applicability year 2028 (January 1, 2028 to December 31, 2028), including the renegotiation
process for MFPs 59 (whether negotiated or renegotiated) to take effect January 1, 2028. This
final guidance also sets forth additional policies regarding manufacturer effectuation of the MFP
in 2026, 2027, and 2028, and specifies the requirements that will be applicable to manufacturers
of drugs that are selected for negotiation or renegotiation. Additionally, this final guidance
58F

59

To the extent applicable, any references in this final guidance to the “MFP” includes a renegotiated MFP.

155
includes information on the successor regulation exception to the IRA’s formulary inclusion
requirement for 2027 and 2028. Finally, this final guidance describes the procedures that may be
applicable to drug manufacturers, Medicare Part D plan sponsors (both Prescription Drug Plans
(PDPs) and Medicare Advantage Prescription Drug (MA-PD) Plans), pharmacies, mail order
services, and other dispensing entities that dispense drugs covered under Medicare Part D, in
addition to hospitals, physicians, and other providers of services and suppliers that furnish or
administer drugs to individuals enrolled under Medicare Part B (including individuals enrolled in
Medicare Advantage plans under Part C). In this final guidance, CMS has made changes to
certain policies in response to comments received, based on the agency’s further consideration of
the relevant issues, or if necessary to incorporate any enacted legislation impacting
administration and operations of the Negotiation Program.
If any provision in this final guidance is held to be invalid or unenforceable, CMS intends that it
shall be severable from the remainder of the final guidance, and shall not affect the remainder
thereof, or the application of the provision to other persons or circumstances. CMS has
determined that all relevant provisions of the final guidance could function independently from
one another.

20. Overview
This final guidance describes how CMS will implement the Negotiation Program for initial price
applicability year 2028, building on policies established in final guidance for initial price
applicability year 2027 and applying the experience of CMS from the first two cycles of
negotiations. As required by law, this final guidance includes policy to incorporate drugs payable
under Part B into the Negotiation Program and implements requirements for renegotiation. This
final guidance also describes refinements to MFP effectuation policies for 2026 and 2027,
including adjustments to Medicare Transaction Facilitator (MTF) operations, and the extension
of such policies to 2028. Furthermore, this final guidance establishes the successor regulation
exception to the IRA’s formulary inclusion requirement for 2027 and 2028.
The MFP effectuation policies established for 2026 and 2027 in final guidance for initial price
applicability year 2027 and manufacturer effectuation of the MFP in 2026 and 2027 are final
policies that remain in effect for 2026 and 2027. In this final guidance, CMS makes updates and
includes supplemental information regarding these policies for 2026 and 2027, and is extending
these same policies to 2028 for drugs covered under Part D. For ease of reference, CMS is
restating the MFP effectuation sections from final guidance for initial price applicability year
2027 and manufacturer effectuation of the MFP in 2026 and 2027 in this final guidance so that
the changes and updates to those policies can more easily be read in context with the policies in
the prior final guidance that CMS is modifying or supplementing.
In accordance with sections 11001 and 11002 of the IRA, which created Part E under Title XI of
the Act (sections 1191 through 1198), the Secretary is required to establish the Negotiation
Program to negotiate MFPs for certain high expenditure, single source drugs covered by
Medicare and to renegotiate the MFP for certain selected drugs. With respect to each initial price
applicability year, CMS shall: (1) publish a list of selected drugs in accordance with section 1192
of the Act; (2) enter into agreements with manufacturers of selected drugs in accordance with
section 1193 of the Act; (3) negotiate MFPs for such selected drugs, in accordance with section
1194 of the Act; (4) publish MFPs for selected drugs in accordance with section 1195 of the Act;
(5) carry out administrative duties, including auditing and compliance monitoring in accordance
with section 1196 of the Act; and (6) impose civil monetary penalties (CMPs) in accordance with
section 1197 of the Act. With respect to initial price applicability year 2028 and subsequent
years, CMS shall also: (1) determine renegotiation-eligible drugs; (2) select drugs for
renegotiation; and (3) renegotiate the MFP for any drug selected for renegotiation. To the extent
applicable, any references in this final guidance to the “MFP” includes a renegotiated MFP.
Section 1198 of the Act establishes certain limitations on administrative and judicial review
relevant to the Negotiation Program.

160

To allow for public input, CMS voluntarily solicited comments on all sections of the draft
guidance, except for section 90.3 (which refers to the Department of the Treasury regulations
that govern the administration of the excise tax 60).
59F

Topics that are not relevant to Negotiation Program implementation for initial price applicability
year 2028 or for MFP effectuation in 2026, 2027, and 2028 are not addressed in this guidance.
The IRA requires implementation of the Negotiation Program for 2026, 2027, and 2028 by
program instruction or other forms of program guidance. CMS intends to engage in rulemaking
to address program policies related to implementation for initial price applicability year 2029 and
subsequent years.

30. Identification of Selected Drugs for Initial Price Applicability Year 2028
Section 1192 of the Act establishes the requirements governing the identification of qualifying
single source drugs, the identification of negotiation-eligible drugs, the ranking of negotiationeligible drugs and identification of selected drugs, and the publication of the list of selected drugs
for an initial price applicability year. First, CMS will identify qualifying single source drugs in
accordance with section 1192(e) of the Act, as described in section 30.1 of this final guidance.
CMS will exclude certain drugs in accordance with section 1192(e)(3) of the Act.
Next, in accordance with section 1192(d)(1)(A) of the Act, CMS will use Total Expenditures 61
under Part D of Title XVIII of the Act for these qualifying single source drugs, calculated using
Part D prescription drug event (PDE) data for dates of service between November 1, 2024 and
October 31, 2025, and other information described below, to identify Part D high spend drugs. In
accordance with section 1192(d)(1)(B) of the Act, CMS will use Total Expenditures 62 under Part
B of Title XVIII of the Act for these qualifying single source drugs, calculated using Medicare
Fee-for-Service (FFS) Part B claims data and Medicare Advantage (MA) encounter data for Part
B items or services (hereinafter collectively referred to as “Part B data”) for the dates of service
between November 1, 2024 and October 31, 2025, and other information described below, to
identify Part B high spend drugs. In these steps, CMS will also exclude certain qualifying single
source drugs in accordance with sections 1192(d)(2) and (3) of the Act.

CMS will calculate Total Expenditures under Part B of Title XVIII of the Act using a

coinsurance and Medicare payment) and a comparable amount calculated using MA encounter
data for Part B items and services, which will reflect the amount that would have been applicable
under FFS. To do so, CMS will first adjust the unit field in MA encounter data for Part B items
and services by referencing the Medically Unlikely Edits (MUEs), which are designed to reduce
improper payments. 65 Because Medicare Administrative Contractors apply these edits to FFS
Part B claims, this will bring the MA encounter data for Part B items and services into closer
alignment. CMS will then multiply the adjusted units by the appropriate published payment limit
(e.g., Average Sales Price (ASP) 66-based) or payment rate (e.g., Outpatient Prospective Payment
System (OPPS), Ambulatory Surgical Center (ASC)) to calculate what would have been
applicable for the Part B items and services under Medicare FFS.

30.1 Identification of Qualifying Single Source Drugs for Initial Price Applicability Year
2028
For initial price applicability year 2028, in accordance with section 1192(e)(1) of the Act, CMS
will define a qualifying single source drug as a covered Part D drug (as defined in section
1860D-2(e) of the Act) (hereinafter “a drug covered under Part D”) or a drug or biological
product for which payment may be made under Part B of Title XVIII of the Act (hereinafter “a
drug payable under Part B”) that meets the following criteria:
• For drug products, a qualifying single source drug is a drug: (1) that is approved under
section 505(c) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (“FD&C Act”) and marketed
pursuant to such approval; (2) for which, as of the selected drug publication date with
respect to a given initial price applicability year, at least 7 years have elapsed since the
date of such approval; 71 and (3) that is not the listed drug for any drug approved and
marketed under an Abbreviated New Drug Application (ANDA) under section 505(j) of
the FD&C Act.
• For biological products, a qualifying single source drug is a biological product: (1) that is
licensed under section 351(a) of the Public Health Service Act (“PHS Act”) and marketed
pursuant to such licensure; (2) for which, as of the selected drug publication date with
respect to a given initial price applicability year, at least 11 years have elapsed since the
date of such licensure; 72 and (3) that is not the reference product for any biological
product that is licensed and marketed under section 351(k) of the PHS Act.

section 351 of the PHS Act, effective March 23, 2020, pursuant to section 7002(e)(4)(A) of
Biologics Price Competition and Innovation Act of 2009 (“BPCI Act”) that are currently licensed
and marketed as biological products under section 351 of the PHS Act (hereinafter “deemed
biologics”), CMS will consider March 23, 2020 to be the licensure date for purposes of
identifying the time since licensure under section 1192(e)(1)(B)(ii) of the Act. 73 This

and CMS treated the earliest New Drug Application (NDA) 74 approval date associated with such

1192(e)(1) of the Act.

such NDA(s); or (3) multi-market approval (MMA) 77 products imported under section
801(d)(1)(B) of the FD&C Act that are marketed pursuant to such NDA(s); 78

This approach to identifying a potential qualifying single source drug aligns with the requirement
in section 1192(d)(3)(B) of the Act to use data aggregated across dosage forms and strengths of
the drug, including new formulations of the drug. Consistent with this statutory instruction, this
approach is also appropriate because CMS is aware that existing NDA / BLA holders have
obtained approval for new dosage forms or different routes of administration of the same active
moiety / active ingredient under different NDAs or BLAs.
Section 1192(e)(2)(A) of the Act states that an authorized generic drug and the qualifying single
source drug that is the listed drug or reference product of that authorized generic drug shall be
treated as the same qualifying single source drug. An authorized generic drug is defined in
section 1192(e)(2)(B) of the Act as: (1) in the case of a drug product, an authorized generic drug
(as such term is defined in section 505(t)(3) of the FD&C Act); and (2) in the case of a biological
product, a product that has been licensed under section 351(a) of the PHS Act 81 and is marketed,
sold, or distributed directly or indirectly to the retail class of trade under a different labeling,
packaging (other than repackaging as the reference product in blister packs, unit doses, or similar
packaging for institutions), product code, labeler code, trade name, or trademark than the
reference product.
80F

If a drug is a fixed combination drug 82 with two or more active moieties / active ingredients, the
distinct combination of active moieties / active ingredients will be considered as one active
moiety / active ingredient for the purpose of identifying potential qualifying single source drugs.
Therefore, all formulations of this distinct combination offered by the same NDA / BLA holder
will be aggregated across all dosage forms and strengths of the fixed combination drug. A
product containing only one (but not all) of the active moieties / active ingredients that is offered
by the same NDA / BLA holder will not be aggregated with the formulations of the fixed
combination drug and will be considered a separate potential qualifying single source drug. For
example, a corticosteroid inhaler would not be aggregated with a fixed combination inhaler from
the same NDA / BLA holder that contains the same corticosteroid combined with a long-acting
beta agonist. In this example, the corticosteroid inhaler would be considered as a separate
potential qualifying single source drug from the fixed combination inhaler.
81F

CMS believes that treating distinct combinations of active moieties / active ingredients as one
active moiety / active ingredient for the purpose of identifying potential qualifying single source
drugs is generally appropriate. However, CMS acknowledges that there may exist fixed
combination drugs for which one of the active ingredients or active moieties contained is not
biologically active against the disease state(s) the drug is indicated for. Accordingly, the current
fixed combination drug policy could create a gaming opportunity in which a Primary
Manufacturer may attempt to avoid the aggregation of its products, thereby decreasing the
likelihood of or avoiding their selection for negotiation, thus undermining the integrity of the
Negotiation Program. An example might include the addition of active moiety / active ingredient
X to a different active moiety / active ingredient Y, where active moiety / active ingredient X

Applying statutory criteria for qualifying single source drugs:
In accordance with section 1192(e)(1) of the Act, to be considered a qualifying single source
drug, at least 7 years (for drug products) or 11 years (for biological products) must have elapsed
between the FDA date of approval or licensure of the potential qualifying single source drug, as
applicable, and the selected drug publication date. 83 To determine the date of approval for a
potential qualifying single source drug that is a drug product with more than one FDA
application number, CMS will use the earliest date of approval of the initial FDA application
number assigned to the NDA holder for the active moiety (or in the case of fixed combination
drugs, for the distinct combination of active moieties). To determine the date of licensure for a
potential qualifying single source drug that is a biological product (subject to the clarification
described below regarding vaccines for infectious disease(s)) with more than one FDA
application number, CMS will use the earliest date of licensure of the initial FDA application
number assigned to the BLA holder for the active ingredient (or in the case of fixed combination
drugs, for the distinct combination of active ingredients). The selected drug publication date for
initial price applicability year 2028 is February 1, 2026, as specified in section 1191(b)(3) of the
Act. As such, for initial price applicability year 2028, the initial approval for a drug product to be
considered a qualifying single source drug must have been on or before February 1, 2019, and
the date of initial licensure for a biological product to be considered a qualifying single source
drug must have been on or before February 1, 2015.
82F

For example, if 12 years had elapsed between the original approval for NDA-1 cited in the
previous example above and February 1, 2026, then the potential qualifying single source drug
defined above would meet this statutory criterion for qualifying single source drugs (even if less
than seven years had elapsed between the approval dates for NDA-2 or NDA-3 and February 1,
2026), consistent with the statutory directive in section 1192(d)(3)(B) of the Act to aggregate
data across dosage forms and strengths of the drug, including new formulations of the drug.
CMS is aware that some manufacturers of vaccines for infectious disease(s) update the antigen
component(s) of their products through supplemental BLAs. For each unique potential qualifying
single source drug that CMS identifies based on its antigen component(s), CMS clarifies that it
will use the earliest date of licensure for any BLA or supplemental BLA for that unique potential
qualifying single source drug for purposes of determining time eligibility.

In accordance with sections 1192(c) and (e) of the Act, for the purpose of identifying qualifying
single source drugs for initial price applicability year 2028, CMS will review PDE data for the
12-month period beginning January 16, 2025 and ending January 15, 2026, as well as Average
Manufacturer Price (AMP) 88 data for the 12-month period beginning December 1, 2024 and
ending November 30, 2025, for a given generic drug or biosimilar for which a potential
qualifying single source drug is the listed drug or reference product. CMS has chosen these time
periods to enable CMS to use the most recent possible data to make this determination while still
allowing for sufficient time for such data to inform the selected drug list published no later than
February 1, 2026, in accordance with section 1192(a) of the Act. CMS believes that review of
additional data sources beyond PDE and AMP data may be merited for assessing utilization, in
particular for drugs payable under Part B. Therefore, CMS will additionally review, when
available, the ASP data available to CMS for the sales quarters of the fourth quarter of 2024
through the third quarter of 2025 (e.g., the 12-month period beginning October 1, 2024 and
ending September 30, 2025) for drugs payable under Part B. CMS may review additional data
sources for utilization for drugs payable under Part B and/or covered under Part D for the most
recent 12-month period for the applicable data source, when available to CMS. The additional
data sources CMS may also review, are Medicaid State Drug Utilization Data (SDUD) and/or
data from nationally representative and commercially available databases.

purchase through the pharmaceutical supply chain and whether any licenses or other agreements

As an example, if a potential qualifying single source drug has at least one approved generic
drug or licensed biosimilar that has high and consistent PDE utilization, AMP sales, and/or ASP
sales, CMS will consider the generic(s) or biosimilar(s) of the potential qualifying single source
drug bona fide marketed. As another example, a potential qualifying single source drug might
have a newly or recently approved generic or licensed biosimilar and the product has relatively
low PDE utilization, AMP sales, and/or ASP sales. In this example, if CMS finds in additional
review of public information that the generic or biosimilar manufacturer has successfully
launched their product, and there is no evidence of agreements limiting distribution of the
generic or biosimilar product, then CMS will consider the generic or biosimilar product of the
potential qualifying single source drug as bona fide marketed. As a third example, a potential
qualifying single source drug might have an approved generic or licensed biosimilar product
with no PDE utilization, AMP sales, and/or ASP sales. In this example, if CMS finds in
additional review of public information that there are ongoing patent disputes and no generic or
biosimilar manufacturer has successfully launched their product, then CMS will consider the
generic or biosimilar product of the potential qualifying single source drug as not bona fide
marketed. While the circumstances illustrated in these examples weigh in favor of, or against, a
determination regarding bona fide marketing, CMS' ultimate determination on any particular
drug will be based on the totality of the circumstances and not on the presence, or absence, of
any single factor.
If any strength or dosage form of a potential qualifying single source drug is the listed drug or
reference product, as applicable, for one or more generic or biosimilar products that CMS
determines are approved or licensed, as applicable, and bona fide marketed based on the process
described in this final guidance, the potential qualifying single source drug will not be
considered a qualifying single source drug for initial price applicability year 2028. If CMS
determines that the potential qualifying single source drug will not be considered a qualifying
single source drug for initial price applicability year 2028 because a manufacturer of such
generic drug or biosimilar product has engaged in bona fide marketing of the generic drug or
biosimilar, CMS will monitor to ensure continued bona fide marketing of the generic drug or
biosimilar based on the approach described in section 90.4 of this final guidance.
